Unit 4: Stress Transformation, Pressure Vessels and Energy Methods - Question Bank Solved

Mechanics of Solids (UE25ME241A)

Level 1: Remember (Q001 to Q020)Level 2: Understand (Q021 to Q040)Level 3: Apply (Q041 to Q060)Level 4: Analyze (Q061 to Q080)Level 5: Evaluate (Q081 to Q100)Level 6: Create (Q101 to Q120)Assignment problems (Unit 4 assignment, 20 questions)

This page solves the Unit 4 question bank (Transformation of Stresses, Pressure Vessels and Energy Methods): 120 questions in six Bloom's levels of 20 each (Q001 to Q120), then the 20 assignment questions and the 20 Q&A model answers (which repeat 20 question-bank IDs and are cross-checked here). Topic codes in the bank: T1 transformation of plane stress, T2 principal stresses and maximum shear, T3 Mohr's circle, P1 thin-walled vessels, P2 thick-walled cylinders, E1 strain energy (normal stress), E2 strain energy (shear and torsion). Types: T theory, D derivation, N numerical, P design or problem.

Conventions of the bank (printed on its page 2). Tension positive; θ\theta positive counter-clockwise; τxy\tau_{xy} positive when it acts upward on the right (+x+x) face (the Beer and Johnston convention used in class). Use E=200E=200 GPa, G=80G=80 GPa and ν=0.3\nu=0.3 for steel unless stated. Stresses are in MPa (N/mm2^2). "Mean radius" is used only where stated; otherwise the inner radius or diameter is meant. Answers are given at the Bloom's level asked, in the exam format: theory answers as definition, principle, formula, explanation, diagram, conclusion; numerical answers as given, to find, assumptions and sign convention, formula, steps, boxed answer. Every numerical was checked by computation.

Level 1: Remember (Q001 to Q020)

Cognitive focus: recall of definitions, formulae, conventions and facts. All 20 are short theory questions (2 or 3 marks), so the answers are short and exact.

U4-Q001Q001 | L1 Remember | T1 | T | 2 marks

Define plane stress. List the stress components that are non-zero in a state of plane stress in the xyxy-plane.

Solution

Definition. A body is in plane stress in the xyxy-plane when only the xx and yy faces of an element carry stress and all stresses act parallel to the xx and yy axes; the stresses on the zz faces are zero (σz=τxz=τyz=0\sigma_z=\tau_{xz}=\tau_{yz}=0).

Non-zero components: σx\sigma_x, σy\sigma_y and τxy\tau_{xy} (with τyx=τxy\tau_{yx}=\tau_{xy}).

Examples. Thin plates loaded in their plane, the free surface of any loaded body, and the surface of shafts, beams and thin pressure vessels.

U4-Q002Q002 | L1 Remember | T1 | T | 2 marks

State the sign convention for normal stress, shear stress and the rotation angle θ\theta used in the stress-transformation equations.

Solution
  • Normal stress σ\sigma: tension is positive, compression negative; the subscript names the face on which it acts.
  • Shear stress τxy\tau_{xy}: the first subscript is the face (normal to xx), the second is the direction (yy). It is positive when it acts on a positive face in the positive direction of an axis, or on a negative face in the negative direction. Moment equilibrium gives τxy=τyx\tau_{xy}=\tau_{yx}. (The bank states the same rule as "positive when it acts upward on the right (+x+x) face".)
  • Angle θ\theta: positive when measured counter-clockwise from the xx axis to the x′x' axis; clockwise rotation is negative.

Note. Mohr's circle plots clockwise-turning shear upward, so the sign of τxy\tau_{xy} is reversed when the point XX is plotted. This agrees with the Q&A model answer (Q1).

U4-Q003Q003 | L1 Remember | T1 | T | 3 marks

Write the transformation equations for σx′\sigma_{x'}, σy′\sigma_{y'} and τx′y′\tau_{x'y'} in terms of 2θ2\theta for a plane-stress element.

Solution

For an element with σx,σy,τxy\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\tau_{xy} rotated counter-clockwise by θ\theta:

σx′\sigma_{x'}​=σx+σy2+σx−σy2cos⁡2θ+τxysin⁡2θ=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}+\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\cos2\theta+\tau_{xy}\sin2\theta

τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−σx−σy2sin⁡2θ+τxycos⁡2θ=-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\sin2\theta+\tau_{xy}\cos2\theta

σy′\sigma_{y'}​=σx+σy2−σx−σy2cos⁡2θ−τxysin⁡2θ=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\cos2\theta-\tau_{xy}\sin2\theta

σy′\sigma_{y'} follows from σx′\sigma_{x'} by putting θ+90∘\theta+90^{\circ} for θ\theta. They satisfy the invariant σx′+σy′=σx+σy\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'}=\sigma_x+\sigma_y and give τy′x′=τx′y′\tau_{y'x'}=\tau_{x'y'}.

U4-Q004Q004 | L1 Remember | T2 | T | 2 marks

Define principal stresses and principal planes.

Solution

The maximum and minimum normal stresses at a point are the principal stresses σ1\sigma_1 (algebraically larger) and σ2\sigma_2 (smaller). The planes on which they act are the principal planes; their normals are the principal axes. The two principal planes are mutually perpendicular and the shear stress on them is zero.

U4-Q005Q005 | L1 Remember | T2 | T | 2 marks

Write the expression that gives the orientation of the principal planes (tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p) in terms of σx\sigma_x, σy\sigma_y, τxy\tau_{xy}.

Solution

tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2τxyσx−σy=\dfrac{2\tau_{xy}}{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}

It has two roots for 2θp2\theta_p differing by 180∘180^{\circ}, so there are two values of θp\theta_p differing by 90∘90^{\circ}: the principal planes are perpendicular. (Agrees with Q&A model answer Q2.) It comes from setting dσx′/dθ=0d\sigma_{x'}/d\theta=0.

U4-Q006Q006 | L1 Remember | T2 | T | 2 marks

Write the expressions for the in-plane principal stresses σ1\sigma_1 and σ2\sigma_2.

Solution

σ1,2\sigma_{1,2}​=σx+σy2±(σx−σy2)2+τxy2=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}\pm\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^{2}+\tau_{xy}^{2}}

σ1\sigma_1 takes the plus sign and σ2\sigma_2 the minus sign; σ1+σ2=σx+σy\sigma_1+\sigma_2=\sigma_x+\sigma_y.

U4-Q007Q007 | L1 Remember | T2 | T | 2 marks

What is the value of shear stress on a principal plane? By what other name are principal planes known?

Solution

The shear stress on a principal plane is zero. (Substituting θp\theta_p in τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−σx−σy2sin⁡2θ+τxycos⁡2θ=-\frac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\sin2\theta+\tau_{xy}\cos2\theta with sin⁡2θp=τxy/R\sin2\theta_p=\tau_{xy}/R and cos⁡2θp=(σx−σy)/2R\cos2\theta_p=\frac{(\sigma_x-\sigma_y)/2}{R} gives 00.)

Principal planes are therefore also called shear-free planes (planes of zero shear stress); their normals are the principal axes.

U4-Q008Q008 | L1 Remember | T2 | T | 3 marks

Write the expressions for the maximum in-plane shear stress and for the normal stress acting on the planes of maximum shear.

Solution

τmax\tau_{max}​=(σx−σy2)2+τxy2=\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^{2}+\tau_{xy}^{2}}​=σ1−σ22=\dfrac{\sigma_1-\sigma_2}{2}

σ′\sigma'​=σavg=\sigma_{avg}​=σx+σy2=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}​=σ1+σ22=\dfrac{\sigma_1+\sigma_2}{2}

The planes of maximum shear are at θs=θp±45∘\theta_s=\theta_p\pm45^{\circ}, with tan⁡2θs\tan2\theta_s​=−σx−σy2τxy=-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2\tau_{xy}}.

U4-Q009Q009 | L1 Remember | T3 | T | 2 marks

State the coordinates of the centre and the radius of Mohr's circle for a plane-stress state (σx,σy,τxy\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\tau_{xy}).

Solution

Centre C=(σx+σy2, 0)C=\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2},\,0\right), radius RR​=(σx−σy2)2+τxy2=\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^{2}+\tau_{xy}^{2}}

The points X=(σx,−τxy)X=(\sigma_x,-\tau_{xy}) and Y=(σy,+τxy)Y=(\sigma_y,+\tau_{xy}) lie on the circle and XYXY is a diameter (clockwise shear is plotted upward).

U4-Q010Q010 | L1 Remember | T3 | T | 2 marks

State the relationship between the angle θ\theta measured on the element and the corresponding angle on Mohr's circle.

Solution

The angle on Mohr's circle is twice the angle on the element: a rotation of the element by θ\theta corresponds to a rotation of the diameter by 2θ2\theta, in the same sense (counter-clockwise on the element is counter-clockwise on the circle). Planes 90∘90^{\circ} apart on the element are 180∘180^{\circ} apart on the circle (the ends XX and YY of a diameter). The doubling occurs because stress is a second-order quantity (it varies as cos⁡2θ\cos2\theta and sin⁡2θ\sin2\theta).

U4-Q011Q011 | L1 Remember | P1 | T | 2 marks

Define a thin-walled pressure vessel and state the thickness-to-radius criterion used to classify it.

Solution

A pressure vessel is thin-walled when its wall thickness is small compared with its radius: t≤r/10t\le r/10 (equivalently r/t≥10r/t\ge10). Then the hoop stress is taken as uniform through the thickness and the radial stress is negligible, so the shell is in biaxial plane stress. A vessel with t>r/10t>r/10 is thick-walled and needs Lamé's theory. (Agrees with Q&A model answer Q3. The class slides use t<d/20t<d/20 for the thick-wall criterion, which is the same limit.)

U4-Q012Q012 | L1 Remember | P1 | T | 2 marks

Write the formulae for hoop stress and longitudinal stress in a thin cylindrical shell under internal pressure pp.

Solution

Hoop stress: σh=pD2t=prt\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t}=\dfrac{pr}{t}. Longitudinal stress: σL=pD4t=pr2t\sigma_L=\dfrac{pD}{4t}=\dfrac{pr}{2t}.

DD is the internal diameter, rr the internal radius and tt the wall thickness. So σh=2σL\sigma_h=2\sigma_L. (The Q&A model answer Q4 awards one mark for each formula; its formulas did not extract from the PDF text, but these are the notes' B.1 and B.2.)

U4-Q013Q013 | L1 Remember | P1 | T | 2 marks

Write the formula for the normal stress in a thin spherical shell of diameter DD and thickness tt under internal pressure pp.

Solution

σ=pD4t=pr2t\sigma=\dfrac{pD}{4t}=\dfrac{pr}{2t}

The stress is the same in every direction in the tangent plane (σ1=σ2=σ\sigma_1=\sigma_2=\sigma); it is half the hoop stress of a cylinder of the same diameter and thickness.

U4-Q014Q014 | L1 Remember | P2 | T | 3 marks

List the assumptions made in Lamé's theory of thick cylinders.

Solution
  1. The material is homogeneous and isotropic and obeys Hooke's law (stresses within the proportional limit).
  2. Plane sections of the cylinder normal to its axis remain plane and normal under pressure (the cylinder is long).
  3. The longitudinal stress and longitudinal strain are constant throughout the wall thickness; hence the sum of hoop and radial stress, σθ+σr\sigma_\theta+\sigma_r, is constant at every point of the wall (=2A=2A).
  4. The pressures act uniformly (axisymmetric loading), so the radial and hoop stresses depend only on the radius; shear stresses vanish.
  5. Deformation is small.
U4-Q015Q015 | L1 Remember | P2 | T | 3 marks

State Lamé's equations for the radial stress σr\sigma_r and hoop stress σθ\sigma_\theta at radius rr in a thick cylinder.

Solution

σr=A−Br2\sigma_r=A-\dfrac{B}{r^{2}}, σθ=A+Br2\qquad\sigma_\theta=A+\dfrac{B}{r^{2}} (tension positive)

AA and BB are constants fixed by the boundary conditions σr=−pi\sigma_r=-p_i at r=rir=r_i and σr=−po\sigma_r=-p_o at r=ror=r_o:

A=piri2−poro2ro2−ri2,B=(pi−po) ri2ro2ro2−ri2.A=\frac{p_ir_i^2-p_or_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2},\qquad B=\frac{(p_i-p_o)\,r_i^2r_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}.

(Class-slide form with the radial pressure pr=−σrp_r=-\sigma_r: pr=br2−ap_r=\dfrac{b}{r^2}-a and σc=br2+a\sigma_c=\dfrac{b}{r^2}+a.)

U4-Q016Q016 | L1 Remember | E1 | T | 2 marks

Define strain energy and state its SI unit.

Solution

Strain energy UU of a member is the increase in energy associated with its deformation; it equals the work done by a slowly (statically) applied load: U=∫0x1P dxU=\int_0^{x_1}P\,dx, the area under the load-deformation diagram.

SI unit: joule (J), where 1 J = 1 N m.

U4-Q017Q017 | L1 Remember | E1 | T | 3 marks

Define strain-energy density, modulus of resilience and modulus of toughness.

Solution
  • Strain-energy density u=dUdVu=\dfrac{dU}{dV}: strain energy per unit volume at a point; it equals the area under the stress-strain diagram, u=∫σ dεu=\int\sigma\,d\varepsilon. In the elastic range u=σ22Eu=\dfrac{\sigma^2}{2E}. Unit: J/m3^3.
  • Modulus of resilience uY=σY22Eu_Y=\dfrac{\sigma_Y^2}{2E}: strain-energy density at the yield point, the energy per unit volume the material can absorb without permanent deformation (the area under the straight-line part).
  • Modulus of toughness: strain-energy density up to fracture, the total area under the σ\sigma-ε\varepsilon curve: the energy per unit volume the material can absorb before breaking.
U4-Q018Q018 | L1 Remember | E1 | T | 2 marks

Write the expression for the elastic strain energy of a prismatic bar (length LL, area AA, modulus EE) carrying an axial load PP.

Solution

U=P2L2AEU=\dfrac{P^{2}L}{2AE}

(From U=∫P22AEdxU=\int\dfrac{P^2}{2AE}dx with constant PP, AA; equivalently U=12PδU=\tfrac12P\delta with δ=PL/AE\delta=PL/AE.)

U4-Q019Q019 | L1 Remember | E2 | T | 2 marks

Write the expression for the strain energy stored in a prismatic circular shaft (length LL, polar moment JJ, modulus GG) subjected to torque TT.

Solution

U=T2L2GJU=\dfrac{T^{2}L}{2GJ}

(From U=∫T22GJdxU=\int\dfrac{T^2}{2GJ}dx with constant TT and JJ; equivalently U=12TφU=\tfrac12T\varphi with φ=TL/GJ\varphi=TL/GJ.)

U4-Q020Q020 | L1 Remember | E1 | T | 2 marks

Write the expression for the elastic strain energy stored in a beam due to the bending moment M(x)M(x) (normal stresses only).

Solution

UU​=∫0LM2(x)2EI dx=\displaystyle\int_0^{L}\frac{M^{2}(x)}{2EI}\,dx

(From σx=My/I\sigma_x=My/I, u=σx2/2Eu=\sigma_x^2/2E and ∫y2dA=I\int y^2dA=I. For a cantilever with tip load PP it gives U=P2L3/6EIU=P^2L^3/6EI.)

Level 2: Understand (Q021 to Q040)

Cognitive focus: explaining ideas, interpreting concepts and stating reasons. All 20 are theory questions, so each answer gives the definition, the principle, the formula, the reasoning, a diagram where it helps, and a short conclusion.

U4-Q021Q021 | L2 Understand | T1 | T | 4 marks

Explain why shear stress exists on inclined planes of a bar in uniaxial tension, and state the plane on which it is maximum and its value.

Solution

Definition. Uniaxial tension: a bar carries only σx=σ=P/A\sigma_x=\sigma=P/A on its cross-section; σy=τxy=0\sigma_y=\tau_{xy}=0.

Principle. Take a cut whose normal makes angle θ\theta with the bar axis. The cut area is A/cos⁡θA/\cos\theta. The internal force PP is the same, but it is not perpendicular to the cut. Resolve PP into a part normal to the cut and a part along (tangent to) the cut. The tangent part is a shear force, so shear stress exists on the cut.

Formula. From the transformation equations with σy=τxy=0\sigma_y=\tau_{xy}=0:

σθ\sigma_\theta​=σcos⁡2θ=\sigma\cos^2\theta​=σ2(1+cos⁡2θ)=\dfrac{\sigma}{2}(1+\cos2\theta), ∣τθ∣=σ2sin⁡2θ\quad|\tau_\theta|=\dfrac{\sigma}{2}\sin2\theta

Explanation. Normal force on the cut: Pcos⁡θP\cos\theta. Shear force along the cut: Psin⁡θP\sin\theta. Dividing by the cut area A/cos⁡θA/\cos\theta gives σcos⁡2θ\sigma\cos^2\theta and σsin⁡θcos⁡θ=σ2sin⁡2θ\sigma\sin\theta\cos\theta=\tfrac{\sigma}{2}\sin2\theta. On the cross-section (θ=0\theta=0) and on the longitudinal plane (θ=90∘\theta=90^{\circ}) the shear is zero, and it is non-zero on every plane between.

Maximum. τθ\tau_\theta is largest when sin⁡2θ=1\sin2\theta=1, i.e. θ=45∘\theta=45^{\circ}:

τmax=σ2=P2A\tau_{max}=\dfrac{\sigma}{2}=\dfrac{P}{2A} on the 45∘45^{\circ} planes, where also σθ=σ2\sigma_\theta=\dfrac{\sigma}{2}.

Conclusion. Shear appears because the force is not perpendicular to an inclined cut. It is maximum, equal to half the axial stress, on planes at 45∘45^{\circ} to the axis. This is why ductile steel yields by slip along 45∘45^{\circ} lines in a tension test.

U4-Q022Q022 | L2 Understand | T1 | T | 3 marks

Explain the invariance of σx+σy\sigma_x+\sigma_y under rotation of axes and how it is used to check numerical answers.

Solution

Definition. The sum of the normal stresses on two perpendicular planes is the same for every orientation of the element. It is called a stress invariant.

Principle. Add the transformation equations for σx′\sigma_{x'} and σy′\sigma_{y'}. The terms in cos⁡2θ\cos2\theta and sin⁡2θ\sin2\theta have opposite signs and cancel:

σx′+σy′\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'}​=σx+σy=\sigma_x+\sigma_y​=σ1+σ2=\sigma_1+\sigma_2​=2 σavg=2\,\sigma_{avg}

Explanation. On Mohr's circle XX and YY are the ends of a diameter, so their mid-point C=(σx+σy)/2C=(\sigma_x+\sigma_y)/2 is fixed whatever the rotation. Hence the two normal stresses always add to 2C2C.

Use as a check. 1. After finding σx′\sigma_{x'} at a given θ\theta, also find σy′\sigma_{y'} (use θ+90∘\theta+90^{\circ}). 2. Check σx′+σy′=σx+σy\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'}=\sigma_x+\sigma_y. The same test applies to σ1+σ2\sigma_1+\sigma_2. 3. If the sum differs, an arithmetic or sign error has been made.

Limit. The check covers only the normal stresses. The shear value is checked separately, for example τx′y′2+(σx′−σavg)2\tau_{x'y'}^2+\left(\sigma_{x'}-\sigma_{avg}\right)^2​=R2=R^2.

Conclusion. The sum of the two normal stresses is constant, equal to twice the centre of Mohr's circle; it is a quick check on any transformed or principal stress.

U4-Q023Q023 | L2 Understand | T2 | T | 4 marks

Explain why principal planes are mutually perpendicular and why the shear stress vanishes on them.

Solution

Definition. Principal planes are the planes on which the normal stress is a maximum or minimum. The normal stresses on them are the principal stresses.

Principle. The normal stress σx′(θ)\sigma_{x'}(\theta) is a smooth function of θ\theta; its extreme values occur where dσx′/dθ=0d\sigma_{x'}/d\theta=0.

Derivation.

dσx′dθ\dfrac{d\sigma_{x'}}{d\theta}​=−(σx−σy)sin⁡2θ+2τxycos⁡2θ=-(\sigma_x-\sigma_y)\sin2\theta+2\tau_{xy}\cos2\theta​=2 τx′y′=2\,\tau_{x'y'}

The slope of σx′\sigma_{x'} is 2τx′y′2\tau_{x'y'}. So the normal stress is stationary exactly where the shear is zero:

tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2τxyσx−σy=\dfrac{2\tau_{xy}}{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}, τx′y′=0\quad\tau_{x'y'}=0 on these planes.

Why perpendicular. The tangent repeats every 180∘180^{\circ} in 2θ2\theta, so there are two roots 2θp2\theta_p and 2θp+180∘2\theta_p+180^{\circ}, that is θp\theta_p and θp+90∘\theta_p+90^{\circ}. One gives the maximum σ1\sigma_1 and the other the minimum σ2\sigma_2. On Mohr's circle the points AA and BB are at the ends of the horizontal diameter, 180∘180^{\circ} apart on the circle, which is 90∘90^{\circ} apart on the element.

Why shear vanishes. AA and BB lie on the σ\sigma axis, where τ=0\tau=0. Physically, if a shear existed on a principal plane, a component of it would change σ\sigma in a neighbouring plane, so σ\sigma could not be extreme there.

Conclusion. Principal planes are at 90∘90^{\circ} to each other and carry zero shear, because the condition for extreme normal stress, dσx′/dθ=0d\sigma_{x'}/d\theta=0, is the same as τx′y′=0\tau_{x'y'}=0.

U4-Q024Q024 | L2 Understand | T2 | T | 4 marks

Distinguish between the maximum in-plane shear stress and the absolute maximum shear stress in a plane-stress state, with an example.

Solution

Definition. - Maximum in-plane shear stress: the largest shear on planes that contain the zz axis (rotation about zz only): τin=R=σ1−σ22\tau_{in}=R=\dfrac{\sigma_1-\sigma_2}{2}. - Absolute maximum shear stress: the largest shear on any plane in three dimensions: τabs\tau_{abs}​=12(σmax−σmin)=\tfrac12(\sigma_{max}-\sigma_{min}) taken over three principal stresses {σ1,σ2,σ3=0}\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3=0\} (since σz=0\sigma_z=0 in plane stress).

Principle. Three Mohr's circles exist in 3D, one for each pair of principal stresses. The largest circle gives the absolute maximum. The in-plane value comes from the circle through σ1\sigma_1 and σ2\sigma_2 only.

Explanation. The two are equal only when σ1\sigma_1 and σ2\sigma_2 have opposite signs (so that zero lies between them). If both principal stresses have the same sign, the circle through σ\sigma and 00 is larger and the absolute maximum is larger than the in-plane maximum.

Case In-plane τ\tau Absolute τ\tau
σ1>0>σ2\sigma_1>0>\sigma_2(σ1−σ2)/2(\sigma_1-\sigma_2)/2same
σ1>σ2>0\sigma_1>\sigma_2>0(σ1−σ2)/2(\sigma_1-\sigma_2)/2σ1/2\sigma_1/2 (larger)

Example. A thin cylinder, σh=100\sigma_h=100 MPa, σL=50\sigma_L=50 MPa, both tension, σz=0\sigma_z=0 on the free surface. - In-plane: (100−50)/2=25(100-50)/2=25 MPa. - Absolute: (100−0)/2=50(100-0)/2=50 MPa, on planes at 45∘45^{\circ} to the radial and hoop directions. (This agrees with τabs\tau_{abs}​=pD/4t=pD/4t​=σh/2=\sigma_h/2 in the formula sheet.)

Conclusion. Always include the zero principal stress when finding the true maximum shear; the in-plane value alone can under-estimate it by a factor of two for same-sign principal stresses.

U4-Q025Q025 | L2 Understand | T2 | T | 3 marks

Explain why the planes of maximum shear stress are inclined at 45∘45^{\circ} to the principal planes.

Solution

Definition. The planes of maximum in-plane shear are the planes on which τx′y′\tau_{x'y'} is largest.

Principle. Shear is extreme where dτx′y′/dθ=0d\tau_{x'y'}/d\theta=0.

Derivation.

dτx′y′dθ\dfrac{d\tau_{x'y'}}{d\theta}​=−(σx−σy)cos⁡2θ−2τxysin⁡2θ=-(\sigma_x-\sigma_y)\cos2\theta-2\tau_{xy}\sin2\theta​=0  =0\;​⇒  tan⁡2θs\Rightarrow\;\tan2\theta_s​=−σx−σy2τxy=-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2\tau_{xy}}

tan⁡2θs\tan2\theta_s​=−1tan⁡2θp  =-\dfrac{1}{\tan2\theta_p}\;​⇒  2θs\Rightarrow\;2\theta_s​=2θp±90∘  =2\theta_p\pm90^{\circ}\;​⇒  θs\Rightarrow\;\theta_s​=θp±45∘=\theta_p\pm45^{\circ}

Explanation on Mohr's circle. The principal points A,BA,B are on the σ\sigma axis. The points of largest ∣τ∣|\tau| are the top and bottom of the circle, DD and EE, which are 90∘90^{\circ} away from AA on the circle. Because angles on the circle are double those on the element, the planes are 45∘45^{\circ} apart.

Conclusion. The two tangent expressions are negative reciprocals, so the doubled angles differ by 90∘90^{\circ}, and the planes of maximum shear are at 45∘45^{\circ} to the principal planes. On them the normal stress is σavg=(σx+σy)/2\sigma_{avg}=(\sigma_x+\sigma_y)/2. (Matches Q&A model answer 5.)

U4-Q026Q026 | L2 Understand | T3 | T | 5 marks

Explain how the equation of Mohr's circle is obtained from the stress-transformation equations.

Solution

Definition. Mohr's circle is the graph of (σx′,τx′y′)\left(\sigma_{x'},\tau_{x'y'}\right) for all values of θ\theta; it is a circle.

Principle. The transformation equations are the parametric equations of a circle with parameter 2θ2\theta. Eliminating 2θ2\theta gives the circle's equation.

Derivation. Write σavg=σx+σy2\sigma_{avg}=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2} and a=σx−σy2a=\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}.

  1. σx′−σavg\sigma_{x'}-\sigma_{avg}​=acos⁡2θ+τxysin⁡2θ=a\cos2\theta+\tau_{xy}\sin2\theta
  2. τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−asin⁡2θ+τxycos⁡2θ=-a\sin2\theta+\tau_{xy}\cos2\theta
  3. Square both and add: the cross terms cancel because sin⁡2θcos⁡2θ\sin2\theta\cos2\theta appears with opposite signs.
  4. (σx′−σavg)2+τx′y′2(\sigma_{x'}-\sigma_{avg})^2+\tau_{x'y'}^2​=(a2+τxy2)(cos⁡22θ+sin⁡22θ)=(a^2+\tau_{xy}^2)(\cos^22\theta+\sin^22\theta)​=a2+τxy2=a^2+\tau_{xy}^2

(σx′−σavg)2+τx′y′2(\sigma_{x'}-\sigma_{avg})^2+\tau_{x'y'}^2​=R2=R^2, R R​=(σx−σy2)2+τxy2=\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^2+\tau_{xy}^2}

Explanation. This is the equation of a circle with centre (σavg,0)(\sigma_{avg},0) on the σ\sigma axis and radius RR. Every point of the circle corresponds to one plane through the element; the σ\sigma coordinate is the normal stress and the τ\tau coordinate the shear on that plane.

Key points read from it. The σ\sigma axis intercepts are σavg±R=σ1,2\sigma_{avg}\pm R=\sigma_{1,2}. The top and bottom points give ±R=τmax\pm R=\tau_{max}.

Conclusion. Squaring and adding the two transformation equations removes 2θ2\theta and gives a circle of centre σavg\sigma_{avg} and radius RR, which is Mohr's circle.

U4-Q027Q027 | L2 Understand | T3 | T | 4 marks

Explain why angles are doubled on Mohr's circle and how the stresses on an arbitrary inclined plane are read from the circle.

Solution

Definition. On Mohr's circle an angle θ\theta on the element appears as 2θ2\theta at the centre of the circle, in the same sense (counter-clockwise on the element is counter-clockwise on the circle for the standard plot).

Why doubled. The transformation equations contain cos⁡2θ\cos2\theta and sin⁡2θ\sin2\theta, not cos⁡θ\cos\theta and sin⁡θ\sin\theta. So when θ\theta increases by Δθ\Delta\theta the point on the circle moves through 2Δθ2\Delta\theta. The two faces of an element at 90∘90^{\circ} (xx and yy) become points 180∘180^{\circ} apart, the two ends XX and YY of a diameter. Faces on the same plane (opposite sides) must give the same stresses, so θ\theta and θ+180∘\theta+180^{\circ} coincide, which fits a circle which repeats after 2θ=360∘2\theta=360^{\circ}.

Procedure. 1. Plot X=(σx,−τxy)X=(\sigma_x,-\tau_{xy}) and Y=(σy,+τxy)Y=(\sigma_y,+\tau_{xy}) (clockwise shear upward). 2. Join them: the diameter XYXY cuts the σ\sigma axis at the centre C=(σx+σy)/2C=(\sigma_x+\sigma_y)/2. 3. Draw the circle through XX and YY. 4. To find the plane turned counter-clockwise by θ\theta: rotate the diameter XYXY counter-clockwise by 2θ2\theta about CC to X′Y′X'Y'. 5. Read X′X': σx′\sigma_{x'} and the shear τx′y′\tau_{x'y'} (with the same sign rule as the plot); Y′Y' gives σy′\sigma_{y'}.

Check: CC is fixed, so σx′+σy′=2C\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'}=2C; radius stays RR.

Conclusion. The doubling comes from the 2θ2\theta in the transformation equations. Stresses on any plane are the coordinates of the point obtained by turning the reference diameter through 2θ2\theta in the same direction as the element.

U4-Q028Q028 | L2 Understand | T3 | T | 4 marks

Sketch and explain Mohr's circles for (a) uniaxial tension, (b) pure shear and (c) equal biaxial tension.

Solution

Definition. Mohr's circle: centre σavg=(σx+σy)/2\sigma_{avg}=(\sigma_x+\sigma_y)/2, radius RR​=(σx−σy2)2+τxy2=\sqrt{\left(\tfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^2+\tau_{xy}^2}.

(a) Uniaxial tension (σx=σ\sigma_x=\sigma, σy=τxy=0\sigma_y=\tau_{xy}=0). Centre σ/2\sigma/2, radius σ/2\sigma/2; the circle touches the origin. σ1=σ\sigma_1=\sigma, σ2=0\sigma_2=0; τmax=σ/2\tau_{max}=\sigma/2 at θ=45∘\theta=45^{\circ} where σ′=σ/2\sigma'=\sigma/2.

(b) Pure shear (σx=σy=0\sigma_x=\sigma_y=0, τxy=τ\tau_{xy}=\tau). Centre at the origin, radius τ\tau. σ1,2=±τ\sigma_{1,2}=\pm\tau on planes at 45∘45^{\circ} to the shear faces; τmax=τ\tau_{max}=\tau on the original faces. Pure shear is the same as equal tension and compression at 45∘45^{\circ}.

(c) Equal biaxial tension (σx=σy=σ\sigma_x=\sigma_y=\sigma, τxy=0\tau_{xy}=0). R=0R=0: the circle degenerates to a point at (σ,0)(\sigma,0). The normal stress is σ\sigma on every plane and the shear is zero on every plane. (In plane stress the absolute maximum shear is still σ/2\sigma/2 from the circle through σ\sigma and 00 in 3D.)

Conclusion. The three circles differ in centre and radius only: the circle for uniaxial tension touches the origin, that for pure shear is centred on it, and that for equal biaxial stress is a single point.

U4-Q029Q029 | L2 Understand | T2 | T | 4 marks

Explain, using principal stresses, why a chalk (brittle) specimen in torsion fails along a 45∘45^{\circ} helical surface while a ductile steel shaft fails by shearing across its section.

Solution

Definition. A shaft in torsion is in pure shear on the surface: σx=σy=0\sigma_x=\sigma_y=0, τxy=τ=Tc/J\tau_{xy}=\tau=Tc/J.

Principle. Principal stresses of pure shear: σ1,2=±R=±τ\sigma_{1,2}=\pm R=\pm\tau on planes at 45∘45^{\circ} to the shaft axis (Mohr's circle centred on the origin, radius τ\tau). The maximum shear τ\tau acts on the cross-section and on the longitudinal planes.

σ1=+τ\sigma_1=+\tau (tension), σ2=−τ\sigma_2=-\tau (compression) on 45∘45^{\circ} planes; τmax=τ\tau_{max}=\tau on the cross-section.

Explanation. - Chalk (brittle). Brittle material is much weaker in tension than in shear. The tensile principal stress σ1=τ\sigma_1=\tau reaches the tensile strength first. The crack opens perpendicular to σ1\sigma_1, that is on a surface at 45∘45^{\circ} to the axis. The result is a helical fracture surface. - Mild steel (ductile). Ductile material is weaker in shear than in tension; yielding is governed by the maximum shear stress. τmax\tau_{max} acts on the transverse cross-section, so the shaft slips and cuts across the section.

Everyday example. Twist a piece of chalk with both hands: it breaks along a spiral. Twist a thick wire repeatedly: it shears across.

Conclusion. Both specimens carry the same state of stress (pure shear); the failure plane differs because brittle materials fail by the maximum tensile stress (on 45∘45^{\circ} planes) and ductile materials fail by the maximum shear stress (on the cross-section).

U4-Q030Q030 | L2 Understand | P1 | T | 4 marks

Explain why the hoop stress in a thin cylinder is twice the longitudinal stress.

Solution

Definition. Thin cylinder: t≤r/10t\le r/10; internal pressure pp, internal diameter DD, length LL. Hoop (circumferential) stress σh\sigma_h acts around the wall; longitudinal stress σL\sigma_L acts along the axis.

Principle. Equilibrium of a free body cut through the cylinder. The pressure force is balanced by the wall force.

Hoop stress (cut along a diameter plane through the axis). Pressure force on the projected area =p D L= p\,D\,L. The wall resists with two strips of area tLtL each:

2 σh t L2\,\sigma_h\,t\,L​=p D L  =p\,D\,L\;​⇒  σh\Rightarrow\;\sigma_h​=pD2t=\dfrac{pD}{2t}

Longitudinal stress (cut across the cylinder). Pressure force on the end area =p πD2/4= p\,\pi D^2/4. The wall resists over the ring area πDt\pi D t:

σL πDt\sigma_L\,\pi D t​=p πD24  =p\,\dfrac{\pi D^2}{4}\;​⇒  σL\Rightarrow\;\sigma_L​=pD4t=\dfrac{pD}{4t}

σh=pD2t=2 σL\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t}=2\,\sigma_L

Explanation. The pressure acts on the same wall in both directions but the area that carries the force differs. For hoop stress, the wall area is 2tL2tL against a pressure area DLDL (ratio D/2tD/2t). For longitudinal stress, the wall area is πDt\pi Dt against a pressure area πD2/4\pi D^2/4 (ratio D/4tD/4t). The wall area carrying the axial load is twice as favourable.

Conclusion. The hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress, so a cylinder under pressure splits along its length first (as a boiled sausage or soda can does).

U4-Q031Q031 | L2 Understand | P1 | T | 3 marks

Explain why a thin spherical shell is more efficient than a cylindrical shell for storing a given pressure.

Solution

Definition. Efficiency here means the least wall thickness (material) for a given pressure pp, radius and allowable stress.

Formulae. Cylinder: σh=pD2t\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t}, σL=pD4t\sigma_L=\dfrac{pD}{4t}. Sphere: σ=pD4t\sigma=\dfrac{pD}{4t}.

For the same pp, DD, tt: σsphere\sigma_{sphere}​=pD4t=\dfrac{pD}{4t}​=12σh, cylinder=\dfrac12\sigma_{h,\,cylinder}

Explanation. In a sphere the pressure force on a hemisphere, pπD2/4p\pi D^2/4, is carried by the wall around the whole great circle, area πDt\pi Dt. In a cylinder the hoop force is carried by only two strips of wall, area 2tL2tL. Hence the maximum stress in a sphere is half that in a cylinder. For the same allowable stress, tspheret_{sphere}​=pD/(4σ)=pD/(4\sigma) is half of tcylindert_{cylinder}​=pD/(2σ)=pD/(2\sigma). A sphere also has no seam under hoop stress and a larger volume per unit of wall material.

Conclusion. The sphere needs half the wall thickness, so it is more material efficient. The drawback is that it is harder to fabricate, so cylinders are used where shape matters. (Consistent with Q&A model answer 6.)

U4-Q032Q032 | L2 Understand | P1 | T | 3 marks

Explain the effect of joint efficiency on the stresses and on the required thickness of a welded cylindrical shell.

Solution

Definition. Joint efficiency η\eta is the ratio of the strength of the welded or riveted joint to the strength of the solid plate. ηl\eta_l is for the longitudinal joint, ηc\eta_c for the circumferential joint; η≤1\eta\le1.

Principle. The joint is weaker than the plate, so the stress in the joint section is higher. The plate stress is unchanged, but the stress at the joint is the plate stress divided by η\eta.

σh=pD2t ηl\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t\,\eta_l} (hoop stress, resisted by the longitudinal joint), σL=pD4t ηc\quad\sigma_L=\dfrac{pD}{4t\,\eta_c} (resisted by the circumferential joint)

Effect on thickness. For an allowable stress σallow\sigma_{allow}:

tht_h​=pD2σallowηl=\dfrac{pD}{2\sigma_{allow}\eta_l}, tL t_L​=pD4σallowηc=\dfrac{pD}{4\sigma_{allow}\eta_c}; use the larger.

Conclusion. Joint efficiency raises the stress at the joint by 1/η1/\eta and therefore increases the required thickness by 1/η1/\eta. A better weld (higher η\eta) allows a thinner shell. Since the hoop stress is double the longitudinal stress, the longitudinal joint usually governs.

U4-Q033Q033 | L2 Understand | P2 | T | 4 marks

Explain why thin-wall formulae are inaccurate for thick cylinders and why the hoop stress in a thick cylinder is non-uniform.

Solution

Definition. A cylinder is thin if t≤r/10t\le r/10; otherwise thick.

Assumptions of the thin-wall theory. 1. Hoop stress is uniform through the thickness. 2. Radial stress is negligible (since p≪σhp\ll\sigma_h).

Why they fail. When the wall is thick, the radial stress goes from −pi-p_i at the inner surface to 00 at the outer surface, which is no longer small compared with σθ\sigma_\theta. The hoop strain also varies with radius. The inner fibres stretch more than the outer fibres but must remain a continuous solid, so the stress adjusts: the inner fibre carries the larger hoop stress.

Why non-uniform (Lamé). Equilibrium and compatibility together give

σr=A−Br2\sigma_r=A-\dfrac{B}{r^2}, σθ=A+Br2\quad\sigma_\theta=A+\dfrac{B}{r^2}

so σθ\sigma_\theta depends on rr through B/r2B/r^2.

Numerical illustration. ro=2rir_o=2r_i, internal pressure pip_i only. Thin-wall formula (t=rit=r_i): σh=piri/t=pi\sigma_h=p_ir_i/t=p_i. Lamé: inner σθ\sigma_\theta​=pi4+14−1=p_i\dfrac{4+1}{4-1}​=1.67 pi=1.67\,p_i; outer σθ=2pi3=0.67 pi\sigma_\theta=\dfrac{2p_i}{3}=0.67\,p_i. The thin formula under-estimates the peak by 40%.

Conclusion. The thin-wall formulae ignore radial stress and the variation of hoop stress, so they are unsafe for thick cylinders; Lamé's equations must be used.

U4-Q034Q034 | L2 Understand | P2 | T | 4 marks

Explain how the radial and hoop stresses vary through the wall of a thick cylinder subjected to internal pressure only. Where is the hoop stress maximum?

Solution

Definition. Thick cylinder, inner radius rir_i, outer radius ror_o, internal pressure pip_i, external pressure zero.

Formulae (Lamé, tension positive).

σθ\sigma_\theta​=piri2ro2−ri2(1+ro2r2)=\dfrac{p_ir_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}\left(1+\dfrac{r_o^2}{r^2}\right), σr\sigma_r​=−piri2ro2−ri2(ro2r2−1)=-\dfrac{p_ir_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}\left(\dfrac{r_o^2}{r^2}-1\right)

Boundary values.

Radius σr\sigma_r σθ\sigma_\theta
r=rir=r_i−pi-p_i (compression)piro2+ri2ro2−ri2p_i\dfrac{r_o^2+r_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2} (maximum)
r=ror=r_o002piri2ro2−ri2\dfrac{2p_ir_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2} (minimum)

Explanation. σθ\sigma_\theta is tensile and falls with 1/r21/r^2 from inner to outer surface. σr\sigma_r is compressive and rises from −pi-p_i to zero. Their sum σr+σθ=2A\sigma_r+\sigma_\theta=2A is constant through the wall (so the axial strain is uniform in a closed or free-end cylinder). Maximum shear (σθ−σr)/2(\sigma_\theta-\sigma_r)/2 is also greatest at the inner surface: piro2/(ro2−ri2)p_ir_o^2/(r_o^2-r_i^2).

Conclusion. The hoop stress is greatest at the inner surface, where the material is first to yield, so design is based on σθ(ri)\sigma_\theta(r_i).

U4-Q035Q035 | L2 Understand | P2 | T | 4 marks

Explain why increasing wall thickness beyond a certain value gives diminishing returns in a thick cylinder, and what happens as pip_i approaches the allowable stress.

Solution

Definition. Design relation for internal pressure with allowable hoop stress σallow\sigma_{allow} at the inner surface:

rori\dfrac{r_o}{r_i}​=σallow+piσallow−pi=\sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_{allow}+p_i}{\sigma_{allow}-p_i}}, σθ,max\sigma_{\theta,max}​=piro2+ri2ro2−ri2=p_i\dfrac{r_o^2+r_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}

Explanation (diminishing returns). The maximum hoop stress is pip_i times the factor k2+1k2−1\dfrac{k^2+1}{k^2-1} with k=ro/rik=r_o/r_i. The factor falls quickly at first, then slowly:

k=ro/rik=r_o/r_i 1.5 2 3 5 10
σθ,max/pi\sigma_{\theta,max}/p_i2.601.671.251.0831.020

The factor never goes below 11, i.e. σθ,max>pi\sigma_{\theta,max}>p_i however thick the wall. Going from k=3k=3 to k=5k=5 almost doubles the wall thickness, but reduces the peak stress by only 13%. The outer layers carry little stress because σθ∝1/r2\sigma_\theta\propto1/r^2, so extra metal there is largely unused.

Limit as pi→σallowp_i\to\sigma_{allow}. The ratio ro/ri→∞r_o/r_i\to\infty: no finite thickness is enough. If pi≥σallowp_i\ge\sigma_{allow}, a single homogeneous cylinder cannot be designed.

Conclusion. Thickness helps strongly at first and very little later; when pip_i is close to σallow\sigma_{allow} the only options are a stronger material or a lower pressure.

U4-Q036Q036 | L2 Understand | E1 | T | 3 marks

Explain the physical meaning of the area under a load-deformation diagram.

Solution

Definition. The load-deformation (PP-xx) diagram plots the axial load against the elongation of a rod while it is loaded slowly.

Principle. The work done by the load over a small elongation dxdx is dU=P dxdU=P\,dx, so the total work is the area under the curve.

U=∫0x1P dxU=\displaystyle\int_0^{x_1}P\,dx (area under the PP-xx curve); linear elastic (P=kxP=kx): U=12P1x1U=\tfrac12P_1x_1 (triangle).

Explanation. This work is stored in the body as strain energy. Within the elastic limit it is fully recoverable: when the load is removed the rod returns the energy, like a spring. Beyond yield, only the recoverable triangle under the unloading line is returned; the rest is lost as plastic work (heat).

Units. N m = J. Dividing by the volume gives the energy density, the area under the stress-strain curve.

Conclusion. The area under the load-deformation diagram is the work done by the load, stored as strain energy; for a linear member it is 12P1x1\tfrac12P_1x_1. (Matches Q&A model answer 7.)

U4-Q037Q037 | L2 Understand | E1 | T | 4 marks

Explain the difference between modulus of resilience and modulus of toughness. Which one governs the ability of a component to resist impact without permanent deformation?

Solution

Definition. - Modulus of resilience uYu_Y: strain energy per unit volume absorbed up to the yield point; the area under the straight (elastic) part of the σ\sigma-ε\varepsilon diagram. - Modulus of toughness: strain energy per unit volume absorbed up to fracture; the whole area under the σ\sigma-ε\varepsilon diagram.

uY=σY22Eu_Y=\dfrac{\sigma_Y^2}{2E}, utoughness u_{toughness}​=∫0εfσ dε=\displaystyle\int_0^{\varepsilon_f}\sigma\,d\varepsilon

Explanation.

Resilience Toughness
Up toyieldfracture
Energyrecoverable (elastic)includes plastic work
Tells usenergy absorbed without permanent setenergy absorbed before breaking
Large forhigh σY\sigma_Y, low EE (springs)ductile steels (couplers, crash barriers)

Which governs. Impact without permanent deformation means the energy must stay within the elastic range, so the modulus of resilience (proof resilience =uY×=u_Y\times volume) governs. If the part may deform permanently but must not break, toughness governs.

Conclusion. Resilience is the elastic energy capacity (σY2/2E\sigma_Y^2/2E); toughness is the total energy to fracture. Resilience decides resistance to impact without permanent deformation.

U4-Q038Q038 | L2 Understand | E1 | T | 4 marks

Explain why a stepped bar of the same material absorbs less strain energy than a uniform bar of the smaller section for the same maximum stress.

Solution

Definition. Strain energy of an axial bar: U=∑Pi2Li2AiEU=\displaystyle\sum\frac{P_i^2L_i}{2A_iE}. The maximum stress is the allowable stress in the smallest section.

Principle. For the same maximum stress σm\sigma_m the load is limited by the small section, P=σmAP=\sigma_mA. The energy density is u=σ2/2Eu=\sigma^2/2E, and it depends on the stress squared in each part.

Explanation. Take length L/2L/2 of area AA and length L/2L/2 of area n2An^2A, same load PP.

  • Uniform bar of area AA: U1=P2L2AEU_1=\dfrac{P^2L}{2AE} (stress σm\sigma_m everywhere).
  • Stepped bar: the large part has stress σm/n2\sigma_m/n^2, so its energy density is only 1/n41/n^4 of the full value:

UnU_n​=P2(L/2)2AE+P2(L/2)2n2AE=\dfrac{P^2(L/2)}{2AE}+\dfrac{P^2(L/2)}{2n^2AE}​=1+n22n2 U1=\dfrac{1+n^2}{2n^2}\,U_1, so U2=58U1U_2=\tfrac58U_1 (n=2n=2).

(Example C.2 in the notes: U1=9000U_1=9000 N mm, U2=5625U_2=5625 N mm.)

Why. The enlarged portion is lightly stressed; it adds volume (and weight) but stores little energy. The peak stress at the small portion still limits the load. Energy per unit volume overall falls.

Application. Bolts have the shank turned down to the thread-root diameter so the whole length is equally stressed and absorbs more shock energy.

Conclusion. Because the large section carries lower stress, it stores less energy per volume. The stepped bar absorbs less energy than a uniform bar of the smaller section for the same peak stress (U2=58U1U_2=\tfrac58U_1 for n=2n=2).

U4-Q039Q039 | L2 Understand | E1 | T | 4 marks

Explain why strain energy is not additive when two loads are applied together, i.e. why U(P1+P2)U(P_1+P_2)​≠U(P1)+U(P2)\ne U(P_1)+U(P_2).

Solution

Definition. Strain energy depends on the square of the load, e.g. U=P2L/2AEU=P^2L/2AE.

Principle. A function of the square is not linear, so the energy of a sum is not the sum of energies.

Derivation (axial rod).

U(P1+P2)U(P_1+P_2)​=(P1+P2)2L2AE=\dfrac{(P_1+P_2)^2L}{2AE}​=P12L2AE+P22L2AE+P1P2LAE=\dfrac{P_1^2L}{2AE}+\dfrac{P_2^2L}{2AE}+\dfrac{P_1P_2L}{AE}​=U(P1)+U(P2)+P1P2LAE=U(P_1)+U(P_2)+\dfrac{P_1P_2L}{AE}

Explanation. The extra term P1P2L/AEP_1P_2L/AE is the work done by one load acting through the deformation caused by the other. It is non-zero whenever both loads act on the same member and produce deformation in the same direction. So the principle of superposition applies to stresses and deflections (linear in load), but not to strain energy (quadratic in load).

Example. P1=P2=PP_1=P_2=P: U(2P)=4U(P)U(2P)=4U(P), but U(P)+U(P)U(P)+U(P)​=2U(P)=2U(P).

Consequence. Do not add the energies of separate load cases; first add the loads (or stresses), then compute UU.

Conclusion. Strain energy varies as load squared, producing a cross term P1P2L/AEP_1P_2L/AE, so it is not additive.

U4-Q040Q040 | L2 Understand | E2 | T | 3 marks

Explain how the strain-energy density for shear, u=τ2/2Gu=\tau^2/2G, is obtained from the shear stress-strain diagram.

Solution

Definition. Strain-energy density uu is the strain energy per unit volume. For shear it is the area under the τ\tau-γ\gamma diagram.

Principle. An element under shear stress τxy\tau_{xy} distorts through shear strain γxy\gamma_{xy}. As the stress grows slowly from 00 to its final value the work per unit volume is τ dγ\tau\,d\gamma.

Derivation. Within the proportional limit τ=Gγ\tau=G\gamma:

uu​=∫0γxyτ dγ=\displaystyle\int_0^{\gamma_{xy}}\tau\,d\gamma​=∫0γxyGγ dγ=\int_0^{\gamma_{xy}}G\gamma\,d\gamma​=12Gγxy2=\tfrac12G\gamma_{xy}^2​=12τxyγxy=\tfrac12\tau_{xy}\gamma_{xy}​=τxy22G=\dfrac{\tau_{xy}^2}{2G}

Explanation. The τ\tau-γ\gamma line is straight through the origin, so the area under it is the triangle 12×γ×τ\tfrac12\times\gamma\times\tau. Replacing γ=τ/G\gamma=\tau/G gives τ2/2G\tau^2/2G. The total energy is U=∫τ22GdVU=\int\dfrac{\tau^2}{2G}dV; for a shaft in torsion this gives U=T2L/2GJU=T^2L/2GJ.

Conclusion. u=τ2/2Gu=\tau^2/2G is the area of the triangle under the linear τ\tau-γ\gamma diagram. (Matches Q&A model answer 8.)

Level 3: Apply (Q041 to Q060)

Cognitive focus: using formulae and methods in routine numerical situations. Each answer states the convention, the formula, every step with units, and a boxed result; each was recomputed in code. Units: stresses in MPa, angles in degrees.

U4-Q041Q041 | L3 Apply | T1 | N | 6 marks

At a point in a plane-stress state σx=80\sigma_x=80 MPa, σy=20\sigma_y=20 MPa and τxy=30\tau_{xy}=30 MPa. Determine σx′\sigma_{x'}, σy′\sigma_{y'} and τx′y′\tau_{x'y'} on an element rotated 30∘30^{\circ} counter-clockwise.

Solution

Given. σx=80\sigma_x=80, σy=20\sigma_y=20, τxy=30\tau_{xy}=30 MPa; θ=+30∘\theta=+30^{\circ} (counter-clockwise).

To find. σx′,σy′,τx′y′\sigma_{x'},\sigma_{y'},\tau_{x'y'}.

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; tension positive; θ\theta counter-clockwise positive; τxy\tau_{xy} as in the bank convention.

Formula. σx′\sigma_{x'}​=σx+σy2+σx−σy2cos⁡2θ+τxysin⁡2θ=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}+\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\cos2\theta+\tau_{xy}\sin2\theta, τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−σx−σy2sin⁡2θ+τxycos⁡2θ=-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\sin2\theta+\tau_{xy}\cos2\theta,   σy′=σx+σy−σx′\;\sigma_{y'}=\sigma_x+\sigma_y-\sigma_{x'}.

Solution.

  1. σx+σy2=50\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}=50 MPa; σx−σy2=30\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}=30 MPa; 2θ=60∘2\theta=60^{\circ}, cos⁡60∘=0.5\cos60^{\circ}=0.5, sin⁡60∘=0.8660\sin60^{\circ}=0.8660.
  2. σx′\sigma_{x'}​=50+30(0.5)+30(0.8660)=50+30(0.5)+30(0.8660)​=50+15+25.98=50+15+25.98​=90.98=90.98 MPa.
  3. τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−30(0.8660)+30(0.5)=-30(0.8660)+30(0.5)​=−25.98+15=-25.98+15​=−10.98=-10.98 MPa.
  4. σy′\sigma_{y'}​=50−15−25.98=50-15-25.98​=9.02=9.02 MPa. Check: σx′+σy′\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'}​=100=100​=σx+σy=\sigma_x+\sigma_y.

σx′=91.0\sigma_{x'}=91.0 MPa,   σy′=9.02\;\sigma_{y'}=9.02 MPa,   τx′y′=−10.98\;\tau_{x'y'}=-10.98 MPa

U4-Q042Q042 | L3 Apply | T1 | N | 6 marks

For σx=−60\sigma_x=-60 MPa, σy=40\sigma_y=40 MPa and τxy=−25\tau_{xy}=-25 MPa, determine the normal and shear stresses on an element rotated 20∘20^{\circ} clockwise.

Solution

Given. σx=−60\sigma_x=-60, σy=40\sigma_y=40, τxy=−25\tau_{xy}=-25 MPa; clockwise rotation so θ=−20∘\theta=-20^{\circ}.

To find. σx′,σy′,τx′y′\sigma_{x'},\sigma_{y'},\tau_{x'y'}.

Assumptions and sign convention. Tension positive, counter-clockwise θ\theta positive, so clockwise 20∘20^{\circ} is θ=−20∘\theta=-20^{\circ} and 2θ=−40∘2\theta=-40^{\circ}.

Formula. As in Q041.

Solution.

  1. σx+σy2=−10\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}=-10 MPa; σx−σy2=−50\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}=-50 MPa; cos⁡(−40∘)=0.7660\cos(-40^{\circ})=0.7660, sin⁡(−40∘)\sin(-40^{\circ})​=−0.6428=-0.6428.
  2. σx′\sigma_{x'}​=−10=-10​+(−50)(0.7660)+(-50)(0.7660)​+(−25)(−0.6428)+(-25)(-0.6428)​=−10−38.30+16.07=-10-38.30+16.07​=−32.23=-32.23 MPa.
  3. τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−(−50)(−0.6428)=-(-50)(-0.6428)​+(−25)(0.7660)+(-25)(0.7660)​=−32.14−19.15=-32.14-19.15​=−51.29=-51.29 MPa.
  4. σy′\sigma_{y'}​=σx+σy−σx′=\sigma_x+\sigma_y-\sigma_{x'}​=−20+32.23=-20+32.23​=12.23=12.23 MPa. Check by formula: −10+38.30−16.07-10+38.30-16.07​=12.23=12.23 MPa.

σx′=−32.2\sigma_{x'}=-32.2 MPa,   σy′=12.2\;\sigma_{y'}=12.2 MPa,   τx′y′=−51.3\;\tau_{x'y'}=-51.3 MPa

U4-Q043Q043 | L3 Apply | T1 | N | 5 marks

A bar is subjected to a uniaxial tensile stress of 120 MPa. Find the normal and shear stresses on a plane whose normal makes 40∘40^{\circ} with the axis of the bar.

Solution

Given. σx=120\sigma_x=120 MPa, σy=τxy=0\sigma_y=\tau_{xy}=0; plane normal at θ=40∘\theta=40^{\circ} to the axis.

To find. σθ\sigma_\theta and τθ\tau_\theta.

Assumptions and sign convention. Uniaxial stress; θ\theta counter-clockwise from the axis to the plane normal; shear magnitude and sense stated.

Formula. σθ=σcos⁡2θ\sigma_\theta=\sigma\cos^2\theta,   τθ=−σ2sin⁡2θ\;\tau_\theta=-\dfrac{\sigma}{2}\sin2\theta (transformation equations with σy=τxy=0\sigma_y=\tau_{xy}=0).

Solution.

  1. cos⁡40∘=0.7660\cos40^{\circ}=0.7660, so cos⁡240∘=0.5868\cos^240^{\circ}=0.5868.
  2. σθ\sigma_\theta​=120(0.5868)=120(0.5868)​=70.42=70.42 MPa.
  3. sin⁡80∘=0.9848\sin80^{\circ}=0.9848, so τθ\tau_\theta​=−60(0.9848)=-60(0.9848)​=−59.09=-59.09 MPa; magnitude 59.0959.09 MPa.
  4. Check: the perpendicular plane (130∘130^{\circ}) carries 120sin⁡240∘=49.58120\sin^240^{\circ}=49.58 MPa, and 70.42+49.5870.42+49.58​=120=120 MPa.

σθ=70.4\sigma_\theta=70.4 MPa (tension),   ∣τθ∣=59.1\;|\tau_\theta|=59.1 MPa (τx′y′=−59.1\tau_{x'y'}=-59.1 MPa)

U4-Q044Q044 | L3 Apply | T1 | N | 6 marks

A wedge-shaped element has a vertical face, a horizontal face and an oblique face inclined at 40∘40^{\circ} to the horizontal. The vertical face carries 50 MPa tension (σx\sigma_x) and shear τxy=20\tau_{xy}=20 MPa (upward on the right face); the horizontal face carries 30 MPa compression (σy\sigma_y). Using equilibrium of the wedge or the transformation equations, find the normal and shear stress on the oblique face (outward normal at 130∘130^{\circ} counter-clockwise from the xx axis).

Solution

Given. σx=+50\sigma_x=+50, σy=−30\sigma_y=-30, τxy=+20\tau_{xy}=+20 MPa; the oblique face has outward normal at θ=130∘\theta=130^{\circ} from +x+x (a face inclined 40∘40^{\circ} to the horizontal has its normal at 40∘+90∘=130∘40^{\circ}+90^{\circ}=130^{\circ}).

To find. σn\sigma_n and τ\tau on the oblique face.

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; tension positive; the plane is specified by its outward normal, so it is the x′x' face with θ=130∘\theta=130^{\circ}; the transformation equations give the same result as force equilibrium of the wedge.

Formula. σx′\sigma_{x'}​=σx+σy2+σx−σy2cos⁡2θ+τxysin⁡2θ=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}+\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\cos2\theta+\tau_{xy}\sin2\theta, τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−σx−σy2sin⁡2θ+τxycos⁡2θ=-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\sin2\theta+\tau_{xy}\cos2\theta.

Solution.

  1. σx+σy2=10\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}=10 MPa; σx−σy2=40\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}=40 MPa; 2θ=260∘2\theta=260^{\circ}: cos⁡260∘=−0.1736\cos260^{\circ}=-0.1736, sin⁡260∘=−0.9848\sin260^{\circ}=-0.9848.
  2. σx′\sigma_{x'}​=10=10​+40(−0.1736)+40(-0.1736)​+20(−0.9848)+20(-0.9848)​=10−6.94−19.70=10-6.94-19.70​=−16.64=-16.64 MPa.
  3. τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−40(−0.9848)+20(−0.1736)=-40(-0.9848)+20(-0.1736)​=39.39−3.47=39.39-3.47​=35.92=35.92 MPa.
  4. Check: for the plane with normal at 40∘40^{\circ} (2θ=80∘2\theta=80^{\circ}) the same formulas give σ=36.64\sigma=36.64 MPa, and −16.64+36.64-16.64+36.64​=20=20​=σx+σy=\sigma_x+\sigma_y MPa.

Oblique face: σn=−16.6\sigma_n=-16.6 MPa (compression),   τ=35.9\;\tau=35.9 MPa

U4-Q045Q045 | L3 Apply | T2 | N | 6 marks

Determine the principal stresses and the principal planes for σx=90\sigma_x=90 MPa, σy=30\sigma_y=30 MPa, τxy=40\tau_{xy}=40 MPa.

Solution

Given. σx=90\sigma_x=90, σy=30\sigma_y=30, τxy=40\tau_{xy}=40 MPa.

To find. σ1,σ2\sigma_1,\sigma_2 and the principal angles θp\theta_p.

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; tension positive; θ\theta counter-clockwise from xx.

Formula. σ1,2\sigma_{1,2}​=σx+σy2±(σx−σy2)2+τxy2=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}\pm\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^2+\tau_{xy}^2}, tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2τxyσx−σy=\dfrac{2\tau_{xy}}{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}.

Solution.

  1. σavg=90+302=60\sigma_{avg}=\dfrac{90+30}{2}=60 MPa; σx−σy2=30\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}=30 MPa.
  2. R=302+402=50R=\sqrt{30^2+40^2}=50 MPa.
  3. σ1=60+50=110\sigma_1=60+50=110 MPa; σ2=60−50=10\sigma_2=60-50=10 MPa.
  4. tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2(40)60=\dfrac{2(40)}{60}​=1.3333=1.3333​⇒2θp\Rightarrow2\theta_p​=53.13∘=53.13^{\circ}, so θp=26.57∘\theta_p=26.57^{\circ} and θp+90∘=116.57∘\theta_p+90^{\circ}=116.57^{\circ}.
  5. Which is which: at θ=26.57∘\theta=26.57^{\circ}, σx′\sigma_{x'}​=60+30cos⁡53.13∘+40sin⁡53.13∘=60+30\cos53.13^{\circ}+40\sin53.13^{\circ}​=60+18+32=60+18+32​=110=110 MPa, so this is the σ1\sigma_1 plane; σ2=10\sigma_2=10 MPa acts on 116.57∘116.57^{\circ}. Shear there is −30sin⁡53.13∘+40cos⁡53.13∘-30\sin53.13^{\circ}+40\cos53.13^{\circ}​=0=0.

σ1=110\sigma_1=110 MPa at θp=26.6∘\theta_p=26.6^{\circ} CCW,   σ2=10\;\sigma_2=10 MPa at 116.6∘116.6^{\circ} CCW (both planes shear-free)

U4-Q046Q046 | L3 Apply | T2 | N | 7 marks

For σx=−45\sigma_x=-45 MPa, σy=75\sigma_y=75 MPa, τxy=−60\tau_{xy}=-60 MPa, determine the principal stresses, the principal angles and the maximum in-plane shear stress.

Solution

Given. σx=−45\sigma_x=-45, σy=75\sigma_y=75, τxy=−60\tau_{xy}=-60 MPa.

To find. σ1,σ2\sigma_1,\sigma_2, θp\theta_p, τmax\tau_{max} (in-plane).

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; tension positive; θ\theta counter-clockwise from xx; τxy\tau_{xy} as in the bank convention.

Formula. σ1,2=σavg±R\sigma_{1,2}=\sigma_{avg}\pm R, RR​=(σx−σy2)2+τxy2=\sqrt{\left(\frac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^2+\tau_{xy}^2}, tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2τxyσx−σy=\dfrac{2\tau_{xy}}{\sigma_x-\sigma_y},   τmax=R\;\tau_{max}=R.

Solution.

  1. σavg=−45+752=15\sigma_{avg}=\dfrac{-45+75}{2}=15 MPa; σx−σy2=−60\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}=-60 MPa.
  2. RR​=(−60)2+(−60)2=\sqrt{(-60)^2+(-60)^2}​=7200=\sqrt{7200}​=84.85=84.85 MPa.
  3. σ1\sigma_1​=15+84.85=15+84.85​=99.85=99.85 MPa; σ2\sigma_2​=15−84.85=15-84.85​=−69.85=-69.85 MPa.
  4. tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2(−60)−45−75=\dfrac{2(-60)}{-45-75}​=−120−120=\dfrac{-120}{-120}​=1=1, so 2θp=45∘2\theta_p=45^{\circ} or −135∘-135^{\circ} (they differ by 180∘180^{\circ}). Test which one gives σ1\sigma_1: σx′\sigma_{x'} at θ=−67.5∘\theta=-67.5^{\circ} is 1515​+(−60)cos⁡(−135∘)+(-60)\cos(-135^{\circ})​+(−60)sin⁡(−135∘)+(-60)\sin(-135^{\circ})​=15+42.43+42.43=15+42.43+42.43​=99.85=99.85 MPa. So σ1\sigma_1 acts at θp1=−67.5∘\theta_{p1}=-67.5^{\circ} (equivalently 112.5∘112.5^{\circ}), and σ2\sigma_2 at θp2=+22.5∘\theta_{p2}=+22.5^{\circ}.
  5. τmax=R=84.85\tau_{max}=R=84.85 MPa on planes θp±45∘\theta_p\pm45^{\circ}, i.e. −22.5∘-22.5^{\circ} and 67.5∘67.5^{\circ}, with σ′=15\sigma'=15 MPa.

σ1=99.9\sigma_1=99.9 MPa at −67.5∘-67.5^{\circ},   σ2=−69.9\;\sigma_2=-69.9 MPa at 22.5∘22.5^{\circ},   τmax=84.9\;\tau_{max}=84.9 MPa

Check: σ1+σ2=30=σx+σy\sigma_1+\sigma_2=30=\sigma_x+\sigma_y MPa.

U4-Q047Q047 | L3 Apply | T2 | N | 6 marks

For σx=120\sigma_x=120 MPa, σy=−40\sigma_y=-40 MPa, τxy=50\tau_{xy}=50 MPa, determine the maximum in-plane shear stress, the normal stress on the planes of maximum shear and the orientation of these planes.

Solution

Given. σx=120\sigma_x=120, σy=−40\sigma_y=-40, τxy=50\tau_{xy}=50 MPa.

To find. τmax\tau_{max}, σ′\sigma' on those planes, θs\theta_s.

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; tension positive; θ\theta counter-clockwise from xx.

Formula. τmax=R\tau_{max}=R,   σ′=σavg\;\sigma'=\sigma_{avg},   θs=θp±45∘\;\theta_s=\theta_p\pm45^{\circ} (or tan⁡2θs\tan2\theta_s​=−σx−σy2τxy=-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2\tau_{xy}}).

Solution.

  1. σavg=120−402=40\sigma_{avg}=\dfrac{120-40}{2}=40 MPa; σx−σy2=80\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}=80 MPa.
  2. RR​=802+502=\sqrt{80^2+50^2}​=8900=\sqrt{8900}​=94.34=94.34 MPa.
  3. tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2(50)160=\dfrac{2(50)}{160}​=0.625=0.625​⇒2θp\Rightarrow2\theta_p​=32.01∘=32.01^{\circ}, θp=16.0∘\theta_p=16.0^{\circ} (this is the σ1=134.3\sigma_1=134.3 MPa plane).
  4. θs=16.0∘±45∘\theta_s=16.0^{\circ}\pm45^{\circ}: 61.0∘61.0^{\circ} and −29.0∘-29.0^{\circ}. Direct check: tan⁡2θs\tan2\theta_s​=−8050=-\dfrac{80}{50}​=−1.6=-1.6​⇒2θs\Rightarrow2\theta_s​=−58.0∘=-58.0^{\circ}, θs=−29.0∘\theta_s=-29.0^{\circ} (and +61.0∘+61.0^{\circ}).
  5. Shear on them: at θ=−29.0∘\theta=-29.0^{\circ}, τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−80sin⁡(−58∘)+50cos⁡(−58∘)=-80\sin(-58^{\circ})+50\cos(-58^{\circ})​=67.84+26.50=67.84+26.50​=+94.34=+94.34 MPa; at 61.0∘61.0^{\circ} it is −94.34-94.34 MPa. The normal stress on both is 4040 MPa.

τmax=94.3\tau_{max}=94.3 MPa on planes at −29.0∘-29.0^{\circ} and 61.0∘61.0^{\circ} (i.e. 45∘45^{\circ} from the principal planes), with σ′=40\sigma'=40 MPa

Note: this is the in-plane value. With σ1=134.3\sigma_1=134.3 and σ2=−54.3\sigma_2=-54.3 of opposite sign, the absolute maximum shear is the same (94.3 MPa).

U4-Q048Q048 | L3 Apply | T3 | N | 8 marks

Using Mohr's circle, determine the principal stresses and the maximum shear stress for σx=70\sigma_x=70 MPa, σy=−30\sigma_y=-30 MPa, τxy=40\tau_{xy}=40 MPa. Show the principal element.

Solution

Given. σx=70\sigma_x=70, σy=−30\sigma_y=-30, τxy=40\tau_{xy}=40 MPa.

To find. σ1,σ2\sigma_1,\sigma_2, τmax\tau_{max}, θp\theta_p, and the principal element.

Assumptions and sign convention. Tension positive; Mohr's circle plots σ\sigma to the right and clockwise-turning shear upward, so X=(σx,−τxy)X=(\sigma_x,-\tau_{xy}), Y=(σy,+τxy)Y=(\sigma_y,+\tau_{xy}); the rotation of the element θ\theta is half the rotation on the circle, in the same sense.

Method (Mohr's circle). Plot XX and YY, join them (diameter), draw the circle, read the points AA, BB on the σ\sigma axis and DD, EE at top and bottom. (Use this when a graph or a quick check is wanted; the analytical formula is the same arithmetic.)

Solution.

  1. X=(70,−40)X=(70,-40), Y=(−30,+40)Y=(-30,+40).
  2. Centre C=70+(−30)2=20C=\dfrac{70+(-30)}{2}=20 MPa.
  3. Radius RR​=(70−(−30)2)2+402=\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{70-(-30)}{2}\right)^2+40^2}​=502+402=\sqrt{50^2+40^2}​=64.03=64.03 MPa.
  4. A=C+R=84.03A=C+R=84.03 MPa; B=C−R=−44.03B=C-R=-44.03 MPa.
  5. τmax=R=64.03\tau_{max}=R=64.03 MPa (points DD, EE) with σ′=20\sigma'=20 MPa.
  6. Angle from CXCX to CACA: XX is 5050 to the right of CC and 4040 below it, so CXCX is 38.66∘38.66^{\circ} below the axis. Rotating to CACA is 38.66∘38.66^{\circ} counter-clockwise on the circle. 2θp=38.66∘2\theta_p=38.66^{\circ}, so θp=19.33∘\theta_p=19.33^{\circ} counter-clockwise from the xx face to the σ1\sigma_1 plane. The σ2\sigma_2 plane is at 109.33∘109.33^{\circ} (or −70.67∘-70.67^{\circ}).
  7. Principal element: rotate the original element 19.33∘19.33^{\circ} counter-clockwise; faces carry 84.084.0 MPa (tension) and −44.0-44.0 MPa (compression) with zero shear.

σ1=84.0\sigma_1=84.0 MPa,   σ2=−44.0\;\sigma_2=-44.0 MPa,   τmax=64.0\;\tau_{max}=64.0 MPa,   θp=19.3∘\;\theta_p=19.3^{\circ} CCW

Check (analytical): tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2(40)100=\dfrac{2(40)}{100}​=0.8=0.8​⇒2θp\Rightarrow2\theta_p​=38.66∘=38.66^{\circ} ✓; σ1+σ2=40=σx+σy\sigma_1+\sigma_2=40=\sigma_x+\sigma_y ✓.

U4-Q049Q049 | L3 Apply | T3 | N | 8 marks

Using Mohr's circle, determine the normal and shear stresses on a plane inclined at 30∘30^{\circ} counter-clockwise from the xx axis for σx=−50\sigma_x=-50 MPa, σy=90\sigma_y=90 MPa, τxy=−35\tau_{xy}=-35 MPa.

Solution

Given. σx=−50\sigma_x=-50, σy=90\sigma_y=90, τxy=−35\tau_{xy}=-35 MPa; θ=30∘\theta=30^{\circ} CCW, so the diameter turns 2θ=60∘2\theta=60^{\circ} CCW.

To find. σx′\sigma_{x'}, τx′y′\tau_{x'y'} (and σy′\sigma_{y'}).

Assumptions and sign convention. As in Q048: X=(σx,−τxy)X=(\sigma_x,-\tau_{xy}), Y=(σy,+τxy)Y=(\sigma_y,+\tau_{xy}); the angle on the circle is twice the element angle in the same sense.

Solution.

  1. X=(−50,+35)X=(-50,+35); Y=(90,−35)Y=(90,-35).
  2. C=−50+902=20C=\dfrac{-50+90}{2}=20 MPa; σx−σy2=−70\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}=-70 MPa.
  3. RR​=702+352=\sqrt{70^2+35^2}​=78.26=78.26 MPa.
  4. CXCX goes 7070 to the left and 3535 up from CC, so it makes β\beta​=atan2(35,−70)=\text{atan2}(35,-70)​=153.43∘=153.43^{\circ} with the +σ+\sigma direction (counter-clockwise).
  5. Rotate 60∘60^{\circ} counter-clockwise: X′X' is at 153.43∘+60∘153.43^{\circ}+60^{\circ}​=213.43∘=213.43^{\circ}.
  6. σx′\sigma_{x'}​=20+78.26cos⁡213.43∘=20+78.26\cos213.43^{\circ}​=20−65.31=20-65.31​=−45.31=-45.31 MPa.
  7. Ordinate of X′X' =78.26sin⁡213.43∘=78.26\sin213.43^{\circ}​=−43.12=-43.12 MPa; the ordinate equals −τx′y′-\tau_{x'y'}, so τx′y′=+43.12\tau_{x'y'}=+43.12 MPa.
  8. σy′\sigma_{y'}​=2C−σx′=2C-\sigma_{x'}​=40+45.31=40+45.31​=85.31=85.31 MPa.

σx′=−45.3\sigma_{x'}=-45.3 MPa,   τx′y′=43.1\;\tau_{x'y'}=43.1 MPa,   σy′=85.3\;\sigma_{y'}=85.3 MPa

Check (analytical): σx′\sigma_{x'}​=20−70cos⁡60∘−35sin⁡60∘=20-70\cos60^{\circ}-35\sin60^{\circ}​=−45.31=-45.31; τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=70sin⁡60∘−35cos⁡60∘=70\sin60^{\circ}-35\cos60^{\circ}​=43.12=43.12 MPa. Agrees with the Q&A model answer 9.

U4-Q050Q050 | L3 Apply | P1 | N | 6 marks

A thin cylindrical shell has an internal diameter of 1.2 m and a wall thickness of 12 mm. It carries an internal pressure of 1.5 MPa. Find the hoop stress, longitudinal stress and maximum in-plane shear stress.

Solution

Given. D=1.2D=1.2 m =1200=1200 mm, t=12t=12 mm, p=1.5p=1.5 MPa (=1.5=1.5 N/mm2^2).

To find. σh\sigma_h, σL\sigma_L, τmax\tau_{max} (in-plane).

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin-walled (t/rt/r​=12/600=12/600​=0.02=0.02​≤0.1\le0.1); internal diameter used; stresses tensile; radial stress neglected.

Formula. σh=pD2t\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t},   σL=pD4t\;\sigma_L=\dfrac{pD}{4t}, τin−plane\tau_{in-plane}​=σh−σL2=\dfrac{\sigma_h-\sigma_L}{2}.

Solution.

  1. σh\sigma_h​=1.5(1200)2(12)=\dfrac{1.5(1200)}{2(12)}​=180024=\dfrac{1800}{24}​=75=75 MPa.
  2. σL\sigma_L​=1.5(1200)4(12)=\dfrac{1.5(1200)}{4(12)}​=37.5=37.5 MPa.
  3. τin−plane\tau_{in-plane}​=75−37.52=\dfrac{75-37.5}{2}​=18.75=18.75 MPa (on planes at 45∘45^{\circ} in the plane of the wall).
  4. Remark: including the zero radial stress, the absolute maximum shear is σh/2=37.5\sigma_h/2=37.5 MPa on planes at 45∘45^{\circ} to the hoop and radial directions.

σh=75\sigma_h=75 MPa,   σL=37.5\;\sigma_L=37.5 MPa, τmax,in−plane\tau_{max,in-plane}​=18.75=18.75 MPa (absolute: 37.5 MPa)

Agrees with the Q&A model answer 10.

U4-Q051Q051 | L3 Apply | P1 | N | 6 marks

A thin spherical shell of diameter 2 m and thickness 10 mm is subjected to an internal pressure of 2 MPa. Find the stress in the shell and the maximum permissible pressure if σallow=120\sigma_{allow}=120 MPa.

Solution

Given. D=2D=2 m =2000=2000 mm, t=10t=10 mm, p=2p=2 MPa; σallow=120\sigma_{allow}=120 MPa.

To find. (a) stress σ\sigma in the shell; (b) pmaxp_{max}.

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin shell (t/rt/r​=10/1000=10/1000​=0.01=0.01); internal diameter; the stress is tensile and the same in every direction in the wall.

Formula. σ=pD4t\sigma=\dfrac{pD}{4t}, so pmaxp_{max}​=4t σallowD=\dfrac{4t\,\sigma_{allow}}{D}.

Solution.

  1. σ\sigma​=2(2000)4(10)=\dfrac{2(2000)}{4(10)}​=400040=\dfrac{4000}{40}​=100=100 MPa.
  2. pmaxp_{max}​=4(10)(120)2000=\dfrac{4(10)(120)}{2000}​=48002000=\dfrac{4800}{2000}​=2.4=2.4 MPa.
  3. Check: σ\sigma at 2.42.4 MPa is 2.4(2000)/402.4(2000)/40​=120=120 MPa ✓.

σ=100\sigma=100 MPa (tension, all directions);   pmax=2.4\;p_{max}=2.4 MPa

Remark: absolute maximum shear in the wall is σ/2=50\sigma/2=50 MPa (using the zero radial stress at the free surface).

U4-Q052Q052 | L3 Apply | P1 | N | 8 marks

A thin cylinder (D=600D=600 mm, t=8t=8 mm, L=3L=3 m) is subjected to p=2.4p=2.4 MPa. Taking E=200E=200 GPa and ν=0.3\nu=0.3, find the changes in diameter, length and volume.

Solution

Given. D=600D=600 mm, t=8t=8 mm, L=3000L=3000 mm, p=2.4p=2.4 MPa, E=200 000E=200\,000 MPa, ν=0.3\nu=0.3.

To find. ΔD\Delta D, ΔL\Delta L, ΔV\Delta V.

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin-walled, closed ends; internal diameter; tension positive; radial stress neglected; Hooke's law for biaxial stress.

Formula. σh=pD2t\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t}, σL=pD4t\sigma_L=\dfrac{pD}{4t}, εh=σh−νσLE\varepsilon_h=\dfrac{\sigma_h-\nu\sigma_L}{E}, εL=σL−νσhE\varepsilon_L=\dfrac{\sigma_L-\nu\sigma_h}{E}, ΔD=εhD\Delta D=\varepsilon_hD, ΔL=εLL\Delta L=\varepsilon_LL, ΔVV=2εh+εL\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}=2\varepsilon_h+\varepsilon_L.

Solution.

  1. σh=2.4(600)2(8)=90\sigma_h=\dfrac{2.4(600)}{2(8)}=90 MPa; σL=45\sigma_L=45 MPa.
  2. εh\varepsilon_h​=90−0.3(45)200 000=\dfrac{90-0.3(45)}{200\,000}​=76.5200 000=\dfrac{76.5}{200\,000}​=3.825×10−4=3.825\times10^{-4}.
  3. εL\varepsilon_L​=45−0.3(90)200 000=\dfrac{45-0.3(90)}{200\,000}​=18200 000=\dfrac{18}{200\,000}​=9.0×10−5=9.0\times10^{-5}.
  4. ΔD\Delta D​=3.825×10−4(600)=3.825\times10^{-4}(600)​=0.2295=0.2295 mm.
  5. ΔL\Delta L​=9.0×10−5(3000)=9.0\times10^{-5}(3000)​=0.270=0.270 mm.
  6. ΔVV\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}​=2(3.825×10−4)+9.0×10−5=2(3.825\times10^{-4})+9.0\times10^{-5}​=8.55×10−4=8.55\times10^{-4}.
  7. VV​=π4(600)2(3000)=\dfrac{\pi}{4}(600)^2(3000)​=8.482×108=8.482\times10^{8} mm3^3, so ΔV\Delta V​=8.55×10−4(8.482×108)=8.55\times10^{-4}(8.482\times10^{8})​=7.25×105=7.25\times10^{5} mm3^3.

ΔD=0.230\Delta D=0.230 mm,   ΔL=0.270\;\Delta L=0.270 mm,   ΔV=7.25×105\;\Delta V=7.25\times10^{5} mm3^3 (=725=725 cm3^3, 0.0855 %0.0855\,\% increase)

Check with the sheet formulae: εh\varepsilon_h​=pr2tE(2−ν)=\dfrac{pr}{2tE}(2-\nu)​=2.4(300)2(8)(200 000)(1.7)=\dfrac{2.4(300)}{2(8)(200\,000)}(1.7)​=3.825×10−4=3.825\times10^{-4} ✓.

U4-Q053Q053 | L3 Apply | P2 | N | 8 marks

A thick cylinder has ri=100r_i=100 mm, ro=200r_o=200 mm and carries an internal pressure of 60 MPa (external pressure zero). Find the hoop and radial stresses at the inner and outer surfaces.

Solution

Given. ri=100r_i=100 mm, ro=200r_o=200 mm, pi=60p_i=60 MPa, po=0p_o=0.

To find. σθ\sigma_\theta and σr\sigma_r at r=rir=r_i and r=ror=r_o.

Assumptions and sign convention. Lamé's theory; tension positive, so σr=−pi\sigma_r=-p_i at the inner surface; plane sections remain plane (closed or free ends not needed for these two stresses).

Formula. σr=A−Br2\sigma_r=A-\dfrac{B}{r^2}, σθ=A+Br2\sigma_\theta=A+\dfrac{B}{r^2}, with A=piri2−poro2ro2−ri2A=\dfrac{p_ir_i^2-p_or_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}, BB​=(pi−po)ri2ro2ro2−ri2=\dfrac{(p_i-p_o)r_i^2r_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}.

Solution.

  1. ri2=104r_i^2=10^4, ro2=4×104r_o^2=4\times10^4 mm2^2; ro2−ri2=3×104r_o^2-r_i^2=3\times10^4 mm2^2.
  2. A=60(104)−03×104=20A=\dfrac{60(10^4)-0}{3\times10^4}=20 MPa.
  3. BB​=60(104)(4×104)3×104=\dfrac{60(10^4)(4\times10^4)}{3\times10^4}​=8×105=8\times10^{5} MPa mm2^2.
  4. Inner surface: σr\sigma_r​=20−8×105104=20-\dfrac{8\times10^5}{10^4}​=20−80=20-80​=−60=-60 MPa ✓ (equals −pi-p_i); σθ=20+80=100\sigma_\theta=20+80=100 MPa.
  5. Outer surface: σr\sigma_r​=20−8×1054×104=20-\dfrac{8\times10^5}{4\times10^4}​=20−20=20-20​=0=0 ✓; σθ=20+20=40\sigma_\theta=20+20=40 MPa.
  6. Check with the direct formula: σθ(ri)\sigma_\theta(r_i)​=piro2+ri2ro2−ri2=p_i\dfrac{r_o^2+r_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}​=6053=60\dfrac{5}{3}​=100=100 MPa ✓; σθ(ro)\sigma_\theta(r_o)​=2piri2ro2−ri2=\dfrac{2p_ir_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}​=40=40 MPa ✓; σr+σθ=2A=40\sigma_r+\sigma_\theta=2A=40 at both surfaces ✓.
Surface σθ\sigma_\theta (MPa) σr\sigma_r (MPa)
Inner (r=100r=100 mm)+100+100−60-60
Outer (r=200r=200 mm)+40+4000

Inner: σθ=100\sigma_\theta=100 MPa, σr=−60\sigma_r=-60 MPa. Outer: σθ=40\sigma_\theta=40 MPa, σr=0\sigma_r=0.

(Thin-wall formula with the inner radius would give 60(100)/100=6060(100)/100=60 MPa, which under-estimates the peak by 40%.)

U4-Q054Q054 | L3 Apply | E1 | N | 6 marks

A steel rod of diameter 25 mm and length 2 m carries an axial tension of 50 kN. Taking E=200E=200 GPa, determine the strain energy stored and the strain-energy density.

Solution

Given. d=25d=25 mm, L=2000L=2000 mm, P=50 000P=50\,000 N, E=200 000E=200\,000 N/mm2^2.

To find. UU and uu.

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic, uniform axial stress, gradually applied load; units N and mm.

Formula. U=P2L2AEU=\dfrac{P^2L}{2AE},   u=σ22E=UV\;u=\dfrac{\sigma^2}{2E}=\dfrac{U}{V}.

Solution.

  1. AA​=π(25)24=\dfrac{\pi(25)^2}{4}​=490.87=490.87 mm2^2; σ=50 000490.87=101.86\sigma=\dfrac{50\,000}{490.87}=101.86 MPa.
  2. UU​=(50 000)2(2000)2(490.87)(200 000)=\dfrac{(50\,000)^2(2000)}{2(490.87)(200\,000)}​=25 465=25\,465 N mm =25.5=25.5 J.
  3. uu​=(101.86)22(200 000)=\dfrac{(101.86)^2}{2(200\,000)}​=0.02594=0.02594 N/mm2^2 =25.9=25.9 kJ/m3^3.
  4. Check: VV​=490.87(2000)=490.87(2000)​=981 748=981\,748 mm3^3, uVuV​=0.02594(981 748)=0.02594(981\,748)​=25 465=25\,465 N mm ✓.

U=25 465U=25\,465 N mm =25.5=25.5 J,   u=0.0259\;u=0.0259 N/mm2=25.9^2=25.9 kJ/m3^3

Agrees with Q&A model answer 11 and with Example C.1 in the notes.

U4-Q055Q055 | L3 Apply | E2 | N | 6 marks

A solid shaft (d=50d=50 mm, L=1.5L=1.5 m, G=80G=80 GPa) transmits a torque of 1.2 kN m. Find the strain energy stored in the shaft.

Solution

Given. d=50d=50 mm, L=1500L=1500 mm, G=80 000G=80\,000 N/mm2^2, T=1.2T=1.2 kN m =1.2×106=1.2\times10^{6} N mm.

To find. Strain energy UU.

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic, uniform torque along the shaft, circular section; units N and mm.

Formula. U=T2L2GJU=\dfrac{T^2L}{2GJ},   J=πd432\;J=\dfrac{\pi d^4}{32}.

Solution.

  1. JJ​=π(50)432=\dfrac{\pi(50)^4}{32}​=6.136×105=6.136\times10^{5} mm4^4.
  2. UU​=(1.2×106)2(1500)2(80 000)(6.136×105)=\dfrac{(1.2\times10^{6})^2(1500)}{2(80\,000)(6.136\times10^{5})}​=2.16×10159.818×1010=\dfrac{2.16\times10^{15}}{9.818\times10^{10}}​=22 002=22\,002 N mm.
  3. U=22.0U=22.0 J.
  4. Check by energy density: τmax\tau_{max}​=TcJ=\dfrac{Tc}{J}​=1.2×106(25)6.136×105=\dfrac{1.2\times10^{6}(25)}{6.136\times10^{5}}​=48.89=48.89 MPa; UV=τmax24G\dfrac{U}{V}=\dfrac{\tau_{max}^2}{4G} and VV​=π4(50)2(1500)=\dfrac{\pi}{4}(50)^2(1500)​=2.945×106=2.945\times10^{6} mm3^3, so UU​=48.8924(80 000)(2.945×106)=\dfrac{48.89^2}{4(80\,000)}(2.945\times10^{6})​=22 002=22\,002 N mm ✓.

U=22 002U=22\,002 N mm ≈22.0\approx22.0 J

Same as Example C.4 in the notes.

U4-Q056Q056 | L3 Apply | E1 | N | 5 marks

A steel has σY=250\sigma_Y=250 MPa and E=200E=200 GPa. Find its modulus of resilience and the elastic energy that 0.002 m3^3 of this steel can absorb up to yield.

Solution

Given. σY=250\sigma_Y=250 MPa, E=200E=200 GPa =200 000=200\,000 MPa, V=0.002V=0.002 m3^3.

To find. uYu_Y and UU.

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic up to yield; uniform stress throughout the volume; stresses in MPa == N/mm2^2 == MJ/m3^3 per unit strain.

Formula. uY=σY22Eu_Y=\dfrac{\sigma_Y^2}{2E},   U=uYV\;U=u_YV.

Solution.

  1. uYu_Y​=25022(200 000)=\dfrac{250^2}{2(200\,000)}​=62 500400 000=\dfrac{62\,500}{400\,000}​=0.15625=0.15625 N/mm2^2.
  2. Since 1 N/mm2=106^2=10^{6} J/m3^3, uY=0.15625×106u_Y=0.15625\times10^{6} J/m3=156.25^3=156.25 kJ/m3^3.
  3. UU​=156 250×0.002=156\,250\times0.002​=312.5=312.5 J.

uY=0.156u_Y=0.156 MJ/m3^3 (156.25(156.25 kJ/m3)^3),   U=312.5\;U=312.5 J

Same as Example C.5 in the notes.

U4-Q057Q057 | L3 Apply | E1 | N | 6 marks

A cantilever of length 1.5 m with flexural rigidity EI=3.4×1011EI=3.4\times10^{11} N mm2^2 carries a 2 kN load at the free end. Find the strain energy stored and the deflection under the load using the energy principle.

Solution

Given. L=1.5L=1.5 m =1500=1500 mm, EI=3.4×1011EI=3.4\times10^{11} N mm2^2, P=2P=2 kN =2000=2000 N at the free end.

To find. UU and the deflection δ\delta under the load.

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic; bending energy only (shear energy neglected); single load, so 12Pδ=U\tfrac12P\delta=U gives the deflection at the load, in its direction.

Formula. M=−PxM=-Px, UU​=∫0LM22EIdx=\displaystyle\int_0^L\dfrac{M^2}{2EI}dx​=P2L36EI=\dfrac{P^2L^3}{6EI};   δ=2UP\;\delta=\dfrac{2U}{P}.

Solution.

  1. UU​=(2000)2(1500)36(3.4×1011)=\dfrac{(2000)^2(1500)^3}{6(3.4\times10^{11})}​=4×106×3.375×1092.04×1012=\dfrac{4\times10^{6}\times3.375\times10^{9}}{2.04\times10^{12}}​=1.35×10162.04×1012=\dfrac{1.35\times10^{16}}{2.04\times10^{12}}​=6617.6=6617.6 N mm.
  2. U=6.62U=6.62 J.
  3. δ\delta​=2UP=\dfrac{2U}{P}​=2(6617.6)2000=\dfrac{2(6617.6)}{2000}​=6.618=6.618 mm (downward, in the direction of PP).
  4. Check with the standard result: PL33EI\dfrac{PL^3}{3EI}​=2000(3.375×109)3(3.4×1011)=\dfrac{2000(3.375\times10^{9})}{3(3.4\times10^{11})}​=6.618=6.618 mm ✓.

U=6618U=6618 N mm ≈6.62\approx6.62 J,   δ=6.62\;\delta=6.62 mm

U4-Q058Q058 | L3 Apply | E1 | N | 7 marks

A rod consists of two portions of equal length 0.5 m. Portion 1 has a diameter of 20 mm and portion 2 has a diameter of 40 mm (E=200E=200 GPa). Find the strain energy stored when an axial load of 30 kN is applied.

Solution

Given. L1=L2=500L_1=L_2=500 mm; d1=20d_1=20 mm, d2=40d_2=40 mm; E=200 000E=200\,000 N/mm2^2; P=30 000P=30\,000 N.

To find. Total strain energy UU.

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic; the same axial force PP in both portions; stress concentration at the step neglected; units N and mm.

Formula. U=∑P2Li2AiEU=\displaystyle\sum\dfrac{P^2L_i}{2A_iE}.

Solution.

  1. A1A_1​=π(20)24=\dfrac{\pi(20)^2}{4}​=314.16=314.16 mm2^2; A2A_2​=π(40)24=\dfrac{\pi(40)^2}{4}​=1256.64=1256.64 mm2^2 (four times A1A_1).
  2. U1U_1​=(30 000)2(500)2(314.16)(200 000)=\dfrac{(30\,000)^2(500)}{2(314.16)(200\,000)}​=4.5×10111.2566×108=\dfrac{4.5\times10^{11}}{1.2566\times10^{8}}​=3581.0=3581.0 N mm.
  3. U2U_2​=(30 000)2(500)2(1256.64)(200 000)=\dfrac{(30\,000)^2(500)}{2(1256.64)(200\,000)}​=895.2=895.2 N mm.
  4. UU​=U1+U2=U_1+U_2​=3581.0+895.2=3581.0+895.2​=4476.2=4476.2 N mm.
  5. Check: stresses are 95.4995.49 MPa and 23.8723.87 MPa; u1V1+u2V2u_1V_1+u_2V_2 with u=σ2/2Eu=\sigma^2/2E gives the same total.

U=4476U=4476 N mm ≈4.48\approx4.48 J (portion 1 stores 80%80\% of it)

Remark: the thick portion has 4 times the area, so it stores only 14\tfrac14 of the energy of an equal length of the thin portion (Q038).

U4-Q059Q059 | L3 Apply | P1 | N | 7 marks

Find the required thickness of a cylindrical boiler shell of 1.5 m diameter subjected to 1.2 MPa if σallow=90\sigma_{allow}=90 MPa, the efficiency of the longitudinal joint is 75% and that of the circumferential joint is 60%.

Solution

Given. D=1500D=1500 mm, p=1.2p=1.2 MPa, σallow=90\sigma_{allow}=90 MPa, ηl=0.75\eta_l=0.75, ηc=0.60\eta_c=0.60.

To find. Required wall thickness tt.

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin shell (to be checked: t/r≪0.1t/r\ll0.1); internal diameter; closed ends; the joint stress is the plate stress divided by the efficiency; stresses tensile.

Formula. Hoop stress resisted by the longitudinal joint: σh=pD2tηl\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t\eta_l}; longitudinal stress resisted by the circumferential joint: σL=pD4tηc\sigma_L=\dfrac{pD}{4t\eta_c}. Use the larger thickness.

Solution.

  1. From hoop stress: tht_h​=pD2σallowηl=\dfrac{pD}{2\sigma_{allow}\eta_l}​=1.2(1500)2(90)(0.75)=\dfrac{1.2(1500)}{2(90)(0.75)}​=1800135=\dfrac{1800}{135}​=13.33=13.33 mm.
  2. From longitudinal stress: tLt_L​=pD4σallowηc=\dfrac{pD}{4\sigma_{allow}\eta_c}​=18004(90)(0.60)=\dfrac{1800}{4(90)(0.60)}​=1800216=\dfrac{1800}{216}​=8.33=8.33 mm.
  3. Governing value: tt​=max⁡(13.33, 8.33)=\max(13.33,\,8.33)​=13.33=13.33 mm.
  4. Thin-wall check: t/rt/r​=13.33/750=13.33/750​=0.018=0.018​<0.1<0.1 ✓.

Required t=13.33t=13.33 mm (hoop stress and longitudinal joint govern); a practical plate would be rounded up (for example 14 mm)

U4-Q060Q060 | L3 Apply | T2 | N | 6 marks

A point in a shaft is in pure shear τxy=50\tau_{xy}=50 MPa. Determine the principal stresses and planes, and the stresses on a plane 22.5∘22.5^{\circ} counter-clockwise from the xx axis.

Solution

Given. σx=σy=0\sigma_x=\sigma_y=0, τxy=50\tau_{xy}=50 MPa; second plane θ=22.5∘\theta=22.5^{\circ} counter-clockwise.

To find. σ1,σ2,θp\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\theta_p; σx′,σy′,τx′y′\sigma_{x'},\sigma_{y'},\tau_{x'y'} at 22.5∘22.5^{\circ}.

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; tension positive; θ\theta counter-clockwise from xx.

Formula. σ1,2=σavg±R\sigma_{1,2}=\sigma_{avg}\pm R; tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2τxyσx−σy=\dfrac{2\tau_{xy}}{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}; σx′=τxysin⁡2θ\sigma_{x'}=\tau_{xy}\sin2\theta, τx′y′=τxycos⁡2θ\tau_{x'y'}=\tau_{xy}\cos2\theta (pure shear).

Solution.

  1. σavg=0\sigma_{avg}=0, R=02+502=50R=\sqrt{0^2+50^2}=50 MPa, so σ1=+50\sigma_1=+50 MPa, σ2=−50\sigma_2=-50 MPa.
  2. tan⁡2θp=1000→∞\tan2\theta_p=\dfrac{100}{0}\to\infty, so 2θp=90∘2\theta_p=90^{\circ} and θp=45∘\theta_p=45^{\circ}: σ1=50\sigma_1=50 MPa on the plane at 45∘45^{\circ}; σ2=−50\sigma_2=-50 MPa on the plane at 135∘135^{\circ}.
  3. At θ=22.5∘\theta=22.5^{\circ}: 2θ=45∘2\theta=45^{\circ}, sin⁡45∘\sin45^{\circ}​=cos⁡45∘=\cos45^{\circ}​=0.7071=0.7071.
  4. σx′\sigma_{x'}​=0+0+50(0.7071)=0+0+50(0.7071)​=35.36=35.36 MPa.
  5. σy′=−35.36\sigma_{y'}=-35.36 MPa.
  6. τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=0+50(0.7071)=0+50(0.7071)​=35.36=35.36 MPa.
  7. Check: σx′+σy′\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'}​=0=0​=σx+σy=\sigma_x+\sigma_y ✓; σx′2+τx′y′2\sigma_{x'}^2+\tau_{x'y'}^2​=2(35.36)2=2(35.36)^2​=2500=2500​=R2=R^2 ✓ (the point lies on the circle of radius 50).

σ1=+50\sigma_1=+50 MPa at 45∘45^{\circ},   σ2=−50\;\sigma_2=-50 MPa at 135∘135^{\circ}; at 22.5∘22.5^{\circ}: σx′=35.4\sigma_{x'}=35.4 MPa, σy′=−35.4\sigma_{y'}=-35.4 MPa, τx′y′=35.4\tau_{x'y'}=35.4 MPa

Level 4: Analyze (Q061 to Q080)

Cognitive focus: breaking problems into parts, deriving relationships, multi-step analysis and comparison. The answers show the reasoning at each step and check the result a second way.

U4-Q061Q061 | L4 Analyze | T1 | D | 8 marks

Derive the stress-transformation equations for σx′\sigma_{x'} and τx′y′\tau_{x'y'} by considering equilibrium of a wedge-shaped element, and show that σx′+σy′=σx+σy\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'}=\sigma_x+\sigma_y.

Solution

Definition and aim. For a plane-stress element with σx,σy,τxy\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\tau_{xy}, find the normal stress σx′\sigma_{x'} and shear stress τx′y′\tau_{x'y'} on a plane whose outward normal x′x' is turned θ\theta counter-clockwise from xx.

Principle. Cut a wedge so that one face lies on the inclined plane. The wedge is in equilibrium, so the sum of forces along x′x' and along y′y' is zero. Force == stress ×\times face area. Tension positive; τxy=τyx\tau_{xy}=\tau_{yx}.

Derivation. Let the inclined face have area dAdA. Then the face normal to xx has area dAcos⁡θdA\cos\theta and the face normal to yy has area dAsin⁡θdA\sin\theta. The outward normals of these two faces are −x-x and −y-y, so the stress vectors on them are (−σx,−τxy)(-\sigma_x,-\tau_{xy}) and (−τxy,−σy)(-\tau_{xy},-\sigma_y). The unit vectors are x′=(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)x'=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta) and y′=(−sin⁡θ,cos⁡θ)y'=(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta).

  1. Forces along x′x': σx′dA\sigma_{x'}dA​−(σxdAcos⁡θ)cos⁡θ-(\sigma_xdA\cos\theta)\cos\theta​−(τxydAcos⁡θ)sin⁡θ-(\tau_{xy}dA\cos\theta)\sin\theta​−(τxydAsin⁡θ)cos⁡θ-(\tau_{xy}dA\sin\theta)\cos\theta​−(σydAsin⁡θ)sin⁡θ-(\sigma_ydA\sin\theta)\sin\theta​=0=0.
  2. Cancel dAdA: σx′\sigma_{x'}​=σxcos⁡2θ+σysin⁡2θ+2τxysin⁡θcos⁡θ=\sigma_x\cos^2\theta+\sigma_y\sin^2\theta+2\tau_{xy}\sin\theta\cos\theta.
  3. Forces along y′y': τx′y′dA\tau_{x'y'}dA​+(σxsin⁡θ−τxycos⁡θ)dAcos⁡θ+(\sigma_x\sin\theta-\tau_{xy}\cos\theta)dA\cos\theta​+(τxysin⁡θ−σycos⁡θ)dAsin⁡θ+(\tau_{xy}\sin\theta-\sigma_y\cos\theta)dA\sin\theta​=0=0.
  4. Cancel dAdA: τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−(σx−σy)sin⁡θcos⁡θ+τxy(cos⁡2θ−sin⁡2θ)=-(\sigma_x-\sigma_y)\sin\theta\cos\theta+\tau_{xy}(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta).
  5. Use cos⁡2θ=12(1+cos⁡2θ)\cos^2\theta=\tfrac12(1+\cos2\theta), sin⁡2θ=12(1−cos⁡2θ)\sin^2\theta=\tfrac12(1-\cos2\theta), 2sin⁡θcos⁡θ=sin⁡2θ2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\sin2\theta:

σx′\sigma_{x'}​=σx+σy2+σx−σy2cos⁡2θ+τxysin⁡2θ=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}+\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\cos2\theta+\tau_{xy}\sin2\theta

τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−σx−σy2sin⁡2θ+τxycos⁡2θ=-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\sin2\theta+\tau_{xy}\cos2\theta

The invariant. The stress on the plane perpendicular to x′x' is found by replacing θ\theta by θ+90∘\theta+90^{\circ}, which changes the sign of cos⁡2θ\cos2\theta and sin⁡2θ\sin2\theta:

σy′\sigma_{y'}​=σx+σy2−σx−σy2cos⁡2θ−τxysin⁡2θ=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\cos2\theta-\tau_{xy}\sin2\theta

Adding: σx′+σy′=σx+σy\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'}=\sigma_x+\sigma_y (the cos⁡2θ\cos2\theta and sin⁡2θ\sin2\theta terms cancel).

Conclusion. Equilibrium of the wedge gives the two transformation equations, and adding the normal stresses on two perpendicular planes gives the invariant σx+σy\sigma_x+\sigma_y.

U4-Q062Q062 | L4 Analyze | T2 | D | 6 marks

Derive the expressions for the orientation of the principal planes and for the principal stresses, and prove that the shear stress on the principal planes is zero.

Solution

Definition. Principal planes carry the maximum and minimum normal stresses; those stresses are σ1\sigma_1 and σ2\sigma_2.

Principle. Normal stress is extreme where dσx′/dθ=0d\sigma_{x'}/d\theta=0.

Derivation.

  1. Start from σx′\sigma_{x'}​=σx+σy2+σx−σy2cos⁡2θ+τxysin⁡2θ=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}+\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\cos2\theta+\tau_{xy}\sin2\theta.
