  2. Differentiate: dσx′dθ\dfrac{d\sigma_{x'}}{d\theta}​=−(σx−σy)sin⁡2θ+2τxycos⁡2θ=-(\sigma_x-\sigma_y)\sin2\theta+2\tau_{xy}\cos2\theta​=0=0.
  3. Hence tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2τxyσx−σy=\dfrac{2\tau_{xy}}{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}. It has two roots 2θp2\theta_p and 2θp+180∘2\theta_p+180^{\circ}, so two planes 90∘90^{\circ} apart.
  4. From the triangle with sides σx−σy2\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2} and τxy\tau_{xy}, hypotenuse RR​=(σx−σy2)2+τxy2=\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^2+\tau_{xy}^2}: cos⁡2θp\cos2\theta_p​=±(σx−σy)/2R=\pm\dfrac{(\sigma_x-\sigma_y)/2}{R}, sin⁡2θp=±τxyR\sin2\theta_p=\pm\dfrac{\tau_{xy}}{R} (same sign).
  5. Put these in σx′\sigma_{x'}: σ\sigma​=σx+σy2±1R[(σx−σy2)2+τxy2]=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}\pm\dfrac{1}{R}\left[\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^2+\tau_{xy}^2\right]​=σx+σy2±R=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}\pm R.

σ1,2\sigma_{1,2}​=σx+σy2±(σx−σy2)2+τxy2=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}\pm\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^2+\tau_{xy}^2}, tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2τxyσx−σy=\dfrac{2\tau_{xy}}{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}

Shear is zero on principal planes. Compare step 2 with τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−σx−σy2sin⁡2θ+τxycos⁡2θ=-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\sin2\theta+\tau_{xy}\cos2\theta: dσx′dθ=2τx′y′\dfrac{d\sigma_{x'}}{d\theta}=2\tau_{x'y'}. So the condition for a principal plane, dσx′/dθ=0d\sigma_{x'}/d\theta=0, is exactly τx′y′=0\tau_{x'y'}=0. Direct check: with tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2τxy/(σx−σy)=2\tau_{xy}/(\sigma_x-\sigma_y), τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=cos⁡2θp[−σx−σy2tan⁡2θp+τxy]=\cos2\theta_p\left[-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\tan2\theta_p+\tau_{xy}\right]​=cos⁡2θp[−τxy+τxy]=\cos2\theta_p[-\tau_{xy}+\tau_{xy}]​=0=0.

Conclusion. The principal angles satisfy tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2τxy/(σx−σy)=2\tau_{xy}/(\sigma_x-\sigma_y), the principal stresses are σavg±R\sigma_{avg}\pm R, and the shear vanishes on both planes because dσx′/dθ=2τx′y′d\sigma_{x'}/d\theta=2\tau_{x'y'}.

U4-Q063Q063 | L4 Analyze | T2 | N | 8 marks

For σx=100\sigma_x=100 MPa, σy=−20\sigma_y=-20 MPa, τxy=−48\tau_{xy}=-48 MPa find the principal stresses and the maximum shear stress, then verify that σx′+σy′\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'} is invariant at θ=35∘\theta=35^{\circ} and that σx′\sigma_{x'} at that angle lies between σ2\sigma_2 and σ1\sigma_1.

Solution

Given. σx=100\sigma_x=100, σy=−20\sigma_y=-20, τxy=−48\tau_{xy}=-48 MPa; θ=35∘\theta=35^{\circ} counter-clockwise.

To find. σ1,σ2,τmax\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\tau_{max}; σx′,σy′\sigma_{x'},\sigma_{y'} at 35∘35^{\circ} and the checks.

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; tension positive; θ\theta counter-clockwise from xx.

Formula. σ1,2=σavg±R\sigma_{1,2}=\sigma_{avg}\pm R, tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2τxyσx−σy=\dfrac{2\tau_{xy}}{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}, transformation equations.

Solution.

  1. σavg=100−202=40\sigma_{avg}=\dfrac{100-20}{2}=40 MPa; σx−σy2=60\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}=60 MPa.
  2. RR​=602+482=\sqrt{60^2+48^2}​=76.84=76.84 MPa.
  3. σ1\sigma_1​=40+76.84=40+76.84​=116.84=116.84 MPa; σ2\sigma_2​=40−76.84=40-76.84​=−36.84=-36.84 MPa; τmax=R=76.84\tau_{max}=R=76.84 MPa.
  4. tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2(−48)120=\dfrac{2(-48)}{120}​=−0.8=-0.8​⇒2θp\Rightarrow2\theta_p​=−38.66∘=-38.66^{\circ}, θp=−19.33∘\theta_p=-19.33^{\circ} (for σ1\sigma_1, as confirmed below) and 70.67∘70.67^{\circ} for σ2\sigma_2.
  5. At θ=35∘\theta=35^{\circ}, 2θ=70∘2\theta=70^{\circ}: cos⁡70∘=0.3420\cos70^{\circ}=0.3420, sin⁡70∘=0.9397\sin70^{\circ}=0.9397.
  6. σx′\sigma_{x'}​=40=40​+60(0.3420)+60(0.3420)​+(−48)(0.9397)+(-48)(0.9397)​=40+20.52−45.11=40+20.52-45.11​=15.42=15.42 MPa.
  7. σy′\sigma_{y'}​=40−20.52+45.11=40-20.52+45.11​=64.58=64.58 MPa.
  8. Invariance: σx′+σy′\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'}​=15.42+64.58=15.42+64.58​=80.00=80.00​=σx+σy=\sigma_x+\sigma_y​=100−20=100-20​=80=80 MPa ✓.
  9. Between the principal values: −36.84-36.84​<15.42<15.42​<116.84<116.84 ✓ (and also 64.5864.58).
  10. Extra check: σx′\sigma_{x'} at θp=−19.33∘\theta_p=-19.33^{\circ} is 116.84116.84 MPa with τ=0\tau=0, confirming the plane for σ1\sigma_1.

σ1=116.8\sigma_1=116.8 MPa, σ2=−36.8\sigma_2=-36.8 MPa, τmax=76.8\tau_{max}=76.8 MPa; at 35∘35^{\circ}: σx′=15.4\sigma_{x'}=15.4 MPa, σy′=64.6\sigma_{y'}=64.6 MPa, sum =80=80 MPa ✓

U4-Q064Q064 | L4 Analyze | T1 | N | 8 marks

At a point the principal stresses are σ1=80\sigma_1=80 MPa and σ2=−40\sigma_2=-40 MPa, with the σ1\sigma_1 plane at 25∘25^{\circ} counter-clockwise from the xx axis. Find σx\sigma_x, σy\sigma_y and τxy\tau_{xy} at the point.

Solution

Given. σ1=80\sigma_1=80, σ2=−40\sigma_2=-40 MPa; θp1=25∘\theta_{p1}=25^{\circ} counter-clockwise from xx.

To find. σx,σy,τxy\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\tau_{xy}.

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; tension positive. This is the inverse problem: use the principal element as the starting state and rotate it by −25∘-25^{\circ} back to the xx-yy axes (or use the Mohr's circle relations).

Formula. On the principal axes σx′=σ1\sigma_x'=\sigma_1, σy′=σ2\sigma_y'=\sigma_2, τ=0\tau=0. The original xx axis is at θ=−25∘\theta=-25^{\circ} from the principal axis, so apply the transformation equations with 2θ=−50∘2\theta=-50^{\circ}. Equivalently σx=σavg+Rcos⁡2θp\sigma_x=\sigma_{avg}+R\cos2\theta_p, σy=σavg−Rcos⁡2θp\sigma_y=\sigma_{avg}-R\cos2\theta_p, τxy=Rsin⁡2θp\tau_{xy}=R\sin2\theta_p.

Solution.

  1. σavg\sigma_{avg}​=80+(−40)2=\dfrac{80+(-40)}{2}​=20=20 MPa; R=80−(−40)2=60R=\dfrac{80-(-40)}{2}=60 MPa.
  2. 2θp=50∘2\theta_p=50^{\circ}: cos⁡50∘=0.6428\cos50^{\circ}=0.6428, sin⁡50∘=0.7660\sin50^{\circ}=0.7660.
  3. σx\sigma_x​=20+60(0.6428)=20+60(0.6428)​=20+38.57=20+38.57​=58.57=58.57 MPa.
  4. σy\sigma_y​=20−38.57=20-38.57​=−18.57=-18.57 MPa.
  5. τxy\tau_{xy}​=60(0.7660)=60(0.7660)​=45.96=45.96 MPa.
  6. Check: σx+σy=40=σ1+σ2\sigma_x+\sigma_y=40=\sigma_1+\sigma_2 ✓. tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2(45.96)58.57+18.57=\dfrac{2(45.96)}{58.57+18.57}​=91.9277.14=\dfrac{91.92}{77.14}​=1.1918=1.1918​=tan⁡50∘=\tan50^{\circ} ✓. And σx′\sigma_{x'} at 25∘25^{\circ} is 2020​+38.57(0.6428)+38.57(0.6428)​+45.96(0.7660)+45.96(0.7660)​=80.0=80.0 MPa ✓ with τx′y′=0\tau_{x'y'}=0.

σx=58.6\sigma_x=58.6 MPa,   σy=−18.6\;\sigma_y=-18.6 MPa,   τxy=46.0\;\tau_{xy}=46.0 MPa

U4-Q065Q065 | L4 Analyze | T2 | N | 7 marks

At a point σx=50\sigma_x=50 MPa (tension) and σy=−10\sigma_y=-10 MPa (compression), the shear stress is unknown and the largest principal stress is 70 MPa. Find ∣τxy∣|\tau_{xy}| and the other principal stress.

Solution

Given. σx=50\sigma_x=50, σy=−10\sigma_y=-10 MPa; σ1=70\sigma_1=70 MPa; τxy\tau_{xy} unknown.

To find. ∣τxy∣|\tau_{xy}| and σ2\sigma_2.

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; tension positive; σ1\sigma_1 is the larger principal stress.

Formula. σ1=σavg+R\sigma_1=\sigma_{avg}+R, RR​=(σx−σy2)2+τxy2=\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^2+\tau_{xy}^2},   σ1+σ2=σx+σy\;\sigma_1+\sigma_2=\sigma_x+\sigma_y.

Solution.

  1. σavg=50−102=20\sigma_{avg}=\dfrac{50-10}{2}=20 MPa; σx−σy2=30\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}=30 MPa.
  2. RR​=σ1−σavg=\sigma_1-\sigma_{avg}​=70−20=70-20​=50=50 MPa.
  3. τxy2\tau_{xy}^2​=R2−302=R^2-30^2​=2500−900=2500-900​=1600=1600, so ∣τxy∣=40|\tau_{xy}|=40 MPa.
  4. σ2\sigma_2​=σavg−R=\sigma_{avg}-R​=20−50=20-50​=−30=-30 MPa (check by the invariant: 70+(−30)70+(-30)​=40=40​=50−10=50-10 ✓).
  5. Check: R=302+402=50R=\sqrt{30^2+40^2}=50 MPa ✓.

∣τxy∣=40|\tau_{xy}|=40 MPa,   σ2=−30\;\sigma_2=-30 MPa (the sign of τxy\tau_{xy} cannot be found from the data given)

U4-Q066Q066 | L4 Analyze | T2 | N | 8 marks

A solid shaft of diameter 40 mm is subjected to an axial tensile force of 30 kN and a torque of 500 N m. Find the principal stresses and the maximum shear stress at a point on the surface.

Solution

Given. d=40d=40 mm, P=30P=30 kN =30 000=30\,000 N, T=500T=500 N m =5×105=5\times10^{5} N mm.

To find. σ1,σ2\sigma_1,\sigma_2 and τmax\tau_{max} at a surface point.

Assumptions and sign convention. Axial stress is uniform (tension positive). Torsion gives the largest shear τ=Tc/J\tau=Tc/J at the surface. Take the shaft axis as xx: σx=P/A\sigma_x=P/A, σy=0\sigma_y=0, τxy=±τ\tau_{xy}=\pm\tau (the sign follows the torque direction and does not change the magnitudes of the principal stresses; +τ+\tau is used for the angle). Units N, mm.

Formula. σx=PA\sigma_x=\dfrac{P}{A}, τ=TcJ\tau=\dfrac{Tc}{J}, J=πd432J=\dfrac{\pi d^4}{32}, then σ1,2\sigma_{1,2}​=σx2±(σx2)2+τ2=\dfrac{\sigma_x}{2}\pm\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x}{2}\right)^2+\tau^2}.

Solution.

  1. AA​=π(40)24=\dfrac{\pi(40)^2}{4}​=1256.6=1256.6 mm2^2; σx=30 0001256.6=23.87\sigma_x=\dfrac{30\,000}{1256.6}=23.87 MPa.
  2. JJ​=π(40)432=\dfrac{\pi(40)^4}{32}​=2.513×105=2.513\times10^{5} mm4^4; τ\tau​=5×105(20)2.513×105=\dfrac{5\times10^{5}(20)}{2.513\times10^{5}}​=39.79=39.79 MPa.
  3. σavg\sigma_{avg}​=23.872=\dfrac{23.87}{2}​=11.94=11.94 MPa.
  4. RR​=11.942+39.792=\sqrt{11.94^2+39.79^2}​=142.5+1583.2=\sqrt{142.5+1583.2}​=41.54=41.54 MPa.
  5. σ1\sigma_1​=11.94+41.54=11.94+41.54​=53.48=53.48 MPa; σ2\sigma_2​=11.94−41.54=11.94-41.54​=−29.60=-29.60 MPa.
  6. τmax,in−plane\tau_{max,in-plane}​=R=R​=41.54=41.54 MPa. Because σ1\sigma_1 and σ2\sigma_2 have opposite signs, this is also the absolute maximum shear.
  7. Angle: tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2(39.79)23.87=\dfrac{2(39.79)}{23.87}​=3.334=3.334​⇒θp\Rightarrow\theta_p​=36.65∘=36.65^{\circ} from the axis (for σ1\sigma_1, with τxy=+39.79\tau_{xy}=+39.79 MPa). Check: σ1+σ2=23.87=σx\sigma_1+\sigma_2=23.87=\sigma_x ✓.

σ1=53.5\sigma_1=53.5 MPa,   σ2=−29.6\;\sigma_2=-29.6 MPa,   τmax=41.5\;\tau_{max}=41.5 MPa

U4-Q067Q067 | L4 Analyze | T3 | N | 8 marks

Construct Mohr's circle for σx=40\sigma_x=40 MPa, σy=−60\sigma_y=-60 MPa, τxy=30\tau_{xy}=30 MPa. Determine the principal stresses, the maximum shear stress and the stresses on a plane 35∘35^{\circ} counter-clockwise from the xx axis, and verify one result analytically.

Solution

Given. σx=40\sigma_x=40, σy=−60\sigma_y=-60, τxy=30\tau_{xy}=30 MPa; θ=35∘\theta=35^{\circ} CCW (2θ=70∘2\theta=70^{\circ}).

To find. σ1,σ2,τmax\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\tau_{max}; σx′,σy′,τx′y′\sigma_{x'},\sigma_{y'},\tau_{x'y'} at 35∘35^{\circ}.

Assumptions and sign convention. Tension positive; σ\sigma plotted to the right and clockwise-turning shear upward, so X=(σx,−τxy)X=(\sigma_x,-\tau_{xy}), Y=(σy,+τxy)Y=(\sigma_y,+\tau_{xy}); the diameter turns 2θ2\theta in the same sense as the element.

Solution (Mohr's circle).

  1. X=(40,−30)X=(40,-30), Y=(−60,+30)Y=(-60,+30).
  2. C=40−602=−10C=\dfrac{40-60}{2}=-10 MPa.
  3. RR​=502+302=\sqrt{50^2+30^2}​=58.31=58.31 MPa.
  4. σ1\sigma_1​=−10+58.31=-10+58.31​=48.31=48.31 MPa; σ2\sigma_2​=−10−58.31=-10-58.31​=−68.31=-68.31 MPa; τmax=R=58.31\tau_{max}=R=58.31 MPa (with σ′=−10\sigma'=-10 MPa on the planes of maximum shear).
  5. CXCX is 5050 right and 3030 below CC: it makes −30.96∘-30.96^{\circ} with the σ\sigma axis. Turning to AA (σ1\sigma_1) is 30.96∘30.96^{\circ} counter-clockwise, so θp=15.48∘\theta_p=15.48^{\circ} CCW for σ1\sigma_1.
  6. Turn XYXY by 70∘70^{\circ} CCW: X′X' is at −30.96∘+70∘-30.96^{\circ}+70^{\circ}​=39.04∘=39.04^{\circ} from the σ\sigma axis.
  7. σx′\sigma_{x'}​=−10+58.31cos⁡39.04∘=-10+58.31\cos39.04^{\circ}​=−10+45.29=-10+45.29​=35.29=35.29 MPa.
  8. The ordinate of X′X' is 58.31sin⁡39.04∘58.31\sin39.04^{\circ}​=36.72=36.72 MPa, equal to −τx′y′-\tau_{x'y'}, so τx′y′=−36.72\tau_{x'y'}=-36.72 MPa.
  9. σy′\sigma_{y'}​=2C−σx′=2C-\sigma_{x'}​=−20−35.29=-20-35.29​=−55.29=-55.29 MPa.

Analytical verification. σx′\sigma_{x'}​=−10+50cos⁡70∘+30sin⁡70∘=-10+50\cos70^{\circ}+30\sin70^{\circ}​=−10+17.10+28.19=-10+17.10+28.19​=35.29=35.29 MPa ✓; τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−50sin⁡70∘+30cos⁡70∘=-50\sin70^{\circ}+30\cos70^{\circ}​=−46.98+10.26=-46.98+10.26​=−36.72=-36.72 MPa ✓.

σ1=48.3\sigma_1=48.3 MPa (at 15.5∘15.5^{\circ}), σ2=−68.3\sigma_2=-68.3 MPa, τmax=58.3\tau_{max}=58.3 MPa; at 35∘35^{\circ}: σx′=35.3\sigma_{x'}=35.3, σy′=−55.3\sigma_{y'}=-55.3, τx′y′=−36.7\tau_{x'y'}=-36.7 MPa

U4-Q068Q068 | L4 Analyze | T3 | N | 7 marks

A shaft is in pure torsion with τ=70\tau=70 MPa. Using Mohr's circle, determine the principal stresses and the stresses on a plane rotated 30∘30^{\circ} counter-clockwise, and infer which planes govern failure of a brittle and of a ductile material.

Solution

Given. σx=σy=0\sigma_x=\sigma_y=0, τxy=70\tau_{xy}=70 MPa; θ=30∘\theta=30^{\circ} CCW (2θ=60∘2\theta=60^{\circ}).

To find. σ1,σ2\sigma_1,\sigma_2; σx′,σy′,τx′y′\sigma_{x'},\sigma_{y'},\tau_{x'y'} at 30∘30^{\circ}; failure planes.

Assumptions and sign convention. Tension positive; Mohr's circle with X=(0,−70)X=(0,-70), Y=(0,+70)Y=(0,+70); angle on circle is twice the element angle.

Solution.

  1. Centre C=0C=0; radius R=70R=70 MPa. The circle is centred on the origin.
  2. A=(70,0)A=(70,0) and B=(−70,0)B=(-70,0): σ1=+70\sigma_1=+70 MPa, σ2=−70\sigma_2=-70 MPa. XX is at −90∘-90^{\circ} on the circle and AA at 0∘0^{\circ}, so 2θp=90∘2\theta_p=90^{\circ} and θp=45∘\theta_p=45^{\circ} CCW for σ1\sigma_1.
  3. At 2θ=60∘2\theta=60^{\circ} CCW: X′X' is at −90∘+60∘=−30∘-90^{\circ}+60^{\circ}=-30^{\circ}.
  4. X′X' abscissa σx′\sigma_{x'}​=70cos⁡(−30∘)=70\cos(-30^{\circ})​=60.62=60.62 MPa; ordinate 70sin⁡(−30∘)=−3570\sin(-30^{\circ})=-35 MPa, so τx′y′=+35\tau_{x'y'}=+35 MPa.
  5. σy′=−60.62\sigma_{y'}=-60.62 MPa. Analytical check: σx′\sigma_{x'}​=70sin⁡60∘=70\sin60^{\circ}​=60.62=60.62, τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=70cos⁡60∘=70\cos60^{\circ}​=35=35 MPa ✓.

Failure planes. - Brittle (chalk, cast iron). Weak in tension, so it fails on the plane of maximum tensile stress σ1=70\sigma_1=70 MPa, at 45∘45^{\circ} to the axis (helical fracture). - Ductile (mild steel). Fails by shear, on the plane of maximum shear τmax=70\tau_{max}=70 MPa, which is the cross-section (and the longitudinal plane): the shaft shears across.

σ1=70\sigma_1=70 MPa at 45∘45^{\circ}, σ2=−70\sigma_2=-70 MPa; at 30∘30^{\circ}: σx′=60.6\sigma_{x'}=60.6 MPa, σy′=−60.6\sigma_{y'}=-60.6 MPa, τx′y′=35\tau_{x'y'}=35 MPa

U4-Q069Q069 | L4 Analyze | T3 | N | 7 marks

The point X(σx,−τxy)X(\sigma_x,-\tau_{xy}) on a Mohr's circle is (65,−30)(65,-30) MPa and the centre is at 25 MPa. Determine σy\sigma_y, τxy\tau_{xy}, the radius, the principal stresses and the maximum shear stress.

Solution

Given. X=(65,−30)X=(65,-30) MPa; centre C=25C=25 MPa.

To find. σy,\sigma_y,​τxy,\tau_{xy},​R,R,​σ1,\sigma_1,​σ2,\sigma_2,​τmax\tau_{max}.

Assumptions and sign convention. XX is plotted as (σx,−τxy)(\sigma_x,-\tau_{xy}), so the ordinate −30-30 means τxy=+30\tau_{xy}=+30 MPa. XX and YY are the ends of a diameter.

Solution.

  1. σx=65\sigma_x=65 MPa and −τxy-\tau_{xy}​=−30=-30​⇒τxy\Rightarrow\tau_{xy}​=+30=+30 MPa.
  2. Centre CC​=σx+σy2=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}​=25=25​⇒σy\Rightarrow\sigma_y​=2(25)−65=2(25)-65​=−15=-15 MPa. So Y=(−15,+30)Y=(-15,+30).
  3. RR​=(65−25)2+302=\sqrt{(65-25)^2+30^2}​=1600+900=\sqrt{1600+900}​=50=50 MPa.
  4. σ1=25+50=75\sigma_1=25+50=75 MPa; σ2=25−50=−25\sigma_2=25-50=-25 MPa.
  5. τmax=R=50\tau_{max}=R=50 MPa.
  6. Checks: σ1+σ2\sigma_1+\sigma_2​=50=50​=σx+σy=\sigma_x+\sigma_y​=65−15=65-15 ✓; tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2(30)65+15=\dfrac{2(30)}{65+15}​=0.75=0.75​⇒θp\Rightarrow\theta_p​=18.43∘=18.43^{\circ} CCW.

σy=−15\sigma_y=-15 MPa,   τxy=30\;\tau_{xy}=30 MPa,   R=50\;R=50 MPa,   σ1=75\;\sigma_1=75 MPa,   σ2=−25\;\sigma_2=-25 MPa,   τmax=50\;\tau_{max}=50 MPa

U4-Q070Q070 | L4 Analyze | T2 | N | 6 marks

The principal stresses at a point in a thin plate are σ1=90\sigma_1=90 MPa and σ2=30\sigma_2=30 MPa (σ3=0\sigma_3=0). Determine the in-plane and absolute maximum shear stresses and explain which governs.

Solution

Given. σ1=90\sigma_1=90, σ2=30\sigma_2=30, σ3=0\sigma_3=0 MPa (free plate surfaces, so σz=0\sigma_z=0).

To find. τin−plane\tau_{in-plane} and τabs\tau_{abs}.

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; tension positive; the three principal stresses are ordered 90>30>090>30>0.

Formula. In-plane: σ1−σ22\dfrac{\sigma_1-\sigma_2}{2}. Absolute: σmax−σmin2\dfrac{\sigma_{max}-\sigma_{min}}{2} over {σ1,σ2,σ3}\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3\}.

Solution.

  1. In-plane: 90−302=30\dfrac{90-30}{2}=30 MPa, on planes 45∘45^{\circ} from the principal planes in the plane of the plate.
  2. The three Mohr circles have diameters 90−30=6090-30=60, 30−0=3030-0=30 and 90−0=9090-0=90 MPa, giving shears 3030, 1515 and 4545 MPa.
  3. Absolute: 90−02=45\dfrac{90-0}{2}=45 MPa, on planes at 45∘45^{\circ} to the σ1\sigma_1 and σ3\sigma_3 axes (out of the plane of the plate).
  4. σ1\sigma_1 and σ2\sigma_2 have the same sign, so the largest circle is the one through σ1\sigma_1 and σ3=0\sigma_3=0.

Which governs. The absolute value, 45 MPa, governs yielding and failure checks. The in-plane value (30 MPa) under-estimates the true maximum shear by 45−3045=33%\dfrac{45-30}{45}=33\%.

τin−plane=30\tau_{in-plane}=30 MPa;   τabs=45\;\tau_{abs}=45 MPa (governs)

Agrees with Q&A model answer 12.

U4-Q071Q071 | L4 Analyze | P1 | N | 8 marks

A thin-walled closed cylinder of mean radius 200 mm and wall thickness 10 mm carries an internal pressure of 3 MPa and is also twisted by a torque of 60 kN m. Find the hoop stress, longitudinal stress, torsional shear stress (τ=T/2πr2t\tau=T/2\pi r^2t) and the resulting principal stresses on the outer surface.

Solution

Given. Mean radius r=200r=200 mm, t=10t=10 mm, p=3p=3 MPa, T=60T=60 kN m =6×107=6\times10^{7} N mm.

To find. σh,σL,τ\sigma_h,\sigma_L,\tau and the principal stresses on the outer surface.

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin wall with mean radius (stated in the question); closed ends so pressure also loads the ends; tension positive; σr≈0\sigma_r\approx0 on the outer surface; take xx along the axis (σx=σL\sigma_x=\sigma_L, σy=σh\sigma_y=\sigma_h) and τxy=+τ\tau_{xy}=+\tau (the sign does not change the principal stresses).

Formula. σh=prt\sigma_h=\dfrac{pr}{t}, σL=pr2t\sigma_L=\dfrac{pr}{2t}, τ=T2πr2t\tau=\dfrac{T}{2\pi r^2t}, σ1,2\sigma_{1,2}​=σh+σL2±(σh−σL2)2+τ2=\dfrac{\sigma_h+\sigma_L}{2}\pm\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_h-\sigma_L}{2}\right)^2+\tau^2}.

Solution.

  1. σh=3(200)10=60\sigma_h=\dfrac{3(200)}{10}=60 MPa.
  2. σL=3(200)2(10)=30\sigma_L=\dfrac{3(200)}{2(10)}=30 MPa.
  3. τ\tau​=6×1072π(200)2(10)=\dfrac{6\times10^{7}}{2\pi(200)^2(10)}​=6×1072.513×106=\dfrac{6\times10^{7}}{2.513\times10^{6}}​=23.87=23.87 MPa.
  4. σavg=60+302=45\sigma_{avg}=\dfrac{60+30}{2}=45 MPa; σh−σL2=15\dfrac{\sigma_h-\sigma_L}{2}=15 MPa.
  5. RR​=152+23.872=\sqrt{15^2+23.87^2}​=225+569.9=\sqrt{225+569.9}​=28.19=28.19 MPa.
  6. σ1\sigma_1​=45+28.19=45+28.19​=73.19=73.19 MPa; σ2\sigma_2​=45−28.19=45-28.19​=16.81=16.81 MPa; σ3≈0\sigma_3\approx0 (radial, free outer surface).
  7. Orientation: with the axis as xx (σx=30\sigma_x=30, σy=60\sigma_y=60 MPa), tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2(23.87)30−60=\dfrac{2(23.87)}{30-60}​=−1.592=-1.592, so 2θp=122.1∘2\theta_p=122.1^{\circ} and θp=61.1∘\theta_p=61.1^{\circ} from the axis for σ1\sigma_1 (σ2\sigma_2 at −28.9∘-28.9^{\circ}); the σ1\sigma_1 direction lies closer to the hoop direction.
  8. In-plane maximum shear =R=28.19=R=28.19 MPa; absolute maximum shear =σ1−σ32=36.60=\dfrac{\sigma_1-\sigma_3}{2}=36.60 MPa.
  9. Check: σ1+σ2=90=σh+σL\sigma_1+\sigma_2=90=\sigma_h+\sigma_L ✓.

σh=60\sigma_h=60 MPa,   σL=30\;\sigma_L=30 MPa,   τ=23.9\;\tau=23.9 MPa;   σ1=73.2\;\sigma_1=73.2 MPa,   σ2=16.8\;\sigma_2=16.8 MPa (absolute τmax=36.6\tau_{max}=36.6 MPa)

U4-Q072Q072 | L4 Analyze | P1 | N | 8 marks

A thin cylinder has a wall thickness of 12 mm and an inner radius of 500 mm. If hemispherical ends are to expand radially by the same amount as the cylinder under internal pressure (ν=0.3\nu=0.3), determine the required thickness of the hemispherical ends.

Solution

Given. tc=12t_c=12 mm, r=500r=500 mm, ν=0.3\nu=0.3, same pp.

To find. Hemispherical end thickness tst_s.

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin walls; same pp, same radius; equal radial expansion, so no bending (discontinuity) stresses at the junction; tension positive.

Formula. Cylinder: σh=prtc\sigma_h=\dfrac{pr}{t_c}, σL=pr2tc\sigma_L=\dfrac{pr}{2t_c}, so the hoop strain is εh\varepsilon_h​=σh−νσLE=\dfrac{\sigma_h-\nu\sigma_L}{E}​=pr2tcE(2−ν)=\dfrac{pr}{2t_cE}(2-\nu). Sphere: σ=pr2ts\sigma=\dfrac{pr}{2t_s}, ε\varepsilon​=(1−ν)σE=\dfrac{(1-\nu)\sigma}{E}​=pr2tsE(1−ν)=\dfrac{pr}{2t_sE}(1-\nu). The radial expansion is rεr\varepsilon in both, so equate the strains.

Solution.

  1. pr2tcE(2−ν)\dfrac{pr}{2t_cE}(2-\nu)​=pr2tsE(1−ν)=\dfrac{pr}{2t_sE}(1-\nu).
  2. tstc\dfrac{t_s}{t_c}​=1−ν2−ν=\dfrac{1-\nu}{2-\nu}​=0.71.7=\dfrac{0.7}{1.7}​=0.4118=0.4118.
  3. tst_s​=0.4118(12)=0.4118(12)​=4.94=4.94 mm.
  4. Check with numbers (p=1p=1 MPa, E=200 000E=200\,000): cylinder εh\varepsilon_h​=1(500)(1.7)2(12)(200 000)=\dfrac{1(500)(1.7)}{2(12)(200\,000)}​=1.771×10−4=1.771\times10^{-4}; sphere ε\varepsilon​=1(500)(0.7)2(4.94)(200 000)=\dfrac{1(500)(0.7)}{2(4.94)(200\,000)}​=1.771×10−4=1.771\times10^{-4} ✓.

ts=4.94t_s=4.94 mm (≈5\approx5 mm), i.e. ts/tct_s/t_c​=1−ν2−ν=\dfrac{1-\nu}{2-\nu}​=0.412=0.412

Flag (course-notes misprint). The lecture notes (B.2.6) write the sphere strain as pr4tsE(1−ν)\dfrac{pr}{4t_sE}(1-\nu) and obtain tstc=1−ν2(2−ν)\dfrac{t_s}{t_c}=\dfrac{1-\nu}{2(2-\nu)}, which would give ts=2.47t_s=2.47 mm. That is inconsistent with the notes' own sphere result (B.8: ε=pr(1−ν)2tE\varepsilon=\dfrac{pr(1-\nu)}{2tE}, from σ=pr2t\sigma=\dfrac{pr}{2t}), which leads to the factor 1−ν2−ν\dfrac{1-\nu}{2-\nu} used here. The verified value is 4.94 mm; the printed formula gives 2.47 mm. Logged in progress.md.

U4-Q073Q073 | L4 Analyze | P1 | N | 7 marks

A strain gauge on the outer surface of a thin cylinder (D=800D=800 mm, t=10t=10 mm, E=200E=200 GPa, ν=0.28\nu=0.28) records a hoop strain of 550 microstrain. Determine the internal pressure, the longitudinal strain and the longitudinal stress.

Solution

Given. D=800D=800 mm, t=10t=10 mm, E=200 000E=200\,000 MPa, ν=0.28\nu=0.28, εh=550×10−6\varepsilon_h=550\times10^{-6}.

To find. pp, εL\varepsilon_L, σL\sigma_L.

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin closed cylinder, internal diameter; σr≈0\sigma_r\approx0; tension positive; Hooke's law for biaxial stress.

Formula. σh=pD2t\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t}, σL=pD4t=σh2\sigma_L=\dfrac{pD}{4t}=\dfrac{\sigma_h}{2}, εh\varepsilon_h​=σh−νσLE=\dfrac{\sigma_h-\nu\sigma_L}{E}​=σhE(1−ν2)=\dfrac{\sigma_h}{E}\left(1-\dfrac{\nu}{2}\right), εL=σL−νσhE\varepsilon_L=\dfrac{\sigma_L-\nu\sigma_h}{E}.

Solution.

  1. σh\sigma_h​=Eεh1−ν/2=\dfrac{E\varepsilon_h}{1-\nu/2}​=200 000(550×10−6)1−0.14=\dfrac{200\,000(550\times10^{-6})}{1-0.14}​=1100.86=\dfrac{110}{0.86}​=127.91=127.91 MPa.
  2. σL\sigma_L​=127.912=\dfrac{127.91}{2}​=63.95=63.95 MPa.
  3. pp​=2tσhD=\dfrac{2t\sigma_h}{D}​=2(10)(127.91)800=\dfrac{2(10)(127.91)}{800}​=3.198=3.198 MPa.
  4. εL\varepsilon_L​=63.95−0.28(127.91)200 000=\dfrac{63.95-0.28(127.91)}{200\,000}​=63.95−35.81200 000=\dfrac{63.95-35.81}{200\,000}​=1.407×10−4=1.407\times10^{-4} (=141=141 microstrain).
  5. Check: εh\varepsilon_h​=127.91−0.28(63.95)200 000=\dfrac{127.91-0.28(63.95)}{200\,000}​=110.0200 000=\dfrac{110.0}{200\,000}​=550×10−6=550\times10^{-6} ✓.

p=3.20p=3.20 MPa,   εL=1.41×10−4\;\varepsilon_L=1.41\times10^{-4} (141 microstrain),   σL=63.9\;\sigma_L=63.9 MPa

U4-Q074Q074 | L4 Analyze | P2 | N | 8 marks

A thick cylinder (ri=80r_i=80 mm, ro=160r_o=160 mm) is subjected to an internal pressure of 40 MPa. Calculate σr\sigma_r and σθ\sigma_\theta at r=80r=80, 120 and 160 mm and verify that σr+σθ\sigma_r+\sigma_\theta is constant through the wall.

Solution

Given. ri=80r_i=80 mm, ro=160r_o=160 mm, pi=40p_i=40 MPa, po=0p_o=0.

To find. σr,σθ\sigma_r,\sigma_\theta at r=80,120,160r=80,120,160 mm; check σr+σθ=2A\sigma_r+\sigma_\theta=2A.

Assumptions and sign convention. Lamé's theory; tension positive (σr=−pi\sigma_r=-p_i at rir_i); the same constants AA and BB for the whole wall.

Formula. σr=A−Br2\sigma_r=A-\dfrac{B}{r^2}, σθ=A+Br2\sigma_\theta=A+\dfrac{B}{r^2}, A=piri2ro2−ri2A=\dfrac{p_ir_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}, B=piri2ro2ro2−ri2B=\dfrac{p_ir_i^2r_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}.

Solution.

  1. ri2=6400r_i^2=6400, ro2=25 600r_o^2=25\,600, ro2−ri2=19 200r_o^2-r_i^2=19\,200 mm2^2.
  2. AA​=40(6400)19 200=\dfrac{40(6400)}{19\,200}​=13.33=13.33 MPa.
  3. BB​=40(6400)(25 600)19 200=\dfrac{40(6400)(25\,600)}{19\,200}​=3.413×105=3.413\times10^{5} MPa mm2^2.
  4. r=80r=80: Br2=53.33\dfrac{B}{r^2}=53.33, so σr\sigma_r​=13.33−53.33=13.33-53.33​=−40.0=-40.0 MPa (equals −pi-p_i ✓); σθ\sigma_\theta​=13.33+53.33=13.33+53.33​=66.67=66.67 MPa.
  5. r=120r=120: Br2\dfrac{B}{r^2}​=3.413×10514 400=\dfrac{3.413\times10^{5}}{14\,400}​=23.70=23.70, so σr=−10.37\sigma_r=-10.37 MPa; σθ=37.04\sigma_\theta=37.04 MPa.
  6. r=160r=160: Br2=13.33\dfrac{B}{r^2}=13.33, so σr=0\sigma_r=0 ✓ (free outer surface); σθ=26.67\sigma_\theta=26.67 MPa.
  7. Sum check: −40+66.67-40+66.67​=26.67=26.67; −10.37+37.04-10.37+37.04​=26.67=26.67; 0+26.67=26.670+26.67=26.67 MPa, all equal to 2A=26.672A=26.67 MPa ✓.
rr (mm) σr\sigma_r (MPa) σθ\sigma_\theta (MPa) sum (MPa)
80−40.0-40.066.766.726.726.7
120−10.4-10.437.037.026.726.7
1600026.726.726.726.7

σθ\sigma_\theta: 66.7, 37.0, 26.7 MPa; σr\sigma_r: −40.0-40.0, −10.4-10.4, 0 MPa; σr+σθ=26.67\sigma_r+\sigma_\theta=26.67 MPa everywhere

U4-Q075Q075 | L4 Analyze | P2 | N | 8 marks

A tube with ri=60r_i=60 mm and ro=120r_o=120 mm is subjected to an external pressure of 30 MPa only. Determine the radial and hoop stresses at the inner and outer surfaces and state where the stress magnitude is greatest.

Solution

Given. ri=60r_i=60 mm, ro=120r_o=120 mm, po=30p_o=30 MPa, pi=0p_i=0.

To find. σr\sigma_r and σθ\sigma_\theta at rir_i and ror_o; location of the greatest magnitude.

Assumptions and sign convention. Lamé's theory; tension positive, so external pressure gives σr=−po\sigma_r=-p_o at ror_o and σr=0\sigma_r=0 at rir_i.

Formula. σr=A−Br2\sigma_r=A-\dfrac{B}{r^2}, σθ=A+Br2\sigma_\theta=A+\dfrac{B}{r^2}, A=piri2−poro2ro2−ri2A=\dfrac{p_ir_i^2-p_or_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}, BB​=(pi−po)ri2ro2ro2−ri2=\dfrac{(p_i-p_o)r_i^2r_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}.

Solution.

  1. ri2=3600r_i^2=3600, ro2=14 400r_o^2=14\,400, ro2−ri2=10 800r_o^2-r_i^2=10\,800 mm2^2.
  2. AA​=0−30(14 400)10 800=\dfrac{0-30(14\,400)}{10\,800}​=−40=-40 MPa.
  3. BB​=(0−30)(3600)(14 400)10 800=\dfrac{(0-30)(3600)(14\,400)}{10\,800}​=−1.44×105=-1.44\times10^{5} MPa mm2^2.
  4. Inner (r=60r=60): Br2=−40\dfrac{B}{r^2}=-40, so σr=−40−(−40)=0\sigma_r=-40-(-40)=0 ✓; σθ\sigma_\theta​=−40+(−40)=-40+(-40)​=−80=-80 MPa.
  5. Outer (r=120r=120): Br2=−10\dfrac{B}{r^2}=-10, so σr=−40+10=−30\sigma_r=-40+10=-30 MPa ✓ (=−po=-p_o); σθ=−40−10=−50\sigma_\theta=-40-10=-50 MPa.
  6. Check with the external-pressure formula: σθ(ri)\sigma_\theta(r_i)​=−2poro2ro2−ri2=-\dfrac{2p_or_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}​=−2(30)(14 400)10 800=-\dfrac{2(30)(14\,400)}{10\,800}​=−80=-80 MPa ✓.
Surface σr\sigma_r (MPa) σθ\sigma_\theta (MPa)
Inner (r=60r=60)00−80-80
Outer (r=120r=120)−30-30−50-50

Where greatest. The magnitude is greatest at the inner surface: the hoop (compressive) stress is 8080 MPa, more than 2.5 times the external pressure. The greatest shear is also there: ∣σθ−σr∣2=40\dfrac{|\sigma_\theta-\sigma_r|}{2}=40 MPa.

Inner: σr=0\sigma_r=0, σθ=−80\sigma_\theta=-80 MPa (greatest). Outer: σr=−30\sigma_r=-30 MPa, σθ=−50\sigma_\theta=-50 MPa.

U4-Q076Q076 | L4 Analyze | P2 | N | 7 marks

A closed-end thick cylinder (ri=100r_i=100 mm, ro=150r_o=150 mm) carries an internal pressure of 50 MPa. Determine the longitudinal stress and the maximum shear stress at the inner surface.

Solution

Given. ri=100r_i=100 mm, ro=150r_o=150 mm, pi=50p_i=50 MPa, po=0p_o=0; closed ends.

To find. σL\sigma_L and τmax\tau_{max} at r=rir=r_i.

Assumptions and sign convention. Lamé's theory; tension positive; closed ends carry the axial pressure force, giving a uniform longitudinal stress; the greatest shear uses the largest and smallest of the three principal stresses (σθ,σL,σr\sigma_\theta,\sigma_L,\sigma_r).

Formula. A=piri2ro2−ri2A=\dfrac{p_ir_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}, B=piri2ro2ro2−ri2B=\dfrac{p_ir_i^2r_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}, σθ=A+Br2\sigma_\theta=A+\dfrac{B}{r^2}, σr=A−Br2\sigma_r=A-\dfrac{B}{r^2}, σL=A\sigma_L=A.

Solution.

  1. ro2−ri2r_o^2-r_i^2​=22 500−10 000=22\,500-10\,000​=12 500=12\,500 mm2^2.
  2. A=50(10 000)12 500=40A=\dfrac{50(10\,000)}{12\,500}=40 MPa; BB​=50(10 000)(22 500)12 500=\dfrac{50(10\,000)(22\,500)}{12\,500}​=9×105=9\times10^{5} MPa mm2^2.
  3. At rir_i: Bri2=90\dfrac{B}{r_i^2}=90, so σθ=40+90=130\sigma_\theta=40+90=130 MPa and σr=40−90=−50\sigma_r=40-90=-50 MPa (=−pi=-p_i ✓).
  4. Longitudinal stress (force balance on the end: piπri2p_i\pi r_i^2​=σLπ(ro2−ri2)=\sigma_L\pi(r_o^2-r_i^2)): σL\sigma_L​=50(10 000)12 500=\dfrac{50(10\,000)}{12\,500}​=40=40 MPa (uniform over the wall, =A=A).
  5. Principal stresses at the inner surface: 130130, 4040, −50-50 MPa. Maximum shear =130−(−50)2=90=\dfrac{130-(-50)}{2}=90 MPa (the other pairs give only 4545 and 2020 MPa).
  6. Check: piro2ro2−ri2\dfrac{p_ir_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}​=50(22 500)12 500=\dfrac{50(22\,500)}{12\,500}​=90=90 MPa ✓.

σL=40\sigma_L=40 MPa,   τmax=90\;\tau_{max}=90 MPa (at the inner surface; σθ=130\sigma_\theta=130, σr=−50\sigma_r=-50 MPa)

Agrees with Q&A model answer 13.

U4-Q077Q077 | L4 Analyze | P2 | N | 8 marks

A cylinder has an inner radius of 100 mm and carries 10 MPa. Compare the maximum hoop stress from the thin-wall formula pri/tpr_i/t with Lamé's value for (a) t=10t=10 mm and (b) t=50t=50 mm, and comment on the percentage errors.

Solution

Given. ri=100r_i=100 mm, pi=10p_i=10 MPa; (a) t=10t=10 mm, ro=110r_o=110 mm; (b) t=50t=50 mm, ro=150r_o=150 mm.

To find. Thin-wall σh\sigma_h and Lamé σθ,max\sigma_{\theta,max} for each, and the percentage error.

Assumptions and sign convention. Internal pressure only; thin formula uses the inner radius (σh=pri/t\sigma_h=pr_i/t); Lamé's maximum hoop stress is at the inner surface; error =σLameˊ−σthinσLameˊ×100=\dfrac{\sigma_{Lam\acute e}-\sigma_{thin}}{\sigma_{Lam\acute e}}\times100 (Lamé taken as the exact value).

Formula. σthin=prit\sigma_{thin}=\dfrac{pr_i}{t}; σθ,max\sigma_{\theta,max}​=piro2+ri2ro2−ri2=p_i\dfrac{r_o^2+r_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}.

Solution.

  1. (a) σthin\sigma_{thin}​=10(100)10=\dfrac{10(100)}{10}​=100.0=100.0 MPa.
  2. (a) ro2=12 100r_o^2=12\,100, ri2=10 000r_i^2=10\,000: σθ,max\sigma_{\theta,max}​=1022 1002100=10\dfrac{22\,100}{2100}​=105.24=105.24 MPa.
  3. (a) Error =105.24−100105.24=\dfrac{105.24-100}{105.24}​=4.98%=4.98\% (the thin formula is low).
  4. (b) σthin\sigma_{thin}​=10(100)50=\dfrac{10(100)}{50}​=20.0=20.0 MPa.
  5. (b) ro2=22 500r_o^2=22\,500: σθ,max\sigma_{\theta,max}​=1032 50012 500=10\dfrac{32\,500}{12\,500}​=26.0=26.0 MPa.
  6. (b) Error =26−2026=23.1%=\dfrac{26-20}{26}=23.1\%.
Case t/rit/r_i Thin (MPa) Lamé (MPa) Error
(a) t=10t=100.10100.0105.25.0%
(b) t=50t=500.5020.026.023.1%

(a) 100 MPa vs 105.2 MPa (5.0% low); (b) 20 MPa vs 26.0 MPa (23.1% low)

Comment. At t/r=0.1t/r=0.1, the usual limit of thin-wall theory, the error is about 5% and acceptable. At t/r=0.5t/r=0.5 the thin formula is 23% too low, which is unsafe. The thin formula under-estimates the peak because it assumes a uniform hoop stress, whereas the true stress is largest at the inner surface (Q033 and Q034).

U4-Q078Q078 | L4 Analyze | E1 | N | 7 marks

A bar of total length 600 mm consists of two equal halves of diameters 40 mm and 20 mm (E=200E=200 GPa). The load is such that the maximum stress is 150 MPa. Find the strain energy and compare it with that of a uniform bar of 20 mm diameter and the same length at the same maximum stress.

Solution

Given. Halves of L/2=300L/2=300 mm: d2=40d_2=40 mm and d1=20d_1=20 mm; E=200 000E=200\,000 MPa; σmax=150\sigma_{max}=150 MPa; comparison bar: d=20d=20 mm, L=600L=600 mm.

To find. UU of the stepped bar and its ratio to UU of the uniform bar.

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic; the same axial force PP in both halves; the maximum stress occurs in the smaller section; stress concentration neglected; units N and mm.

Formula. P=σmaxA1P=\sigma_{max}A_1, U=∑P2Li2AiEU=\displaystyle\sum\dfrac{P^2L_i}{2A_iE}.

Solution.

  1. A1A_1​=π(20)24=\dfrac{\pi(20)^2}{4}​=314.16=314.16 mm2^2; A2A_2​=π(40)24=\dfrac{\pi(40)^2}{4}​=1256.64=1256.64 mm2^2.
  2. PP​=150(314.16)=150(314.16)​=47 124=47\,124 N; the stress in the 40 mm half is 47 1241256.64=37.5\dfrac{47\,124}{1256.64}=37.5 MPa.
  3. U1U_1​=(47 124)2(300)2(314.16)(200 000)=\dfrac{(47\,124)^2(300)}{2(314.16)(200\,000)}​=5301=5301 N mm (20 mm half).
  4. U2U_2​=(47 124)2(300)2(1256.64)(200 000)=\dfrac{(47\,124)^2(300)}{2(1256.64)(200\,000)}​=1325=1325 N mm (40 mm half).
  5. UU​=5301+1325=5301+1325​=6627=6627 N mm =6.63=6.63 J.
  6. Uniform 20 mm bar: U0U_0​=15022(200 000)(314.16)(600)=\dfrac{150^2}{2(200\,000)}(314.16)(600)​=10 603=10\,603 N mm =10.60=10.60 J.
  7. Ratio: UU0\dfrac{U}{U_0}​=662710 603=\dfrac{6627}{10\,603}​=0.625=0.625​=58=\dfrac58 (check with 1+n22n2\dfrac{1+n^2}{2n^2}, n=2n=2).

Ustepped=6627U_{stepped}=6627 N mm =6.63=6.63 J;   Uuniform=10 603\;U_{uniform}=10\,603 N mm =10.60=10.60 J; the stepped bar stores 62.5%62.5\% of it

Comparison. Enlarging one half does not raise the permissible load (the 20 mm half still carries 150 MPa) but adds lightly stressed material, so the energy-absorbing capacity falls. Agrees with Q&A model answer 14.

U4-Q079Q079 | L4 Analyze | E2 | N | 8 marks

Compare the strain energy per unit volume of a solid circular shaft and a hollow circular shaft with ri/ro=0.6r_i/r_o=0.6 for the same maximum shear stress of 80 MPa (G=80G=80 GPa). Which is better as a torsional energy absorber per unit volume?

Solution

Given. τmax=80\tau_{max}=80 MPa, G=80 000G=80\,000 MPa, hollow shaft k=ri/ro=0.6k=r_i/r_o=0.6.

To find. U/VU/V for each shaft and the comparison.

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic torsion; shear stress varies linearly with radius, τ=Tρ/J\tau=T\rho/J; the same τmax\tau_{max} at the outer surface.

Formula. UV=τmax24G\dfrac{U}{V}=\dfrac{\tau_{max}^2}{4G} (solid); UV\dfrac{U}{V}​=(1+k2)τmax24G=(1+k^2)\dfrac{\tau_{max}^2}{4G} (hollow). (Course notes N 23.)

Derivation (hollow, for the factor). U=∫τ22GdVU=\displaystyle\int\dfrac{\tau^2}{2G}dV with τ=τmaxρ/ro\tau=\tau_{max}\rho/r_o: UV\dfrac UV​=τmax22Gro2⋅∫ρ2dAA=\dfrac{\tau_{max}^2}{2Gr_o^2}\cdot\dfrac{\int\rho^2dA}{A}​=τmax22Gro2⋅ro2+ri22=\dfrac{\tau_{max}^2}{2Gr_o^2}\cdot\dfrac{r_o^2+r_i^2}{2}​=τmax24G(1+k2)=\dfrac{\tau_{max}^2}{4G}(1+k^2) (since J/AJ/A​=12(ro2+ri2)=\tfrac12(r_o^2+r_i^2)). For k=0k=0 it reduces to the solid shaft.

Solution.

  1. Solid: UV\dfrac UV​=8024(80 000)=\dfrac{80^2}{4(80\,000)}​=6400320 000=\dfrac{6400}{320\,000}​=0.0200=0.0200 N/mm2^2 =20=20 kJ/m3^3.
  2. Hollow: 1+k21+k^2​=1+0.36=1+0.36​=1.36=1.36, so UV\dfrac UV​=1.36(0.0200)=1.36(0.0200)​=0.0272=0.0272 N/mm2^2 =27.2=27.2 kJ/m3^3.
  3. Ratio hollow/solid =1.36=1.36.

Solid: 0.02000.0200 N/mm2^2 (20 kJ/m3^3); hollow: 0.02720.0272 N/mm2^2 (27.2 kJ/m3^3), 36%36\% more

Conclusion. The hollow shaft is better per unit volume because the material near the axis of a solid shaft is lightly stressed (stress ∝ρ\propto\rho), whereas in a hollow shaft all the material is closer to the peak stress. As k→1k\to1 the factor tends to 2, i.e. the shear stress is almost uniform.

U4-Q080Q080 | L4 Analyze | E1 | N | 8 marks

In a two-bar frame, rod BC (length 0.6 l0.6\,l) and rod BD (length 0.8 l0.8\,l), of area 300 mm2^2 and E=70E=70 GPa, support a vertical load P=24P=24 kN at B with l=1.25l=1.25 m. The forces are FBC=+0.6PF_{BC}=+0.6P and FBD=−0.8PF_{BD}=-0.8P. Find the strain energy and the deflection of B along the line of the load.

Solution

Given. A=300A=300 mm2^2, E=70 000E=70\,000 MPa, P=24 000P=24\,000 N, l=1250l=1250 mm; LBC=0.6l=750L_{BC}=0.6l=750 mm, LBD=0.8l=1000L_{BD}=0.8l=1000 mm; FBCF_{BC}​=+0.6P=+0.6P​=14 400=14\,400 N (tension), FBDF_{BD}​=−0.8P=-0.8P​=−19 200=-19\,200 N (compression).

To find. UU and the deflection δB\delta_B in the direction of PP.

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic; axial forces only (no bending); single load, so work 12PδB=U\tfrac12P\delta_B=U gives the deflection at B in the direction of PP only; forces given in the question.

Formula. U=∑Fi2Li2AEU=\displaystyle\sum\dfrac{F_i^2L_i}{2AE},   δB=2UP\;\delta_B=\dfrac{2U}{P}.

Solution.

  1. FBC2LBC2AE\dfrac{F_{BC}^2L_{BC}}{2AE}​=(14 400)2(750)2(300)(70 000)=\dfrac{(14\,400)^2(750)}{2(300)(70\,000)}​=1.5552×10114.2×107=\dfrac{1.5552\times10^{11}}{4.2\times10^{7}}​=3702.9=3702.9 N mm.
  2. FBD2LBD2AE\dfrac{F_{BD}^2L_{BD}}{2AE}​=(19 200)2(1000)4.2×107=\dfrac{(19\,200)^2(1000)}{4.2\times10^{7}}​=3.6864×10114.2×107=\dfrac{3.6864\times10^{11}}{4.2\times10^{7}}​=8777.1=8777.1 N mm.
  3. UU​=3702.9+8777.1=3702.9+8777.1​=12 480=12\,480 N mm =12.48=12.48 J.
  4. δB\delta_B​=2UP=\dfrac{2U}{P}​=2(12 480)24 000=\dfrac{2(12\,480)}{24\,000}​=1.04=1.04 mm (downward, along PP).
  5. Check with the symbolic result: UU​=P2l[(0.6)3+(0.8)3]2AE=\dfrac{P^2l\left[(0.6)^3+(0.8)^3\right]}{2AE}​=0.364P2lAE=0.364\dfrac{P^2l}{AE} and δ\delta​=0.728PlAE=0.728\dfrac{Pl}{AE}​=0.72824 000(1250)300(70 000)=0.728\dfrac{24\,000(1250)}{300(70\,000)}​=1.04=1.04 mm ✓ (Example C.6 of the notes).

U=12 480U=12\,480 N mm =12.5=12.5 J,   δB=1.04\;\delta_B=1.04 mm (vertical, along the load)

Stresses: σBC=48\sigma_{BC}=48 MPa (T) and σBD=−64\sigma_{BD}=-64 MPa (C). The method gives only the deflection along the load, not the horizontal movement of B.

Level 5: Evaluate (Q081 to Q100)

Cognitive focus: judging, verifying claims, checking safety and recommending decisions on the basis of calculation. Each answer states the claim or criterion, tests it with numbers, and ends with a clear, justified verdict.

U4-Q081Q081 | L5 Evaluate | T1 | N | 5 marks

A student claims that σx′+σy′\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'} changes with θ\theta. For σx=60\sigma_x=60, σy=−20\sigma_y=-20, τxy=30\tau_{xy}=30 MPa, evaluate this claim by computing σx′+σy′\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'} at θ=0∘\theta=0^{\circ}, 30∘30^{\circ}, 60∘60^{\circ} and 90∘90^{\circ}.

Solution

Claim to test. σx′+σy′\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'} depends on θ\theta.

Given. σx=60\sigma_x=60, σy=−20\sigma_y=-20, τxy=30\tau_{xy}=30 MPa.

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; tension positive; θ\theta counter-clockwise; σy′\sigma_{y'} from the transformation equation with θ+90∘\theta+90^{\circ}.

Formula. σx′\sigma_{x'}​=σavg+σx−σy2cos⁡2θ+τxysin⁡2θ=\sigma_{avg}+\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\cos2\theta+\tau_{xy}\sin2\theta, σy′\sigma_{y'}​=σavg−σx−σy2cos⁡2θ−τxysin⁡2θ=\sigma_{avg}-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\cos2\theta-\tau_{xy}\sin2\theta.

Solution. σavg=20\sigma_{avg}=20 MPa, σx−σy2=40\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}=40 MPa, τxy=30\tau_{xy}=30 MPa.

θ\theta 2θ2\theta σx′\sigma_{x'} (MPa) σy′\sigma_{y'} (MPa) Sum (MPa)
0∘0^{\circ}0∘0^{\circ}20+40(1)+020+40(1)+0​=60.00=60.0020−40=−20.0020-40=-20.0040.0040.00
30∘30^{\circ}60∘60^{\circ}20+20+25.9820+20+25.98​=65.98=65.9820−20−25.9820-20-25.98​=−25.98=-25.9840.0040.00
60∘60^{\circ}120∘120^{\circ}20−20+25.9820-20+25.98​=25.98=25.9820+20−25.9820+20-25.98​=14.02=14.0240.0040.00
90∘90^{\circ}180∘180^{\circ}20−40+0=−20.0020-40+0=-20.0020+40=60.0020+40=60.0040.0040.00

Judgement. The sum is 4040 MPa =σx+σy=\sigma_x+\sigma_y at every angle. The claim is false.

Reason. Adding the two equations cancels the cos⁡2θ\cos2\theta and sin⁡2θ\sin2\theta terms, leaving 2σavg2\sigma_{avg}; on Mohr's circle the centre does not move when the diameter turns.

Claim rejected: σx′+σy′=40\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'}=40 MPa for all θ\theta (invariant). The student probably confused it with the individual stresses, which do change.

U4-Q082Q082 | L5 Evaluate | T2 | T | 6 marks

A student states that for principal stresses σ1=80\sigma_1=80 MPa and σ2=40\sigma_2=40 MPa the maximum shear stress is (80−40)/2=20(80-40)/2=20 MPa. Critically evaluate this statement.

Solution

Claim to test. τmax\tau_{max}​=(σ1−σ2)/2=(\sigma_1-\sigma_2)/2​=20=20 MPa.

Principle. (σ1−σ2)/2(\sigma_1-\sigma_2)/2 is the maximum in-plane shear, from the circle through σ1\sigma_1 and σ2\sigma_2. The true (absolute) maximum shear in a body considers all three principal stresses {σ1,σ2,σ3}\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3\}; in plane stress σ3=0\sigma_3=0 (the free surface).

Evaluation.

Circle (pair) Diameter (MPa) Shear (MPa)
σ1,σ2\sigma_1,\sigma_2 (80, 40)4020
σ2,σ3\sigma_2,\sigma_3 (40, 0)4020
σ1,σ3\sigma_1,\sigma_3 (80, 0)8040
  1. The student's value, 20 MPa, is correct only as the in-plane maximum shear.
  2. Both principal stresses are tensile (same sign), so the largest circle is the one through σ1\sigma_1 and σ3=0\sigma_3=0, which gives 80−02=40\dfrac{80-0}{2}=40 MPa on planes at 45∘45^{\circ} to the σ1\sigma_1 axis, out of the plane.
  3. Using 20 MPa in a yield check (for example τmax≤σY/2\tau_{max}\le\sigma_Y/2) would under-estimate the shear by 50%, which is unsafe.

Verdict. The statement is incomplete and unsafe if the state is plane stress. The absolute maximum shear is 40 MPa; 20 MPa is only the in-plane value. (If the problem were genuinely three-dimensional with a third principal stress between 40 and 80, the answer would differ, but no third stress is given, so σ3=0\sigma_3=0 is the natural reading, as in Q070.)

In-plane τmax=20\tau_{max}=20 MPa; absolute τmax=40\tau_{max}=40 MPa (governs). The student's statement is correct only for in-plane shear.

U4-Q083Q083 | L5 Evaluate | T2 | N | 7 marks

A machine member of ductile steel (σY=250\sigma_Y=250 MPa) is in plane stress with σx=120\sigma_x=120, σy=−40\sigma_y=-40 and τxy=60\tau_{xy}=60 MPa. Yielding occurs when τmax=σY/2\tau_{max}=\sigma_Y/2. Evaluate whether the member is safe and compute the factor of safety.

Solution

Given. σx=120\sigma_x=120, σy=−40\sigma_y=-40, τxy=60\tau_{xy}=60 MPa; σY=250\sigma_Y=250 MPa; criterion: yield when τmax=σY/2=125\tau_{max}=\sigma_Y/2=125 MPa.

To find. τmax\tau_{max} at the point, safety verdict, factor of safety.

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; tension positive; maximum-shear (Tresca) criterion using the absolute maximum shear, found from all three principal stresses.

Formula. σ1,2=σavg±R\sigma_{1,2}=\sigma_{avg}\pm R; τmax\tau_{max}​=12(σmax−σmin)=\tfrac12(\sigma_{max}-\sigma_{min}) over {σ1,σ2,0}\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2,0\}; FS=σY/2τmaxFS=\dfrac{\sigma_Y/2}{\tau_{max}}.

Solution.

  1. σavg=120−402=40\sigma_{avg}=\dfrac{120-40}{2}=40 MPa; σx−σy2=80\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}=80 MPa.
  2. R=802+602=100R=\sqrt{80^2+60^2}=100 MPa.
  3. σ1=140\sigma_1=140 MPa; σ2=−60\sigma_2=-60 MPa; σ3=0\sigma_3=0.
  4. σ1\sigma_1 and σ2\sigma_2 have opposite signs, so the absolute maximum equals the in-plane one: τmax\tau_{max}​=140−(−60)2=\dfrac{140-(-60)}{2}​=100=100 MPa.
  5. Limit: σY/2=125\sigma_Y/2=125 MPa. Since 100<125100<125 MPa the member does not yield.
  6. FS=125100=1.25FS=\dfrac{125}{100}=1.25.

Evaluation. The member is safe against yielding, but the margin is small: 1.25 is below the 1.5 to 2 usually wanted for machine parts, so the design is acceptable only if loads and material strength are well known. (The factor of safety of 1.5 or higher is a general design practice, not a course value; the verdict above rests on the given criterion.)

τmax=100\tau_{max}=100 MPa <125<125 MPa: safe; FS=1.25FS=1.25

U4-Q084Q084 | L5 Evaluate | T3 | T | 5 marks

Critically compare the analytical and Mohr's-circle methods of stress transformation and state when each is preferable.

Solution

Definition. Both methods give the same stresses on an inclined plane from σx,σy,τxy\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\tau_{xy}. Analytical: apply the transformation equations. Mohr's circle: plot X(σx,−τxy)X(\sigma_x,-\tau_{xy}) and Y(σy,τxy)Y(\sigma_y,\tau_{xy}), draw the circle and turn the diameter 2θ2\theta.

Principle. Mohr's circle is the graphical form of the transformation equations (they are the parametric equations of the circle with parameter 2θ2\theta, Q026).

Comparison.

Aspect Analytical Mohr's circle
Accuracyexact, limited only by arithmeticexact if computed with the circle's geometry; graph-reading is approximate
Speedquick for one plane with a calculatorquick for several planes or a full picture
Sign errorspossible with sin⁡\sin, cos⁡\cos and signspossible with the −τxy-\tau_{xy} plotting rule and rotation sense
Insightlittleshows principal planes, max shear, invariance, where σ\sigma is extreme
Checkσx′+σy′\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'}the circle itself, the diameter, centre =σavg=\sigma_{avg}
Computer useeasy to programnot needed

Evaluation. - Prefer the analytical method when a numerical answer on one specified plane is needed, when high accuracy is required, or when programming. - Prefer Mohr's circle when the whole stress state is wanted (principal and maximum shear together), to see the effect of rotation, for 3-D comparisons (three circles), or for quick checking. - Best practice: solve with one method and verify with the other, as in Q049 and Q067.

Conclusion. Neither is superior in all cases: the analytical method is the more precise tool for one plane, Mohr's circle gives understanding and a check; both rest on the same equations.

U4-Q085Q085 | L5 Evaluate | T2 | N | 6 marks

Evaluate the statement "the maximum shear stress always acts on planes at 45∘45^{\circ} to the xx axis" for σx=100\sigma_x=100, σy=20\sigma_y=20, τxy=40\tau_{xy}=40 MPa.

Solution

Claim to test. τmax\tau_{max} acts on planes at 45∘45^{\circ} to the xx axis.

Given. σx=100\sigma_x=100, σy=20\sigma_y=20, τxy=40\tau_{xy}=40 MPa.

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; θ\theta counter-clockwise from xx; in-plane maximum shear.

Formula. tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2τxyσx−σy=\dfrac{2\tau_{xy}}{\sigma_x-\sigma_y},   θs=θp±45∘\;\theta_s=\theta_p\pm45^{\circ},   τmax=R\;\tau_{max}=R, τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−σx−σy2sin⁡2θ+τxycos⁡2θ=-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\sin2\theta+\tau_{xy}\cos2\theta.

Solution.

  1. σavg=60\sigma_{avg}=60 MPa, σx−σy2=40\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}=40 MPa, RR​=402+402=\sqrt{40^2+40^2}​=56.57=56.57 MPa.
  2. tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=8080=\dfrac{80}{80}​=1=1​⇒2θp\Rightarrow2\theta_p​=45∘=45^{\circ}, θp=22.5∘\theta_p=22.5^{\circ} (σ1=116.57\sigma_1=116.57 MPa).
  3. Planes of maximum shear: θs\theta_s​=22.5∘±45∘=22.5^{\circ}\pm45^{\circ}​=67.5∘=67.5^{\circ} and −22.5∘-22.5^{\circ}. Check: τx′y′\tau_{x'y'} at −22.5∘-22.5^{\circ} is −40sin⁡(−45∘)+40cos⁡(−45∘)-40\sin(-45^{\circ})+40\cos(-45^{\circ})​=28.28+28.28=28.28+28.28​=56.57=56.57 MPa ✓.
  4. What happens at θ=45∘\theta=45^{\circ} from xx: τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−40sin⁡90∘+40cos⁡90∘=-40\sin90^{\circ}+40\cos90^{\circ}​=−40=-40 MPa, with σx′\sigma_{x'}​=60+0+40=60+0+40​=100=100 MPa. This is only 71% of the true maximum, 56.57 MPa.

Judgement. The statement is false. The maximum shear acts at 45∘45^{\circ} to the principal planes, not to the xx axis. It is at 45∘45^{\circ} to xx only when the xx and yy axes are themselves the principal axes (τxy=0\tau_{xy}=0, θp=0\theta_p=0), as in a bar in uniaxial tension (Q021).

τmax=56.6\tau_{max}=56.6 MPa at θ=67.5∘\theta=67.5^{\circ} and −22.5∘-22.5^{\circ} from xx (not 45∘45^{\circ}); at 45∘45^{\circ} the shear is only 40 MPa

U4-Q086Q086 | L5 Evaluate | T1 | N | 6 marks

The grain of a timber member makes 15∘15^{\circ} with the vertical. The member is under compressive stresses of 3 MPa (horizontal) and 1.8 MPa (vertical), no shear. The allowable shear stress along the grain is 0.35 MPa and the allowable compressive stress normal to the grain is 3.5 MPa. Evaluate whether the member is safe.

Solution

Given. σx=−3\sigma_x=-3 MPa (horizontal), σy=−1.8\sigma_y=-1.8 MPa (vertical), τxy=0\tau_{xy}=0; grain 15∘15^{\circ} from the vertical; τallow=0.35\tau_{allow}=0.35 MPa along the grain; σallow=3.5\sigma_{allow}=3.5 MPa (compression) normal to the grain.

To find. Shear stress along the grain and normal stress on the plane across the grain; verdict.

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; compression negative; xx horizontal. A grain direction 15∘15^{\circ} from the vertical means the grain plane has its normal 15∘15^{\circ} from the horizontal, so θ=15∘\theta=15^{\circ} (the sign of θ\theta changes only the sign of the shear, not its size).

Formula. σx′\sigma_{x'}​=σx+σy2+σx−σy2cos⁡2θ+τxysin⁡2θ=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}+\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\cos2\theta+\tau_{xy}\sin2\theta, τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−σx−σy2sin⁡2θ+τxycos⁡2θ=-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\sin2\theta+\tau_{xy}\cos2\theta.

Solution.

  1. σavg\sigma_{avg}​=−3−1.82=\dfrac{-3-1.8}{2}​=−2.40=-2.40 MPa; σx−σy2=−0.60\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}=-0.60 MPa; 2θ=30∘2\theta=30^{\circ}.
  2. σx′\sigma_{x'}​=−2.40+(−0.60)(0.8660)=-2.40+(-0.60)(0.8660)​=−2.92=-2.92 MPa (compression normal to the grain plane).
  3. τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−(−0.60)(0.5)=-(-0.60)(0.5)​=+0.30=+0.30 MPa (shear along the grain).
  4. Comparison: normal compression 2.92<3.52.92<3.5 MPa ✓; shear 0.30<0.350.30<0.35 MPa ✓.
  5. Margins: 3.52.92=1.20\dfrac{3.5}{2.92}=1.20 and 0.350.30=1.17\dfrac{0.35}{0.30}=1.17.

Verdict. The member is safe against both limits. The shear along the grain is the more critical check (margin 1.17, utilisation 86%).

Normal stress across grain: 2.922.92 MPa <3.5<3.5 MPa; shear along grain: 0.300.30 MPa <0.35<0.35 MPa. Safe (smallest margin 1.17, in shear).

U4-Q087Q087 | L5 Evaluate | P1 | N | 6 marks

A cylinder (D=1D=1 m, t=10t=10 mm) and a sphere of the same diameter and thickness hold air at 2 MPa. Compare the stresses and evaluate which vessel makes better use of material.

Solution

Given. D=1000D=1000 mm, t=10t=10 mm, p=2p=2 MPa for both vessels.

To find. The stresses in each and the better use of material.

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin walls (t/r=0.02t/r=0.02); internal diameter; tension positive; closed ends.

Formula. Cylinder: σh=pD2t\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t}, σL=pD4t\sigma_L=\dfrac{pD}{4t}. Sphere: σ=pD4t\sigma=\dfrac{pD}{4t}.

Solution.

  1. Cylinder: σh=2(1000)2(10)=100\sigma_h=\dfrac{2(1000)}{2(10)}=100 MPa; σL=50\sigma_L=50 MPa.
  2. Sphere: σ=2(1000)4(10)=50\sigma=\dfrac{2(1000)}{4(10)}=50 MPa in every direction.
  3. Absolute maximum shear: cylinder σh2=50\dfrac{\sigma_h}{2}=50 MPa; sphere σ2=25\dfrac{\sigma}{2}=25 MPa.
  4. Thickness needed for an allowable stress σa\sigma_{a}: cylinder tc=pD2σat_c=\dfrac{pD}{2\sigma_a}; sphere ts=pD4σa=12tct_s=\dfrac{pD}{4\sigma_a}=\tfrac12t_c. For the same wall the sphere's maximum stress is half.
  5. For example, if σa=100\sigma_a=100 MPa, the sphere needs only 5 mm against 10 mm for the cylinder.
Max stress (MPa) Max shear (MPa) Thickness for 100 MPa
Cylinder1005010 mm
Sphere50255 mm

Verdict. The sphere makes better use of material: for the same wall it has half the stress, or for the same allowable stress it needs half the thickness (and its stress is uniform, with no seam carrying hoop stress). Its drawbacks are cost of fabrication and poor use of space; the cylinder is chosen for convenience of shape.

Cylinder σh=100\sigma_h=100, σL=50\sigma_L=50 MPa; sphere σ=50\sigma=50 MPa. The sphere is the more efficient shell (half the stress, half the thickness).

U4-Q088Q088 | L5 Evaluate | P1 | N | 7 marks

A cylindrical vessel (D=800D=800 mm, t=10t=10 mm) holds 3.5 MPa. The yield stress is 240 MPa and a factor of safety of 2 is required. Evaluate whether the design is adequate and, if not, recommend a thickness.

Solution

Given. D=800D=800 mm, t=10t=10 mm, p=3.5p=3.5 MPa, σY=240\sigma_Y=240 MPa, required FS=2FS=2.

To find. Adequacy of the design and a recommended thickness.

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin closed cylinder; internal diameter; the larger principal stress (hoop) governs; allowable stress =σY/FS=\sigma_Y/FS; joint efficiencies taken as 1 (none given).

Formula. σh=pD2t\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t}, σallow=σYFS\sigma_{allow}=\dfrac{\sigma_Y}{FS}, treqt_{req}​=pD2σallow=\dfrac{pD}{2\sigma_{allow}}.

Solution.

  1. σallow=2402=120\sigma_{allow}=\dfrac{240}{2}=120 MPa.
  2. σh\sigma_h​=3.5(800)2(10)=\dfrac{3.5(800)}{2(10)}​=140=140 MPa; σL=70\sigma_L=70 MPa.
  3. Actual factor of safety =240140=1.71<2=\dfrac{240}{140}=1.71<2; the stress 140>120140>120 MPa.
  4. Required thickness: treqt_{req}​=3.5(800)2(120)=\dfrac{3.5(800)}{2(120)}​=2800240=\dfrac{2800}{240}​=11.67=11.67 mm.
  5. Recommend the next standard plate, 12 mm. Check: σh=28002(12)=116.7\sigma_h=\dfrac{2800}{2(12)}=116.7 MPa <120<120 ✓, FS=240116.7=2.06FS=\dfrac{240}{116.7}=2.06.
  6. Thin-wall check: t/rt/r​=12/400=12/400​=0.03=0.03​<0.1<0.1 ✓.

Verdict. The design is not adequate (FS 1.71 instead of 2). Increase the thickness to at least 11.67 mm; use 12 mm.

σh=140\sigma_h=140 MPa >120>120 MPa allowed: inadequate (FS=1.71FS=1.71). Recommended t≥11.67t\ge11.67 mm, i.e. 12 mm (FS=2.06FS=2.06).

U4-Q089Q089 | L5 Evaluate | P1 | T | 5 marks

For a cylindrical vessel with equal efficiency of longitudinal and circumferential welds, evaluate which seam is more critical and why.

Solution

Definition. The longitudinal seam runs along the axis of the cylinder; the circumferential seam runs around it.

Principle. The stress that a seam must carry is the stress acting across it. - The longitudinal seam is loaded by the hoop stress σh=pD2tηl\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t\eta_l} (hoop force tries to open the seam). - The circumferential seam is loaded by the longitudinal stress σL=pD4tηc\sigma_L=\dfrac{pD}{4t\eta_c}.

Evaluation. With ηl=ηc=η\eta_l=\eta_c=\eta, σh=2σL\sigma_h=2\sigma_L. The longitudinal seam carries twice the stress of the circumferential seam, so it is the more critical and fails first (the cylinder splits along its length).

Design consequences. - The shell thickness is governed by the hoop requirement, t=pD2σallowηt=\dfrac{pD}{2\sigma_{allow}\eta}. - A circumferential joint could have about half the efficiency with the same thickness (ηc≈ηl/2\eta_c\approx\eta_l/2). - Inspection effort should be concentrated on the longitudinal welds.

Conclusion. The longitudinal seam is more critical because it resists the hoop stress, twice the longitudinal stress. (Matches Q&A model answer 16; compare Q030 and Q032.)

U4-Q090Q090 | L5 Evaluate | P2 | N | 7 marks

A thick cylinder (ri=100r_i=100 mm, ro=160r_o=160 mm) carries 70 MPa. The allowable tensile stress is 150 MPa. Evaluate whether it is safe using Lamé's equations and calculate the factor of safety.

Solution

Given. ri=100r_i=100 mm, ro=160r_o=160 mm, internal pressure pi=70p_i=70 MPa (external zero); σallow=150\sigma_{allow}=150 MPa. (Dimensions read from the question-bank page: ro=160r_o=160 mm.)

To find. Maximum stress, verdict, factor of safety.

Assumptions and sign convention. Lamé's theory; tension positive; the greatest tensile stress is the hoop stress at the inner surface; FS=σallow/σmaxFS=\sigma_{allow}/\sigma_{max} (the allowable stress already includes any margin).

Formula. σθ,max\sigma_{\theta,max}​=piro2+ri2ro2−ri2=p_i\dfrac{r_o^2+r_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}; design relation rori\dfrac{r_o}{r_i}​=σallow+piσallow−pi=\sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_{allow}+p_i}{\sigma_{allow}-p_i}}.

Solution.

  1. ro2=25 600r_o^2=25\,600, ri2=10 000r_i^2=10\,000, ro2−ri2=15 600r_o^2-r_i^2=15\,600 mm2^2.
  2. σθ,max\sigma_{\theta,max}​=7025 600+10 00015 600=70\dfrac{25\,600+10\,000}{15\,600}​=70(2.282)=70(2.282)​=159.7=159.7 MPa at r=rir=r_i.
  3. 159.7>150159.7>150 MPa, so the cylinder is over-stressed.
  4. FSFS​=150159.7=\dfrac{150}{159.7}​=0.94=0.94​<1<1.
  5. Outer surface for reference: σθ\sigma_\theta​=2(70)(10 000)15 600=\dfrac{2(70)(10\,000)}{15\,600}​=89.7=89.7 MPa; σr=−70\sigma_r=-70 MPa at the inner surface.
  6. Required outer radius: rori\dfrac{r_o}{r_i}​=150+70150−70=\sqrt{\dfrac{150+70}{150-70}}​=2.75=\sqrt{2.75}​=1.658=1.658, so ro≥165.8r_o\ge165.8 mm (against 160 mm provided).

Verdict. The cylinder is not safe: σθ,max=159.7\sigma_{\theta,max}=159.7 MPa exceeds the 150 MPa allowable, FS=0.94FS=0.94. It would need ro≥166r_o\ge166 mm (wall at least 66 mm instead of 60 mm) or a lower pressure.

σθ,max=159.7\sigma_{\theta,max}=159.7 MPa >150>150 MPa: unsafe, FS=0.94FS=0.94; required ro≥165.8r_o\ge165.8 mm

U4-Q091Q091 | L5 Evaluate | P2 | N | 6 marks

Evaluate the claim "doubling the wall thickness of a thick cylinder halves the maximum hoop stress" for ri=100r_i=100 mm, pi=50p_i=50 MPa by comparing ro=150r_o=150 mm with ro=200r_o=200 mm.

Solution

Claim to test. Doubling tt halves σθ,max\sigma_{\theta,max}.

Given. ri=100r_i=100 mm, pi=50p_i=50 MPa; case 1: ro=150r_o=150 mm (t=50t=50 mm); case 2: ro=200r_o=200 mm (t=100t=100 mm, twice as thick).

Assumptions and sign convention. Lamé's theory, internal pressure only; tension positive; maximum hoop stress at the inner surface.

Formula. σθ,max\sigma_{\theta,max}​=piro2+ri2ro2−ri2=p_i\dfrac{r_o^2+r_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}.

Solution.

  1. Case 1: σθ,max\sigma_{\theta,max}​=5022 500+10 00022 500−10 000=50\dfrac{22\,500+10\,000}{22\,500-10\,000}​=5032 50012 500=50\dfrac{32\,500}{12\,500}​=130.0=130.0 MPa.
  2. Case 2: σθ,max\sigma_{\theta,max}​=5040 000+10 00040 000−10 000=50\dfrac{40\,000+10\,000}{40\,000-10\,000}​=5050 00030 000=50\dfrac{50\,000}{30\,000}​=83.3=83.3 MPa.
  3. Ratio =83.3130.0=0.641=\dfrac{83.3}{130.0}=0.641; the stress falls by 36%36\%, not 50%50\%.
  4. Why: the factor k2+1k2−1\dfrac{k^2+1}{k^2-1} is not proportional to thickness; it tends to 1 (never to zero), so each extra bit of thickness helps less (Q035).

Verdict. The claim is false: doubling the thickness reduces the maximum hoop stress by only 36%. It would halve the stress only for the thin-wall formula pr/tpr/t, which is not valid here.

σθ,max=130.0\sigma_{\theta,max}=130.0 MPa (ro=150r_o=150) and 83.383.3 MPa (ro=200r_o=200): reduction 36%36\%, not 50%50\%

U4-Q092Q092 | L5 Evaluate | P2 | N | 6 marks

For a thick cylinder (ri=50r_i=50 mm, ro=100r_o=100 mm, pi=40p_i=40 MPa) evaluate the maximum shear stress at the inner and outer surfaces and decide which surface governs yielding of a ductile material.

Solution

Given. ri=50r_i=50 mm, ro=100r_o=100 mm, pi=40p_i=40 MPa, po=0p_o=0.

To find. τmax\tau_{max} at rir_i and ror_o; governing surface.

Assumptions and sign convention. Lamé's theory; tension positive; the radial and hoop stresses are principal; the maximum-shear criterion governs a ductile material; the closed-end axial stress lies between σr\sigma_r and σθ\sigma_\theta and does not change the result.

Formula. σθ=A+Br2\sigma_\theta=A+\dfrac{B}{r^2}, σr=A−Br2\sigma_r=A-\dfrac{B}{r^2}, τmax=σθ−σr2=Br2\tau_{max}=\dfrac{\sigma_\theta-\sigma_r}{2}=\dfrac{B}{r^2}.

Solution.

  1. ro2−ri2r_o^2-r_i^2​=10 000−2500=10\,000-2500​=7500=7500 mm2^2; AA​=40(2500)7500=\dfrac{40(2500)}{7500}​=13.33=13.33 MPa; BB​=40(2500)(10 000)7500=\dfrac{40(2500)(10\,000)}{7500}​=1.333×105=1.333\times10^{5} MPa mm2^2.
  2. Inner (r=50r=50): Br2=53.33\dfrac{B}{r^2}=53.33, so σθ=66.67\sigma_\theta=66.67 MPa, σr=−40\sigma_r=-40 MPa, τmax\tau_{max}​=66.67+402=\dfrac{66.67+40}{2}​=53.33=53.33 MPa. Check: piro2ro2−ri2\dfrac{p_ir_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}​=40(10 000)7500=\dfrac{40(10\,000)}{7500}​=53.33=53.33 ✓.
  3. Outer (r=100r=100): Br2=13.33\dfrac{B}{r^2}=13.33, so σθ=26.67\sigma_\theta=26.67 MPa, σr=0\sigma_r=0, τmax=13.33\tau_{max}=13.33 MPa.
  4. Ratio inner/outer =53.3313.33=4.0=\dfrac{53.33}{13.33}=4.0.

Verdict. The inner surface carries four times the shear, so yielding of a ductile material begins at the inner surface.

Inner τmax=53.3\tau_{max}=53.3 MPa; outer τmax=13.3\tau_{max}=13.3 MPa; the inner surface governs

Agrees with Q&A model answer 17.

U4-Q093Q093 | L5 Evaluate | E1 | N | 7 marks

A bolt has a shank of diameter 20 mm and length 80 mm and a threaded root portion of diameter 16 mm and length 30 mm. Design B has the shank turned down to 16 mm. For a maximum stress of 200 MPa in the threaded root (E=200E=200 GPa), evaluate which design absorbs more energy and by what percentage.

Solution

Given. Design A: shank d=20d=20 mm, L=80L=80 mm; root d=16d=16 mm, L=30L=30 mm. Design B: shank d=16d=16 mm, L=80L=80 mm; root d=16d=16 mm, L=30L=30 mm (so 16 mm throughout, 110 mm). σmax=200\sigma_{max}=200 MPa in the root, E=200 000E=200\,000 MPa.

To find. UAU_A, UBU_B and the percentage difference.

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic; the same axial force in all portions; stress concentration at threads and the step neglected; units N and mm.

Formula. P=σmaxArootP=\sigma_{max}A_{root},   U=∑P2Li2AiE\;U=\displaystyle\sum\dfrac{P^2L_i}{2A_iE}.

Solution.

  1. ArootA_{root}​=π(16)24=\dfrac{\pi(16)^2}{4}​=201.06=201.06 mm2^2; Ashank,AA_{shank,A}​=π(20)24=\dfrac{\pi(20)^2}{4}​=314.16=314.16 mm2^2.
  2. PP​=200(201.06)=200(201.06)​=40 212=40\,212 N (the same for both designs, since the root governs).
  3. Design A: UAU_A​=P22E(80314.16+30201.06)=\dfrac{P^2}{2E}\left(\dfrac{80}{314.16}+\dfrac{30}{201.06}\right)​=(40 212)2400 000(0.2546+0.1492)=\dfrac{(40\,212)^2}{400\,000}(0.2546+0.1492)​=4042.4(0.4038)=4042.4(0.4038)​=1632.6=1632.6 N mm. The shank stress is only 40 212314.16=128\dfrac{40\,212}{314.16}=128 MPa.
  4. Design B: UBU_B​=P22E(110201.06)=\dfrac{P^2}{2E}\left(\dfrac{110}{201.06}\right)​=4042.4(0.5471)=4042.4(0.5471)​=2211.7=2211.7 N mm.
  5. Difference: 2211.7−1632.61632.6\dfrac{2211.7-1632.6}{1632.6}​=35.5%=35.5\% more energy for B (UB/UA=1.355U_B/U_A=1.355).

UA=1633U_A=1633 N mm (1.631.63 J); UB=2212U_B=2212 N mm (2.212.21 J). Design B absorbs 35%35\% more energy.

Verdict. Design B (shank turned down to the root diameter) is better as an impact absorber: the whole length works at the same stress, while the larger shank in A is lightly stressed and stores little energy (Q038). The price is a weaker shank in B in bending or axial stiffness, which the question does not ask about.

U4-Q094Q094 | L5 Evaluate | E1 | N | 6 marks

A student computes the energy of a rod under two sequential loads P1=10P_1=10 kN and P2=20P_2=20 kN (applied together) as U1+U2U_1+U_2. Evaluate this claim by comparing with the correct strain energy for the combined load (P1+P2P_1+P_2).

Solution

Given. P1=10P_1=10 kN, P2=20P_2=20 kN, applied together on the same rod; the rod's LL, AA, EE are not given, so the comparison is made as a ratio (it does not depend on them).

To find. U(P1+P2)U(P_1+P_2) against U(P1)+U(P2)U(P_1)+U(P_2).

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic axial rod; both loads axial and applied together, so the force in the rod is P1+P2P_1+P_2; U=P2L2AEU=\dfrac{P^2L}{2AE}.

Formula. U(P)=P2L2AE=cP2U(P)=\dfrac{P^2L}{2AE}=cP^2 with c=L2AEc=\dfrac{L}{2AE}.

Solution.

  1. U1=c(10)2=100cU_1=c(10)^2=100c; U2=c(20)2=400cU_2=c(20)^2=400c (loads in kN).
  2. Student: U1+U2=500cU_1+U_2=500c.
  3. Correct: U(P1+P2)U(P_1+P_2)​=c(30)2=c(30)^2​=900c=900c.
  4. Ratio =900500=1.8=\dfrac{900}{500}=1.8: the correct energy is 80%80\% larger.
  5. The missing part is the cross term: P1P2LAE\dfrac{P_1P_2L}{AE}​=2P1P2 c=2P_1P_2\,c​=400c=400c, the work done by each load through the deformation caused by the other. 900c900c​=100c+400c+400c=100c+400c+400c ✓.

U(P1+P2)U(P_1+P_2)​=1.8 [U1+U2]=1.8\,[U_1+U_2]; the student's sum is 44%44\% too low (it omits P1P2L/AE=400cP_1P_2L/AE=400c)

Verdict. The claim is wrong. Strain energy is quadratic in load, so energies cannot be added (Q039); add the loads first, then find UU. Numerical value in N mm needs the rod's L,A,EL,A,E, which are not printed in the question (logged in progress.md as data not given).

U4-Q095Q095 | L5 Evaluate | E1 | N | 7 marks

Material A has σY=300\sigma_Y=300 MPa, σU=450\sigma_U=450 MPa, E=200E=200 GPa and fracture strain 0.25; material B has σY=800\sigma_Y=800 MPa, σU=850\sigma_U=850 MPa, E=205E=205 GPa and fracture strain 0.02. Estimate the modulus of resilience and toughness (toughness ≈12(σY+σU)εf\approx\tfrac12(\sigma_Y+\sigma_U)\varepsilon_f) of each and evaluate which suits a railway coupler and which a spring.

Solution

Given. A: σY=300\sigma_Y=300, σU=450\sigma_U=450 MPa, E=200 000E=200\,000 MPa, εf=0.25\varepsilon_f=0.25. B: σY=800\sigma_Y=800, σU=850\sigma_U=850 MPa, E=205 000E=205\,000 MPa, εf=0.02\varepsilon_f=0.02.

To find. uYu_Y and uTu_T of each; best choice for coupler and spring.

Assumptions and sign convention. Resilience uY=σY22Eu_Y=\dfrac{\sigma_Y^2}{2E} (elastic energy to yield); toughness estimated by the given formula uTu_T​≈12(σY+σU)εf\approx\tfrac12(\sigma_Y+\sigma_U)\varepsilon_f (average stress times fracture strain); 1 N/mm2=1^2=1 MJ/m3^3 per unit strain.

Solution.

  1. A resilience: uYu_Y​=30022(200 000)=\dfrac{300^2}{2(200\,000)}​=0.225=0.225 MJ/m3^3.
  2. A toughness: uTu_T​≈12(300+450)(0.25)\approx\tfrac12(300+450)(0.25)​=93.75=93.75 MJ/m3^3.
  3. B resilience: uYu_Y​=80022(205 000)=\dfrac{800^2}{2(205\,000)}​=1.561=1.561 MJ/m3^3.
  4. B toughness: uTu_T​≈12(800+850)(0.02)\approx\tfrac12(800+850)(0.02)​=16.5=16.5 MJ/m3^3.
uYu_Y (MJ/m3^3) uTu_T (MJ/m3^3)
A0.22593.75
B1.56116.5

Evaluation. - Railway coupler: must absorb large impact energy and may deform before breaking, so toughness matters: material A (about 5.7 times tougher). - Spring: must store and return energy elastically, so resilience matters: material B (about 7 times higher uYu_Y), with high yield strength and low plastic strain.

A: uY=0.225u_Y=0.225, uT≈93.8u_T\approx93.8 MJ/m3^3; B: uY=1.56u_Y=1.56, uT≈16.5u_T\approx16.5 MJ/m3^3. Choose A for the coupler and B for the spring.

U4-Q096Q096 | L5 Evaluate | E1 | N | 6 marks

A cantilever of length 1 m, EI=2×106EI=2\times10^{6} N m2^2, carries 1 kN at its free end. Verify the deflection using U=12PδU=\tfrac12P\delta and evaluate the limitations of this method.

Solution

Given. L=1L=1 m, EI=2×106EI=2\times10^{6} N m2^2, P=1P=1 kN =1000=1000 N at the free end.

To find. UU and δ\delta by the energy principle; check against the standard result; limitations.

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic; bending energy only; one load; units N and m (so UU in J, δ\delta in m).

Formula. M=−PxM=-Px, UU​=∫0LM22EIdx=\displaystyle\int_0^L\dfrac{M^2}{2EI}dx​=P2L36EI=\dfrac{P^2L^3}{6EI}; single load: 12Pδ=U⇒δ=2UP\tfrac12P\delta=U\Rightarrow\delta=\dfrac{2U}{P}.

Solution.

  1. UU​=(1000)2(1)36(2×106)=\dfrac{(1000)^2(1)^3}{6(2\times10^{6})}​=1061.2×107=\dfrac{10^{6}}{1.2\times10^{7}}​=0.0833=0.0833 J.
  2. δ\delta​=2(0.0833)1000=\dfrac{2(0.0833)}{1000}​=1.667×10−4=1.667\times10^{-4} m =0.167=0.167 mm.
  3. Check: PL33EI\dfrac{PL^3}{3EI}​=1000(1)3(2×106)=\dfrac{1000(1)}{3(2\times10^{6})}​=1.667×10−4=1.667\times10^{-4} m ✓ (the two agree, so the energy method is verified for this case).

U=0.0833U=0.0833 J,   δ=0.167\;\delta=0.167 mm (verified by PL3/3EIPL^3/3EI)

Limitations of δ=2U/P\delta=2U/P (course notes N 23). 1. It gives the deflection only at the point and in the direction of the single load; the deflection at other points, or the slope, cannot be found. 2. It applies only to one load: with several loads UU depends on all of them and 12∑Piδi=U\tfrac12\sum P_i\delta_i=U cannot be solved for each δi\delta_i (other methods such as Castigliano's theorem or the unit-load method are needed). 3. It needs a linear elastic member, and UU must include every significant energy component; here shear energy has been neglected (small for a slender beam).

Verdict. The energy method gives the right deflection here because the beam has a single tip load; it should not be relied on for several loads or for a point without a load.

U4-Q097Q097 | L5 Evaluate | T3 | N | 7 marks

Using Mohr's circles, evaluate and rank by in-plane maximum shear and by absolute maximum shear the states (a) σx=σy=80\sigma_x=\sigma_y=80 MPa, τ=0\tau=0; (b) σx=80\sigma_x=80 MPa, σy=0\sigma_y=0, τ=0\tau=0; (c) σx=σy=0\sigma_x=\sigma_y=0, τxy=40\tau_{xy}=40 MPa.

Solution

Given. Three plane-stress states (a), (b), (c) as above; σz=0\sigma_z=0 in each.

To find. In-plane τmax=R\tau_{max}=R and absolute τmax\tau_{max}; ranking.

Assumptions and sign convention. Tension positive; plane stress so σ3=0\sigma_3=0; absolute maximum =12(σmax−σmin)=\tfrac12(\sigma_{max}-\sigma_{min}) over {σ1,σ2,0}\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2,0\}.

Solution.

State Circle (in-plane) Principal σ1,σ2\sigma_1,\sigma_2 In-plane τmax=R\tau_{max}=R Absolute τmax\tau_{max}
(a) equal biaxial 80a point at (80,0)(80,0), R=0R=080, 800080−02=40\dfrac{80-0}{2}=40 MPa
(b) uniaxial 80centre 40, R=40R=4080, 04040 MPa80−02=40\dfrac{80-0}{2}=40 MPa
(c) pure shear 40centre 0, R=40R=40+40,−40+40,-404040 MPa40−(−40)2=40\dfrac{40-(-40)}{2}=40 MPa

Ranking. - By in-plane shear: (b) == (c) =40=40 MPa >> (a) =0=0. - By absolute shear: all three equal, 40 MPa.

Evaluation. State (a) looks harmless on the in-plane circle (a point, no shear) but in 3-D it has the same maximum shear as the others because the circle through σ=80\sigma=80 and σ3=0\sigma_3=0 has radius 40. Ranking by in-plane shear alone would wrongly call (a) the safest; for yielding by the maximum-shear criterion all three are equally severe.

In-plane: (b) = (c) = 40 > (a) = 0 MPa. Absolute: (a) = (b) = (c) = 40 MPa

U4-Q098Q098 | L5 Evaluate | E2 | N | 7 marks

Two shafts of equal length and equal cross-sectional area carry the same maximum shear stress of 100 MPa: shaft A is solid with d=40d=40 mm, shaft B is hollow with outer diameter 50 mm and inner diameter 30 mm (G=80G=80 GPa, L=1L=1 m). Evaluate which stores more energy.

Solution

Given. A: solid d=40d=40 mm. B: do=50d_o=50 mm, di=30d_i=30 mm. τmax=100\tau_{max}=100 MPa, G=80 000G=80\,000 MPa, L=1000L=1000 mm.

To find. UAU_A and UBU_B.

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic torsion; same τmax\tau_{max} at the outer surface; units N and mm.

Formula. UV=τmax24G\dfrac UV=\dfrac{\tau_{max}^2}{4G} (solid); UV\dfrac UV​=(1+k2)τmax24G=(1+k^2)\dfrac{\tau_{max}^2}{4G} (hollow, k=di/dok=d_i/d_o); V=ALV=AL.

Solution.

  1. AAA_A​=π(40)24=\dfrac{\pi(40)^2}{4}​=1256.6=1256.6 mm2^2; ABA_B​=π(502−302)4=\dfrac{\pi(50^2-30^2)}{4}​=π(1600)4=\dfrac{\pi(1600)}{4}​=1256.6=1256.6 mm2^2 (equal areas ✓, so equal volumes V=1.2566×106V=1.2566\times10^{6} mm3^3).
  2. A: UV\dfrac UV​=10024(80 000)=\dfrac{100^2}{4(80\,000)}​=0.03125=0.03125 N/mm2^2.
  3. B: k=3050=0.6k=\dfrac{30}{50}=0.6, 1+k2=1.361+k^2=1.36, so UV\dfrac UV​=1.36(0.03125)=1.36(0.03125)​=0.0425=0.0425 N/mm2^2.
  4. UAU_A​=0.03125(1.2566×106)=0.03125(1.2566\times10^{6})​=39 270=39\,270 N mm =39.3=39.3 J.
  5. UBU_B​=0.0425(1.2566×106)=0.0425(1.2566\times10^{6})​=53 407=53\,407 N mm =53.4=53.4 J.
  6. UBUA=1.36\dfrac{U_B}{U_A}=1.36.

UA=39.3U_A=39.3 J; UB=53.4U_B=53.4 J. The hollow shaft stores 36%36\% more energy.

Evaluation. For the same volume of material and the same peak stress the hollow shaft is the better energy absorber: more of its material works at a stress near τmax\tau_{max}. (Same conclusion as Q079; the torque capacity is also larger, but that is not asked.)

U4-Q099Q099 | L5 Evaluate | T2 | N | 7 marks

A cast-iron shaft is subjected to an axial compression of 30 MPa and a torsional shear of 40 MPa. The allowable tensile stress is 40 MPa. Evaluate whether it is safe against tensile fracture.

Solution

Given. σx=−30\sigma_x=-30 MPa (axial, compression), σy=0\sigma_y=0, τxy=40\tau_{xy}=40 MPa; σt,allow=40\sigma_{t,allow}=40 MPa.

To find. The largest principal (tensile) stress and the factor of safety.

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress at the surface; compression negative; cast iron is brittle, so the governing criterion is the maximum principal tensile stress compared with the allowable tension.

Formula. σ1,2\sigma_{1,2}​=σx+σy2±(σx−σy2)2+τxy2=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}\pm\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^2+\tau_{xy}^2}.

Solution.

  1. σavg=−302=−15\sigma_{avg}=\dfrac{-30}{2}=-15 MPa; σx−σy2=−15\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}=-15 MPa.
  2. RR​=152+402=\sqrt{15^2+40^2}​=42.72=42.72 MPa.
  3. σ1\sigma_1​=−15+42.72=-15+42.72​=27.72=27.72 MPa (tension); σ2\sigma_2​=−15−42.72=-15-42.72​=−57.72=-57.72 MPa (compression).
  4. Compare: 27.72<4027.72<40 MPa, so the shaft is safe against tensile fracture.
  5. FS=4027.72=1.44FS=\dfrac{40}{27.72}=1.44.
  6. Note: the axial compression reduces the tension; the same shear without the compression would give σ1=40\sigma_1=40 MPa, right at the limit. (The compressive principal stress 57.757.7 MPa should also be checked against the compressive strength, not given here.)

σ1=27.7\sigma_1=27.7 MPa <40<40 MPa: safe against tensile fracture, FS=1.44FS=1.44 (σ2=−57.7\sigma_2=-57.7 MPa)

U4-Q100Q100 | L5 Evaluate | T3 | N | 6 marks

At a point in a beam web σx=75\sigma_x=75 MPa, σy=0\sigma_y=0 and τxy=30\tau_{xy}=30 MPa. Using Mohr's circle, evaluate the error in taking σx\sigma_x as the maximum principal stress.

Solution

Given. σx=75\sigma_x=75, σy=0\sigma_y=0, τxy=30\tau_{xy}=30 MPa.

To find. σ1\sigma_1 and the error of using σx\sigma_x in its place.

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; tension positive; Mohr's circle with X=(75,−30)X=(75,-30) and Y=(0,+30)Y=(0,+30).

Solution.

  1. Centre C=75+02=37.5C=\dfrac{75+0}{2}=37.5 MPa.
  2. Radius RR​=37.52+302=\sqrt{37.5^2+30^2}​=48.02=48.02 MPa.
  3. σ1=C+R=85.52\sigma_1=C+R=85.52 MPa; σ2=C−R=−10.52\sigma_2=C-R=-10.52 MPa; τmax=R=48.02\tau_{max}=R=48.02 MPa.
  4. θp\theta_p: tan⁡2θp=2(30)75=0.8\tan2\theta_p=\dfrac{2(30)}{75}=0.8, θp=19.33∘\theta_p=19.33^{\circ} for σ1\sigma_1.
  5. Error: σ1−σx\sigma_1-\sigma_x​=85.52−75=85.52-75​=10.52=10.52 MPa, i.e. 10.5285.52=12.3%\dfrac{10.52}{85.52}=12.3\% of σ1\sigma_1 (or 14.0%14.0\% relative to σx\sigma_x).

Evaluation. Taking σx\sigma_x as the maximum principal stress under-estimates it by 10.5 MPa (12.3%), which is non-conservative. The error is large wherever the shear is comparable with the bending stress (near the neutral axis or at the web-flange junction), so the principal stress must be found from the full plane-stress state.

σ1=85.5\sigma_1=85.5 MPa vs σx=75\sigma_x=75 MPa: error 10.510.5 MPa (12.3%12.3\% of σ1\sigma_1), unsafe side

Agrees with Q&A model answer 18.

Level 6: Create (Q101 to Q120)

Cognitive focus: designing, constructing, developing procedures and generating new solutions. Each answer states the design problem, the method built from the course formulae, the calculation, a justified choice and a check. Every number was computed.

U4-Q101Q101 | L6 Create | T2 | P | 8 marks

Develop an algorithm (flow-chart or spreadsheet formulae) that takes σx\sigma_x, σy\sigma_y and τxy\tau_{xy} and returns σ1\sigma_1, σ2\sigma_2, θp\theta_p, τmax\tau_{max} and θs\theta_s. Test it for σx=80\sigma_x=80, σy=−40\sigma_y=-40, τxy=30\tau_{xy}=30 MPa.

Solution

Design problem. Turn the principal-stress formulae into a fixed sequence of steps (a procedure that gives the right quadrant for the angle and the right sign for each stress).

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; tension positive; θ\theta counter-clockwise from xx; τxy\tau_{xy} as in the bank; angles in degrees; θp\theta_p is the angle of the σ1\sigma_1 plane.

Algorithm (flow of steps).

  1. Input σx,σy,τxy\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\tau_{xy}.
  2. σavg=σx+σy2\sigma_{avg}=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}.
  3. a=σx−σy2a=\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}.
  4. R=a2+τxy2R=\sqrt{a^2+\tau_{xy}^2} (this is τmax\tau_{max}).
  5. σ1=σavg+R\sigma_1=\sigma_{avg}+R; σ2=σavg−R\sigma_2=\sigma_{avg}-R.
  6. θp\theta_p​=12 atan2(τxy, a)=\tfrac12\,\mathrm{atan2}(\tau_{xy},\,a) (the two-argument arctangent puts 2θp2\theta_p in the correct quadrant, so the plane is that of σ1\sigma_1).
  7. The σ2\sigma_2 plane is θp+90∘\theta_p+90^{\circ}.
  8. θs=θp+45∘\theta_s=\theta_p+45^{\circ} (a second plane of maximum shear is θp−45∘\theta_p-45^{\circ}); σ′=σavg\sigma'=\sigma_{avg} on these planes.
  9. Check: σ1+σ2=σx+σy\sigma_1+\sigma_2=\sigma_x+\sigma_y; transform to θp\theta_p and confirm σx′=σ1\sigma_{x'}=\sigma_1 and τx′y′=0\tau_{x'y'}=0.
  10. Output.

Spreadsheet formulae (cells A1, A2, A3 hold σx,σy,τxy\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\tau_{xy}): =(A1+A2)/2 for σavg\sigma_{avg}; =SQRT(((A1-A2)/2)^2+A3^2) for RR; =B1+B2 and =B1-B2 for σ1,σ2\sigma_1,\sigma_2; =0.5*DEGREES(ATAN2((A1-A2)/2,A3)) for θp\theta_p (spreadsheets take ATAN2 with the arguments in the order xx, yy); =B4+45 for θs\theta_s.

Test. σx=80\sigma_x=80, σy=−40\sigma_y=-40, τxy=30\tau_{xy}=30 MPa:

  1. σavg=20\sigma_{avg}=20 MPa; a=60a=60 MPa.
  2. RR​=602+302=\sqrt{60^2+30^2}​=67.08=67.08 MPa =τmax=\tau_{max}.
  3. σ1=87.08\sigma_1=87.08 MPa; σ2=−47.08\sigma_2=-47.08 MPa.
  4. θp\theta_p​=12atan2(30,60)=\tfrac12\mathrm{atan2}(30,60)​=12(26.57∘)=\tfrac12(26.57^{\circ})​=13.28∘=13.28^{\circ} (for σ1\sigma_1); σ2\sigma_2 at 103.28∘103.28^{\circ}.
  5. θs\theta_s​=13.28∘+45∘=13.28^{\circ}+45^{\circ}​=58.28∘=58.28^{\circ} (and −31.72∘-31.72^{\circ}); σ′=20\sigma'=20 MPa.
  6. Check: 87.08−47.0887.08-47.08​=40=40​=80−40=80-40 ✓. At 13.28∘13.28^{\circ}: σx′\sigma_{x'}​=20+60cos⁡26.57∘+30sin⁡26.57∘=20+60\cos26.57^{\circ}+30\sin26.57^{\circ}​=20+53.67+13.42=20+53.67+13.42​=87.08=87.08 ✓, τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−60(0.4472)+30(0.8944)=-60(0.4472)+30(0.8944)​=0=0 ✓.

Test result: σ1=87.1\sigma_1=87.1 MPa, σ2=−47.1\sigma_2=-47.1 MPa, θp=13.3∘\theta_p=13.3^{\circ}, τmax=67.1\tau_{max}=67.1 MPa, θs=58.3∘\theta_s=58.3^{\circ}

Justification. The atan2 form avoids the common error of getting θp\theta_p in the wrong quadrant from a plain arctangent, and the final check catches sign mistakes.

U4-Q102Q102 | L6 Create | T3 | P | 10 marks

Construct, to scale, Mohr's circle for σx=80\sigma_x=80 MPa, σy=−20\sigma_y=-20 MPa and τxy=−40\tau_{xy}=-40 MPa. From the construction obtain the principal stresses, the maximum shear stress, and sketch the principal and maximum-shear elements.

Solution

Design problem. Build the circle step by step so that every reading can be checked by calculation.

Assumptions and sign convention. Tension positive; σ\sigma axis to the right, clockwise-turning shear plotted upward: X=(σx,−τxy)X=(\sigma_x,-\tau_{xy}), Y=(σy,+τxy)Y=(\sigma_y,+\tau_{xy}). Scale: 1 mm =1=1 MPa (or 1 cm =10=10 MPa); element angle is half the circle angle.

Construction.

  1. Draw the σ\sigma and τ\tau axes through the origin.
  2. Plot X=(80,+40)X=(80,+40) (since −τxy=+40-\tau_{xy}=+40) and Y=(−20,−40)Y=(-20,-40).
  3. Join XYXY; it cuts the σ\sigma axis at the centre C=80+(−20)2=30C=\dfrac{80+(-20)}{2}=30 MPa.
  4. With centre CC and radius CXCX draw the circle. Radius by measurement or calculation: RR​=502+402=\sqrt{50^2+40^2}​=64.03=64.03 MPa.
  5. Mark AA (right end of the horizontal diameter) and BB (left end), and DD, EE at the top and bottom of the circle.

Readings.

Point Reading
AA σ1\sigma_1​=30+64.03=30+64.03​=94.03=94.03 MPa
BB σ2\sigma_2​=30−64.03=30-64.03​=−34.03=-34.03 MPa
DD, EE τmax=R=64.03\tau_{max}=R=64.03 MPa, with σ′=30\sigma'=30 MPa

Angles. CXCX runs 5050 to the right and 4040 up, so it lies 38.66∘38.66^{\circ} above the σ\sigma axis. Turning from XX to AA is 38.66∘38.66^{\circ} clockwise on the circle, so 2θp=−38.66∘2\theta_p=-38.66^{\circ} and θp1=−19.33∘\theta_{p1}=-19.33^{\circ} (the σ1\sigma_1 plane is 19.33∘19.33^{\circ} clockwise from xx). The σ2\sigma_2 plane is at +70.67∘+70.67^{\circ}. From XX to DD the turn is 90∘−38.66∘90^{\circ}-38.66^{\circ}​=51.34∘=51.34^{\circ} counter-clockwise, so θs=25.67∘\theta_s=25.67^{\circ} (and −64.33∘-64.33^{\circ}). These are 45∘45^{\circ} from the principal planes ✓.

Elements to sketch. - Principal element: turn the element 19.33∘19.33^{\circ} clockwise; its faces carry 94.094.0 MPa (tension) and −34.0-34.0 MPa (compression), no shear. - Maximum-shear element: turn it 25.67∘25.67^{\circ} counter-clockwise; each face carries a normal stress of 3030 MPa and a shear of 64.064.0 MPa.

Check (analytical). tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2(−40)100=\dfrac{2(-40)}{100}​=−0.8=-0.8​⇒2θp\Rightarrow2\theta_p​=−38.66∘=-38.66^{\circ} ✓; σ1+σ2=60=σx+σy\sigma_1+\sigma_2=60=\sigma_x+\sigma_y ✓.

σ1=94.0\sigma_1=94.0 MPa at −19.3∘-19.3^{\circ}; σ2=−34.0\sigma_2=-34.0 MPa; τmax=64.0\tau_{max}=64.0 MPa at 25.7∘25.7^{\circ} (with σ′=30\sigma'=30 MPa)

U4-Q103Q103 | L6 Create | T2 | P | 10 marks

Design a thin-walled test tube (mean diameter 50 mm, thickness 3 mm) under combined axial force FF and torque TT that produces principal stresses of 100 MPa and −40-40 MPa. Determine the required FF and TT.

Solution
