Design problem. Find the axial force and torque that give a prescribed principal-stress state in a thin-walled tube (no internal pressure, so σhoop=0\sigma_{hoop}=0).

Given. Mean D=50D=50 mm, mean radius r=25r=25 mm, t=3t=3 mm; σ1=100\sigma_1=100, σ2=−40\sigma_2=-40 MPa.

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin tube: A=2πrtA=2\pi rt, τ=T2πr2t\tau=\dfrac{T}{2\pi r^2t}; stress state on the surface: σx=FA\sigma_x=\dfrac{F}{A} (axial), σy=0\sigma_y=0, τxy=τ\tau_{xy}=\tau; tension positive; units N, mm.

Formula. σ1+σ2=σx\sigma_1+\sigma_2=\sigma_x; σ1σ2\sigma_1\sigma_2​=σxσy−τ2=\sigma_x\sigma_y-\tau^2​=−τ2=-\tau^2 (invariants of the stress state when σy=0\sigma_y=0).

Solution.

  1. σx\sigma_x​=σ1+σ2=\sigma_1+\sigma_2​=100−40=100-40​=60=60 MPa.
  2. τ2=−σ1σ2=4000\tau^2=-\sigma_1\sigma_2=4000, so τ=63.25\tau=63.25 MPa.
  3. Check with the circle: centre σx/2=30\sigma_x/2=30 MPa, radius RR​=302+63.252=\sqrt{30^2+63.25^2}​=70.0=70.0 MPa, giving σ1,2\sigma_{1,2}​=30±70=30\pm70​=100,=100,​−40-40 MPa ✓.
  4. Area: AA​=2π(25)(3)=2\pi(25)(3)​=471.24=471.24 mm2^2.
  5. FF​=σxA=\sigma_xA​=60(471.24)=60(471.24)​=28 274=28\,274 N =28.3=28.3 kN.
  6. TT​=τ(2πr2t)=\tau(2\pi r^2t)​=63.25 (2π×625×3)=63.25\,(2\pi\times625\times3)​=63.25(11 781)=63.25(11\,781)​=7.451×105=7.451\times10^{5} N mm =745=745 N m.
  7. Principal angle: tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2(63.25)60=\dfrac{2(63.25)}{60}​=2.108=2.108, so θp=32.3∘\theta_p=32.3^{\circ} from the tube axis (for σ1=100\sigma_1=100 MPa, with τxy>0\tau_{xy}>0); the shear sign follows the torque direction.

F=28.3F=28.3 kN (tension),   T=745\;T=745 N m. Surface stresses: σx=60\sigma_x=60 MPa, τ=63.2\tau=63.2 MPa.

Justification. Thin-wall stresses are uniform through the thickness (t/r=0.12t/r=0.12 is close to the usual limit 0.10.1, so the values are approximate; with the mean radius the error is small). Two unknowns (FF and TT) fixed by two prescribed principal stresses give a unique design.

U4-Q104Q104 | L6 Create | T1 | P | 10 marks

Two timber bars (cross-sectional area 5000 mm2^2) are spliced by a glued scarf joint. The glue can carry 2.5 MPa normal and 1.5 MPa shear stress. Develop a design rule for the joint angle θ\theta (measured between the axis and the normal to the glue plane) so that the joint carries an axial tension of 20 kN.

Solution

Design problem. Choose the joint angle so that the stresses on the glue plane stay within the glue's capacity.

Given. A=5000A=5000 mm2^2; P=20 000P=20\,000 N; σglue≤2.5\sigma_{glue}\le2.5 MPa (normal), τglue≤1.5\tau_{glue}\le1.5 MPa (shear); θ\theta between the bar axis and the glue-plane normal.

Assumptions and sign convention. Uniaxial stress σ=P/A\sigma=P/A in the bars; shear taken as a magnitude; the plane has its normal at θ\theta to the axis, so θ=0\theta=0 is a butt joint (cross-section) and θ→90∘\theta\to90^{\circ} is a plane almost parallel to the axis.

Formula. σθ=σcos⁡2θ\sigma_\theta=\sigma\cos^2\theta, ∣τθ∣|\tau_\theta|​=σsin⁡θcos⁡θ=\sigma\sin\theta\cos\theta​=σ2sin⁡2θ=\dfrac{\sigma}{2}\sin2\theta.

Solution.

  1. σ=20 0005000=4.0\sigma=\dfrac{20\,000}{5000}=4.0 MPa.
  2. Normal-stress rule: 4cos⁡2θ4\cos^2\theta​≤2.5\le2.5​⇒cos⁡2θ\Rightarrow\cos^2\theta​≤0.625\le0.625​⇒θ\Rightarrow\theta​≥37.76∘\ge37.76^{\circ}.
  3. Shear-stress rule: 2sin⁡2θ2\sin2\theta​≤1.5\le1.5​⇒sin⁡2θ\Rightarrow\sin2\theta​≤0.75\le0.75, so 2θ≤48.59∘2\theta\le48.59^{\circ} or 2θ≥131.41∘2\theta\ge131.41^{\circ}, i.e. θ≤24.30∘\theta\le24.30^{\circ} or θ≥65.70∘\theta\ge65.70^{\circ}.
  4. Both together: the first rule needs θ≥37.76∘\theta\ge37.76^{\circ}, so the shear rule leaves only θ≥65.70∘\theta\ge65.70^{\circ}.
  5. Table:
θ\theta σθ\sigma_\theta (MPa) τθ\tau_\theta (MPa) OK?
60∘60^{\circ}1.001.73no (shear)
65.7∘65.7^{\circ}0.681.50limit
70∘70^{\circ}0.471.29yes
75∘75^{\circ}0.271.00yes
80∘80^{\circ}0.120.68yes

Design rule: θ≥65.7∘\theta\ge65.7^{\circ} (the glue plane at ≤24.3∘\le24.3^{\circ} to the axis); recommended θ≈70∘\theta\approx70^{\circ} to 75∘75^{\circ} (shear 1.291.29 to 1.001.00 MPa, normal 0.470.47 to 0.270.27 MPa)

Justification. Shear on the glue is the governing check. A longer, shallower scarf lowers both stresses but needs a longer cut, so the practical choice is the smallest angle that gives a margin, about 70∘70^{\circ} (margin on shear 1.5/1.29=1.171.5/1.29=1.17). For a different load PP the rule is sin⁡2θ≤2(1.5)AP\sin2\theta\le\dfrac{2(1.5)A}{P} and cos⁡2θ≤2.5AP\cos^2\theta\le\dfrac{2.5A}{P}.

U4-Q105Q105 | L6 Create | P1 | P | 10 marks

Design a cylindrical air receiver of internal volume 2 m3^3 with length =3×=3\times diameter, working pressure 1.2 MPa, σallow=80\sigma_{allow}=80 MPa, joint efficiency 0.85 and a corrosion allowance of 3 mm. Specify diameter, length and plate thickness.

Solution

Design problem. Size a thin cylindrical shell for a given volume and pressure.

Given. V=2V=2 m3^3, L=3DL=3D, p=1.2p=1.2 MPa, σallow=80\sigma_{allow}=80 MPa, η=0.85\eta=0.85, corrosion allowance c=3c=3 mm.

Assumptions and sign convention. Internal diameter DD; thin-walled; the syllabus formulas are σh=pD2tηl\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t\eta_l} and σL=pD4tηc\sigma_L=\dfrac{pD}{4t\eta_c}, and only one efficiency (0.85) is given, so it is taken as the longitudinal-joint value used for the hoop stress; the circumferential seam does not govern as long as ηc≥ηl/2=0.425\eta_c\ge\eta_l/2=0.425 (the hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress, Q089); the corrosion allowance is added to the pressure thickness; dished ends are ignored for the volume (cylinder only); tension positive.

Formula. V=π4D2LV=\dfrac{\pi}{4}D^2L,   th=pD2σallowη\;t_h=\dfrac{pD}{2\sigma_{allow}\eta},   tL=pD4σallowη\;t_L=\dfrac{pD}{4\sigma_{allow}\eta}.

Solution.

  1. Volume: VV​=π4D2(3D)=\dfrac{\pi}{4}D^2(3D)​=3π4D3=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}D^3​=2=2​⇒D3\Rightarrow D^3​=83π=\dfrac{8}{3\pi}​=0.8488=0.8488 m3^3, so D=0.947D=0.947 m.
  2. Adopt D=950D=950 mm and L=2850L=2850 mm (=3D=3D). Check: VV​=π4(0.95)2(2.85)=\dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.95)^2(2.85)​=2.02=2.02 m3≥2^3\ge2 ✓.
  3. Hoop requirement: tht_h​=1.2(950)2(80)(0.85)=\dfrac{1.2(950)}{2(80)(0.85)}​=1140136=\dfrac{1140}{136}​=8.38=8.38 mm.
  4. Longitudinal requirement: tLt_L​=1.2(950)4(80)(0.85)=\dfrac{1.2(950)}{4(80)(0.85)}​=4.19=4.19 mm (half, so the hoop stress governs).
  5. Add the corrosion allowance: 8.38+3=11.388.38+3=11.38 mm.
  6. Standard plate: 12 mm. Thin-wall check: t/rt/r​=12/475=12/475​=0.025=0.025​<0.1<0.1 ✓. Stress in the plate at the working thickness (after 3 mm corrosion, t=9t=9 mm): σh\sigma_h​=1.2(950)2(9)(0.85)=\dfrac{1.2(950)}{2(9)(0.85)}​=74.5=74.5 MPa <80<80 ✓.

D=950D=950 mm, L=2850L=2850 mm, plate thickness t=12t=12 mm (8.38 mm for pressure +3+3 mm corrosion, rounded up)

Justification. The hoop stress (twice the longitudinal) governs thickness. The 12 mm plate still satisfies the stress limit when 3 mm has corroded away.

U4-Q106Q106 | L6 Create | P1 | P | 8 marks

Design a spherical storage vessel for 268 m3^3 of gas at 1.8 MPa with σallow=120\sigma_{allow}=120 MPa and joint efficiency 0.9. Determine the radius and thickness.

Solution

Design problem. Size a thin sphere for a given volume and pressure.

Given. V=268V=268 m3^3, p=1.8p=1.8 MPa, σallow=120\sigma_{allow}=120 MPa, η=0.9\eta=0.9.

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin-walled; internal radius; the seam stress is the plate stress divided by η\eta; tension positive; no corrosion allowance (none given).

Formula. V=43πr3V=\dfrac43\pi r^3,   σ=pD4tη\;\sigma=\dfrac{pD}{4t\eta}, so t=pD4σallowηt=\dfrac{pD}{4\sigma_{allow}\eta}.

Solution.

  1. r3r^3​=3V4π=\dfrac{3V}{4\pi}​=3(268)4π=\dfrac{3(268)}{4\pi}​=63.98=63.98 m3^3, so r=4.00r=4.00 m and D=8.00D=8.00 m (=8000=8000 mm).
  2. tt​=1.8(8000)4(120)(0.9)=\dfrac{1.8(8000)}{4(120)(0.9)}​=14 400432=\dfrac{14\,400}{432}​=33.3=33.3 mm.
  3. Thin-wall check: t/rt/r​=33.3/4000=33.3/4000​=0.008=0.008​<0.1<0.1 ✓.
  4. Adopt the next whole millimetre: 34 mm (the syllabus has no table of standard plate sizes).
  5. Comparison (why a sphere): a cylinder under the same conditions would need t=pD2ση=66.7t=\dfrac{pD}{2\sigma\eta}=66.7 mm, twice as thick (Q031).

r=4.00r=4.00 m (D=8D=8 m), t=33.3t=33.3 mm, use 34 mm

U4-Q107Q107 | L6 Create | P1 | P | 8 marks

Propose an experimental scheme using strain gauges to determine the working pressure of a thin cylinder (D=500D=500 mm, t=6t=6 mm, E=205E=205 GPa, ν=0.29\nu=0.29). Calculate the expected hoop and longitudinal strains at p=2p=2 MPa and state which gauge you would use.

Solution

Design problem. Measure the pressure indirectly from the wall strain.

Given. D=500D=500 mm, t=6t=6 mm, E=205 000E=205\,000 MPa, ν=0.29\nu=0.29, test pressure p=2p=2 MPa.

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin-walled closed cylinder; internal diameter; outer-surface stress state σh\sigma_h, σL\sigma_L with σr≈0\sigma_r\approx0; tension positive; the gauges are on a region away from the ends and seams.

Scheme. 1. Bond one gauge in the hoop direction and one in the axial direction on the outer surface, away from ends, welds and fittings. Add a dummy gauge on an unstressed piece of the same material for temperature compensation. 2. Connect each to a Wheatstone bridge (quarter bridge with the dummy) and zero it at atmospheric pressure. 3. Raise the pressure and record εh\varepsilon_h (and εL\varepsilon_L). 4. Calibrate: compare the pressure from the gauge with a standard pressure gauge.

Formula. σh=pD2t\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t}, σL=pD4t\sigma_L=\dfrac{pD}{4t}, εh=σh−νσLE\varepsilon_h=\dfrac{\sigma_h-\nu\sigma_L}{E}, εL=σL−νσhE\varepsilon_L=\dfrac{\sigma_L-\nu\sigma_h}{E}; inverse: p=2tEεhD(1−ν/2)p=\dfrac{2tE\varepsilon_h}{D(1-\nu/2)}.

Solution.

  1. σh\sigma_h​=2(500)2(6)=\dfrac{2(500)}{2(6)}​=83.33=83.33 MPa; σL=41.67\sigma_L=41.67 MPa.
  2. εh\varepsilon_h​=83.33−0.29(41.67)205 000=\dfrac{83.33-0.29(41.67)}{205\,000}​=71.25205 000=\dfrac{71.25}{205\,000}​=3.48×10−4=3.48\times10^{-4} (348 microstrain).
  3. εL\varepsilon_L​=41.67−0.29(83.33)205 000=\dfrac{41.67-0.29(83.33)}{205\,000}​=17.50205 000=\dfrac{17.50}{205\,000}​=8.5×10−5=8.5\times10^{-5} (85 microstrain).
  4. Ratio εh/εL=4.07\varepsilon_h/\varepsilon_L=4.07.
  5. Check of the inverse relation: pp​=2(6)(205 000)(3.476×10−4)500(1−0.145)=\dfrac{2(6)(205\,000)(3.476\times10^{-4})}{500(1-0.145)}​=855.0427.5=\dfrac{855.0}{427.5}​=2.00=2.00 MPa ✓.

At p=2p=2 MPa: εh=348\varepsilon_h=348 microstrain, εL=85\varepsilon_L=85 microstrain. Use the hoop gauge for pp: p=2tEεhD(1−ν/2)p=\dfrac{2tE\varepsilon_h}{D(1-\nu/2)}.

Justification. The hoop strain is about four times the axial strain, so it gives better resolution for the same measuring error. The axial gauge is kept as a check: εL/εh\varepsilon_L/\varepsilon_h should be close to 0.25, which confirms the thin-wall closed-end assumption.

U4-Q108Q108 | L6 Create | P2 | P | 8 marks

Design a hydraulic cylinder with inner radius 50 mm for a working pressure of 70 MPa and allowable tensile stress of 180 MPa. Determine the outer radius using Lamé's theory and recommend a standard value.

Solution

Design problem. Choose the outer radius so that the maximum hoop stress at the bore does not exceed 180 MPa.

Given. ri=50r_i=50 mm, pi=70p_i=70 MPa, po=0p_o=0, σallow=180\sigma_{allow}=180 MPa.

Assumptions and sign convention. Lamé's theory; tension positive; the maximum hoop stress at the inner surface governs; the course material has no table of standard sizes, so the "standard value" is taken as the minimum rounded up to the next whole millimetre, checked by the Lamé formula.

Formula. rori\dfrac{r_o}{r_i}​=σallow+piσallow−pi=\sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_{allow}+p_i}{\sigma_{allow}-p_i}}, from σθ,max\sigma_{\theta,max}​=piro2+ri2ro2−ri2=p_i\dfrac{r_o^2+r_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}.

Solution.

  1. rori\dfrac{r_o}{r_i}​=180+70180−70=\sqrt{\dfrac{180+70}{180-70}}​=2.273=\sqrt{2.273}​=1.5076=1.5076.
  2. ror_o​=1.5076(50)=1.5076(50)​=75.4=75.4 mm (minimum), wall 25.425.4 mm.
  3. Check at the minimum: σθ\sigma_\theta​=7075.382+50275.382−502=70\dfrac{75.38^2+50^2}{75.38^2-50^2}​=180.0=180.0 MPa ✓.
  4. The syllabus gives the minimum from the design relation; no table of standard sizes is in the course material, so the value is rounded up to the next whole millimetre: ro=76r_o=76 mm. Check: σθ(ri)\sigma_\theta(r_i)​=70762+502762−502=70\dfrac{76^2+50^2}{76^2-50^2}​=7082763276=70\dfrac{8276}{3276}​=176.8=176.8 MPa ≤180\le180 MPa ✓ (factor on the allowable =180176.8=1.02=\dfrac{180}{176.8}=1.02).
  5. Other stresses at ro=76r_o=76 mm: outer-surface hoop stress =2(70)(2500)5776−2500=\dfrac{2(70)(2500)}{5776-2500}​=106.8=106.8 MPa and radial stress at the bore =−70=-70 MPa.

Minimum ro=75.4r_o=75.4 mm; adopt ro=76r_o=76 mm (OD 152 mm), σθ,max=176.8\sigma_{\theta,max}=176.8 MPa <180<180 MPa

Justification. The minimum is set by the bore hoop stress; rounding up to 76 mm keeps the stress just inside the limit. A larger size would add margin but is not required by the syllabus method. Note how much thicker the wall must be as pi→σallowp_i\to\sigma_{allow} (Q035).

U4-Q109Q109 | L6 Create | P2 | P | 10 marks

A sleeve with inner radius 60 mm carries an internal pressure of 40 MPa and an external pressure of 10 MPa. Determine the minimum outer radius so that the maximum hoop stress does not exceed 100 MPa.

Solution

Design problem. Find ror_o for a thick tube loaded by both internal and external pressure so that the largest hoop stress stays within 100 MPa.

Given. ri=60r_i=60 mm, pi=40p_i=40 MPa, po=10p_o=10 MPa, σθ,max≤100\sigma_{\theta,max}\le100 MPa.

Assumptions and sign convention. Lamé's theory; tension positive; radial stress −pi-p_i at rir_i and −po-p_o at ror_o; the hoop stress is largest at the inner surface (checked below).

Formula. A=piri2−poro2ro2−ri2A=\dfrac{p_ir_i^2-p_or_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}, BB​=(pi−po)ri2ro2ro2−ri2=\dfrac{(p_i-p_o)r_i^2r_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2},   σθ=A+Br2\;\sigma_\theta=A+\dfrac{B}{r^2}.

Solution.

  1. At the inner surface (r=rir=r_i): σθ\sigma_\theta​=A+Bri2=A+\dfrac{B}{r_i^2}​=piri2−poro2+(pi−po)ro2ro2−ri2=\dfrac{p_ir_i^2-p_or_o^2+(p_i-p_o)r_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}​=piri2+(pi−2po)ro2ro2−ri2=\dfrac{p_ir_i^2+(p_i-2p_o)r_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}.
  2. Substitute: σθ(ri)\sigma_\theta(r_i)​=40(3600)+(40−20)ro2ro2−3600=\dfrac{40(3600)+(40-20)r_o^2}{r_o^2-3600}​=144 000+20ro2ro2−3600=\dfrac{144\,000+20r_o^2}{r_o^2-3600}.
  3. Set σθ(ri)≤100\sigma_\theta(r_i)\le100: 144 000+20ro2144\,000+20r_o^2​≤100ro2−360 000\le100r_o^2-360\,000​⇒80ro2\Rightarrow80r_o^2​≥504 000\ge504\,000​⇒ro2\Rightarrow r_o^2​≥6300\ge6300.
  4. ro≥6300=79.4r_o\ge\sqrt{6300}=79.4 mm.
  5. Check at ro=79.37r_o=79.37 mm: σθ(ri)\sigma_\theta(r_i)​=144 000+126 0002700=\dfrac{144\,000+126\,000}{2700}​=100.0=100.0 MPa ✓.
  6. Check the outer surface: σθ(ro)\sigma_\theta(r_o)​=252 000−10ro2ro2−3600=\dfrac{252\,000-10r_o^2}{r_o^2-3600}​=252 000−63 0002700=\dfrac{252\,000-63\,000}{2700}​=70=70 MPa <100<100 ✓, so the inner surface governs. Radial stresses are −40-40 and −10-10 MPa.

Minimum ro=79.4r_o=79.4 mm (wall 19.419.4 mm); the inner-surface hoop stress is exactly 100 MPa and the outer-surface hoop stress is 70 MPa. A round value of 80 mm gives 144 000+20(6400)6400−3600\dfrac{144\,000+20(6400)}{6400-3600}​=97.1=97.1 MPa.

Justification. The external pressure helps (it lowers the hoop stress), so the wall can be thinner than with pip_i alone: with po=0p_o=0 the same limit would need ror_o​=14060 (60)=\sqrt{\dfrac{140}{60}}\,(60)​=91.7=91.7 mm (from rori=100+40100−40\dfrac{r_o}{r_i}=\sqrt{\dfrac{100+40}{100-40}}).

U4-Q110Q110 | L6 Create | P2 | P | 8 marks

Develop a table of σr\sigma_r and σθ\sigma_\theta at r=100r=100, 112.5, 125, 137.5 and 150 mm for a thick cylinder with ri=100r_i=100 mm, ro=150r_o=150 mm and pi=50p_i=50 MPa, and sketch the distributions.

Solution

Design problem. Build a table and plot of the Lamé stresses through the wall.

Given. ri=100r_i=100, ro=150r_o=150 mm, pi=50p_i=50 MPa, po=0p_o=0.

Assumptions and sign convention. Lamé's theory; tension positive (radial stress is compressive); closed or open ends do not change σr\sigma_r and σθ\sigma_\theta.

Formula. σr=A−Br2\sigma_r=A-\dfrac{B}{r^2}, σθ=A+Br2\sigma_\theta=A+\dfrac{B}{r^2}, A=piri2ro2−ri2A=\dfrac{p_ir_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}, B=piri2ro2ro2−ri2B=\dfrac{p_ir_i^2r_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}.

Solution.

  1. ro2−ri2r_o^2-r_i^2​=22 500−10 000=22\,500-10\,000​=12 500=12\,500 mm2^2.
  2. A=50(10 000)12 500=40A=\dfrac{50(10\,000)}{12\,500}=40 MPa; BB​=50(10 000)(22 500)12 500=\dfrac{50(10\,000)(22\,500)}{12\,500}​=9×105=9\times10^{5} MPa mm2^2.
  3. Table:
rr (mm) B/r2B/r^2 (MPa) σr\sigma_r (MPa) σθ\sigma_\theta (MPa) σr+σθ\sigma_r+\sigma_\theta (MPa)
100.090.00−50.0-50.0130.080.0
112.571.11−31.1-31.1111.180.0
125.057.60−17.6-17.697.680.0
137.547.60−7.6-7.687.680.0
150.040.000.080.080.0

Reading the sketch. σθ\sigma_\theta (tensile) is greatest, 130 MPa, at the inner surface and falls non-linearly (as 1/r21/r^2) to 80 MPa at the outer surface. σr\sigma_r (compressive) is −50-50 MPa (=−pi=-p_i) at the bore and rises to 0 at the free outer surface. The sum σr+σθ=2A=80\sigma_r+\sigma_\theta=2A=80 MPa is constant, as Lamé's solution requires.

σθ\sigma_\theta: 130.0, 111.1, 97.6, 87.6, 80.0 MPa; σr\sigma_r: −50.0-50.0, −31.1-31.1, −17.6-17.6, −7.6-7.6, 0 MPa; sum =80=80 MPa throughout

Agrees with Q&A model answer 20.

U4-Q111Q111 | L6 Create | E2 | P | 10 marks

Design a solid steel torsion bar (G=80G=80 GPa) of length 800 mm that must store 150 J of strain energy at a maximum shear stress of 300 MPa. Find the diameter and the torque at this condition.

Solution

Design problem. Choose the diameter so that the bar stores 150 J when the surface shear stress reaches 300 MPa.

Given. G=80 000G=80\,000 MPa, L=800L=800 mm, U=150U=150 J =1.5×105=1.5\times10^{5} N mm, τmax=300\tau_{max}=300 MPa.

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic torsion; solid circular section; the stress and energy are for the same torque; units N and mm.

Formula. UV=τmax24G\dfrac UV=\dfrac{\tau_{max}^2}{4G} (solid shaft), V=πd24LV=\dfrac{\pi d^2}{4}L, τmax=16Tπd3\tau_{max}=\dfrac{16T}{\pi d^3}, and the check U=T2L2GJU=\dfrac{T^2L}{2GJ}.

Solution.

  1. UV\dfrac UV​=30024(80 000)=\dfrac{300^2}{4(80\,000)}​=0.28125=0.28125 N/mm2^2.
  2. Required volume: VV​=1.5×1050.28125=\dfrac{1.5\times10^{5}}{0.28125}​=5.333×105=5.333\times10^{5} mm3^3.
  3. Area: AA​=VL=\dfrac VL​=5.333×105800=\dfrac{5.333\times10^{5}}{800}​=666.7=666.7 mm2^2.
  4. Diameter: dd​=4Aπ=\sqrt{\dfrac{4A}{\pi}}​=848.8=\sqrt{848.8}​=29.13=29.13 mm.
  5. Torque: JJ​=π(29.13)432=\dfrac{\pi(29.13)^4}{32}​=7.074×104=7.074\times10^{4} mm4^4; TT​=τmaxJc=\dfrac{\tau_{max}J}{c}​=300(7.074×104)14.57=\dfrac{300(7.074\times10^{4})}{14.57}​=1.457×106=1.457\times10^{6} N mm =1.457=1.457 kN m.
  6. Check: UU​=T2L2GJ=\dfrac{T^2L}{2GJ}​=(1.457×106)2(800)2(80 000)(7.074×104)=\dfrac{(1.457\times10^{6})^2(800)}{2(80\,000)(7.074\times10^{4})}​=1.50×105=1.50\times10^{5} N mm =150=150 J ✓.

Exact: d=29.1d=29.1 mm, T=1.46T=1.46 kN m. Practical choice d=30d=30 mm: UU​=0.28125×5.655×105=0.28125\times5.655\times10^{5}​=159=159 J (at τ=300\tau=300 MPa), TT​=π(300)(30)316=\dfrac{\pi(300)(30)^3}{16}​=1.59=1.59 kN m

Justification. The energy per unit volume is fixed by the allowable stress, so the volume (and hence dd for a given length) is fixed. Choosing the next round size (30 mm) gives the required energy with a 6% margin. A hollow bar of the same volume would store more (Q079), but the question asks for a solid one.

U4-Q112Q112 | L6 Create | E1 | P | 10 marks

A bolt of total length 100 mm has a threaded root portion 25 mm long (root diameter 12 mm) and a plain shank 75 mm long. It must absorb at least 0.8 J with a maximum stress of 180 MPa in the root (E=200E=200 GPa). Determine the largest permissible shank diameter.

Solution

Design problem. Find the shank diameter dd for which the bolt still stores at least 0.8 J when the root carries 180 MPa.

Given. Root: dr=12d_r=12 mm, Lr=25L_r=25 mm. Shank: diameter dd (unknown), Ls=75L_s=75 mm. σroot=180\sigma_{root}=180 MPa, E=200 000E=200\,000 MPa, U≥0.8U\ge0.8 J =800=800 N mm.

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic; the same axial force in both portions; stress concentration at threads neglected; the root is the smallest section so it limits the load; units N and mm.

Formula. P=σrootArP=\sigma_{root}A_r,   U=P22E(LrAr+LsAs)\;U=\dfrac{P^2}{2E}\left(\dfrac{L_r}{A_r}+\dfrac{L_s}{A_s}\right).

Solution.

  1. ArA_r​=π(12)24=\dfrac{\pi(12)^2}{4}​=113.10=113.10 mm2^2; PP​=180(113.10)=180(113.10)​=20 358=20\,358 N.
  2. P22E\dfrac{P^2}{2E}​=(20 358)2400 000=\dfrac{(20\,358)^2}{400\,000}​=1036.1=1036.1 N.
  3. Condition: 1036.1(25113.10+75As)1036.1\left(\dfrac{25}{113.10}+\dfrac{75}{A_s}\right)​≥800\ge800.
  4. 25113.10=0.2210\dfrac{25}{113.10}=0.2210, so 0.2210+75As0.2210+\dfrac{75}{A_s}​≥0.7721\ge0.7721​⇒75As\Rightarrow\dfrac{75}{A_s}​≥0.5511\ge0.5511​⇒As\Rightarrow A_s​≤136.1\le136.1 mm2^2.
  5. dd​≤4(136.1)π\le\sqrt{\dfrac{4(136.1)}{\pi}}​=13.16=13.16 mm.
  6. Checks: d=13d=13 mm gives UU​=1036.1(0.2210+75132.73)=1036.1\left(0.2210+\dfrac{75}{132.73}\right)​=814=814 N mm ≥800\ge800 ✓; d=13.16d=13.16 mm gives 800800 N mm; d=12d=12 mm (uniform bolt) gives 916916 N mm.

Largest permissible shank diameter d=13.16d=13.16 mm (use 13 mm: U=0.814U=0.814 J ≥0.8\ge0.8 J)

Justification. A bigger shank is stiffer but absorbs less energy for the same root stress, because its extra area is lightly stressed (Q038, Q093). Energy is highest if the shank is no larger than the root; 0.8 J is met only with a shank up to about 13 mm.

U4-Q113Q113 | L6 Create | T3 | P | 10 marks

A cylinder (hoop stress 100 MPa, longitudinal stress 50 MPa, from p=2.5p=2.5 MPa and r/t=40r/t=40) has a helical weld seam inclined at 30∘30^{\circ} to the cylinder axis. Construct Mohr's circle and determine the normal and shear stresses on the seam; design the allowable pressure if the weld permits 80 MPa normal and 25 MPa shear.

Solution

Design problem. Find the stresses on the weld plane and the largest pressure for which they stay within the weld's limits.

Given. p=2.5p=2.5 MPa, r/t=40r/t=40: σh=prt=100\sigma_h=\dfrac{pr}{t}=100 MPa, σL=pr2t=50\sigma_L=\dfrac{pr}{2t}=50 MPa. Seam at 30∘30^{\circ} to the axis. Weld limits: 8080 MPa normal, 2525 MPa shear.

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin-walled closed cylinder; xx along the axis (σx=σL=50\sigma_x=\sigma_L=50), yy in the hoop direction (σy=σh=100\sigma_y=\sigma_h=100), τxy=0\tau_{xy}=0; the seam line makes 30∘30^{\circ} with xx, so the seam plane has its normal at 60∘60^{\circ} to xx (the symmetric seam gives the same magnitudes); tension positive.

Construction. 1. X=(50,0)X=(50,0) and Y=(100,0)Y=(100,0) are on the σ\sigma axis (τxy=0\tau_{xy}=0); centre C=75C=75 MPa, radius R=25R=25 MPa. 2. The seam normal is at 60∘60^{\circ} to xx, so turn the diameter 2θ=120∘2\theta=120^{\circ} counter-clockwise. 3. Read X′X' from the figure: abscissa σn\sigma_n and ordinate −τ-\tau (values calculated below and checked against the plot).

Solution.

  1. σn\sigma_n​=σx+σy2+σx−σy2cos⁡2θ=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}+\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\cos2\theta​=75+(−25)cos⁡120∘=75+(-25)\cos120^{\circ}​=75+12.5=75+12.5​=87.5=87.5 MPa.
  2. τ\tau​=−σx−σy2sin⁡2θ=-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\sin2\theta​=25sin⁡120∘=25\sin120^{\circ}​=21.65=21.65 MPa (magnitude).
  3. Check: σn\sigma_n on the perpendicular plane is 62.562.5 MPa and 87.5+62.5=15087.5+62.5=150 ✓.
  4. Stresses scale with pp (σh=40p\sigma_h=40p, σL=20p\sigma_L=20p): σn=35p\sigma_n=35p and τ=8.66p\tau=8.66p (MPa for pp in MPa).
  5. Normal limit: 35p≤80⇒p≤2.28635p\le80\Rightarrow p\le2.286 MPa.
  6. Shear limit: 8.66p8.66p​≤25\le25​⇒p\Rightarrow p​≤2.887\le2.887 MPa.
  7. Allowable pressure =min⁡=2.29=\min=2.29 MPa (the normal stress governs).

At p=2.5p=2.5 MPa: σn=87.5\sigma_n=87.5 MPa, τ=21.7\tau=21.7 MPa on the seam (normal stress exceeds 80 MPa, so 2.52.5 MPa is too high). Allowable p=2.29p=2.29 MPa.

Justification. The seam normal stress, 87.5 MPa, exceeds the weld's 80 MPa, so the design pressure must be reduced by 8087.5=91%\dfrac{80}{87.5}=91\% to 2.29 MPa. A smaller seam angle to the axis would raise the normal stress towards the hoop value, so the angle should be chosen with this check in mind.

U4-Q114Q114 | L6 Create | T1 | P | 8 marks

Prepare a table of σx′\sigma_{x'}, τx′y′\tau_{x'y'} and σy′\sigma_{y'} for σx=80\sigma_x=80, σy=−20\sigma_y=-20, τxy=30\tau_{xy}=30 MPa at θ=0∘\theta=0^{\circ}, 15°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 75°, 90°, plot the variation and identify the principal and maximum-shear orientations.

Solution

Design problem. Tabulate and plot the transformation equations to locate the extremes.

Given. σx=80\sigma_x=80, σy=−20\sigma_y=-20, τxy=30\tau_{xy}=30 MPa; θ=0∘\theta=0^{\circ} to 90∘90^{\circ} in 15∘15^{\circ} steps.

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; tension positive; θ\theta counter-clockwise from xx.

Formula. σx′\sigma_{x'}​=30+50cos⁡2θ+30sin⁡2θ=30+50\cos2\theta+30\sin2\theta, σy′\sigma_{y'}​=30−50cos⁡2θ−30sin⁡2θ=30-50\cos2\theta-30\sin2\theta, τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−50sin⁡2θ+30cos⁡2θ=-50\sin2\theta+30\cos2\theta.

Solution. (σavg=30\sigma_{avg}=30 MPa, σx−σy2=50\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}=50 MPa.)

θ\theta σx′\sigma_{x'} (MPa) σy′\sigma_{y'} (MPa) τx′y′\tau_{x'y'} (MPa)
0∘0^{\circ}80.0−20.0-20.030.0
15∘15^{\circ}88.3−28.3-28.31.0
30∘30^{\circ}81.0−21.0-21.0−28.3-28.3
45∘45^{\circ}60.00.0−50.0-50.0
60∘60^{\circ}31.029.0−58.3-58.3
75∘75^{\circ}1.758.3−51.0-51.0
90∘90^{\circ}−20.0-20.080.0−30.0-30.0

Extremes. 1. RR​=502+302=\sqrt{50^2+30^2}​=58.31=58.31 MPa. 2. tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2(30)100=\dfrac{2(30)}{100}​=0.6=0.6​⇒θp\Rightarrow\theta_p​=15.48∘=15.48^{\circ}: σ1\sigma_1​=30+58.31=30+58.31​=88.31=88.31 MPa (maximum of σx′\sigma_{x'}, where τx′y′=0\tau_{x'y'}=0, as the table shows at 15∘15^{\circ}); σ2=−28.31\sigma_2=-28.31 MPa at 105.48∘105.48^{\circ} (the minimum, where σy′\sigma_{y'} reaches its maximum 88.3 MPa). 3. Maximum shear τmax=R=58.31\tau_{max}=R=58.31 MPa at θs\theta_s​=θp+45∘=\theta_p+45^{\circ}​=60.48∘=60.48^{\circ} (value −58.31-58.31 MPa in the table at 60∘60^{\circ}) and at −29.52∘-29.52^{\circ} (+58.31+58.31 MPa), with σ′=30\sigma'=30 MPa (table: σx′≈31\sigma_{x'}\approx31 at 60∘60^{\circ} ✓). 4. Invariance check: σx′+σy′\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'}​=60=60​=σx+σy=\sigma_x+\sigma_y in every row ✓.

σ1=88.3\sigma_1=88.3 MPa at 15.5∘15.5^{\circ}, σ2=−28.3\sigma_2=-28.3 MPa at 105.5∘105.5^{\circ}; τmax=58.3\tau_{max}=58.3 MPa at 60.5∘60.5^{\circ} and −29.5∘-29.5^{\circ} (σ′=30\sigma'=30 MPa)

U4-Q115Q115 | L6 Create | E1 | P | 8 marks

Design a rectangular cantilever (depth h=2bh=2b) that must deflect no more than 2 mm under a 300 N end load over L=0.8L=0.8 m (E=200E=200 GPa), using the strain-energy expression U=P2L3/6EIU=P^2L^3/6EI to obtain the deflection. Find bb.

Solution

Design problem. Choose the width bb so that the tip deflection does not exceed 2 mm.

Given. P=300P=300 N, L=800L=800 mm, E=200 000E=200\,000 MPa, h=2bh=2b (hh is the depth in the bending direction), δ≤2\delta\le2 mm.

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic; bending energy only; a single tip load, so 12Pδ=U\tfrac12P\delta=U gives the deflection at the load; units N and mm.

Formula. U=P2L36EIU=\dfrac{P^2L^3}{6EI},   δ=2UP=PL33EI\;\delta=\dfrac{2U}{P}=\dfrac{PL^3}{3EI},   I=bh312\;I=\dfrac{bh^3}{12}.

Solution.

  1. II​=b(2b)312=\dfrac{b(2b)^3}{12}​=8b412=\dfrac{8b^4}{12}​=2b43=\dfrac{2b^4}{3}.
  2. δ\delta​=PL33E(23b4)=\dfrac{PL^3}{3E\left(\tfrac23b^4\right)}​=PL32Eb4=\dfrac{PL^3}{2Eb^4}.
  3. Require δ≤2\delta\le2: b4b^4​≥PL32Eδ\ge\dfrac{PL^3}{2E\delta}​=300(800)32(200 000)(2)=\dfrac{300(800)^3}{2(200\,000)(2)}​=1.536×10118×105=\dfrac{1.536\times10^{11}}{8\times10^{5}}​=1.92×105=1.92\times10^{5} mm4^4.
  4. bb​≥(1.92×105)1/4\ge(1.92\times10^{5})^{1/4}​=20.93=20.93 mm, so h=2b≥41.9h=2b\ge41.9 mm.
  5. Adopt b=21b=21 mm, h=42h=42 mm: II​=21(42)312=\dfrac{21(42)^3}{12}​=1.296×105=1.296\times10^{5} mm4^4; δ\delta​=300(800)33(200 000)(1.296×105)=\dfrac{300(800)^3}{3(200\,000)(1.296\times10^{5})}​=1.97=1.97 mm ≤2\le2 ✓.
  6. Strain energy at this size: UU​=12Pδ=\dfrac12P\delta​=12(300)(1.974)=\tfrac12(300)(1.974)​=296=296 N mm.
  7. Strength check (flexure formula, from Unit 3): σ\sigma​=6PLbh2=\dfrac{6PL}{bh^2}​=6(300)(800)21(42)2=\dfrac{6(300)(800)}{21(42)^2}​=38.9=38.9 MPa, well within the strength of steel.

b=20.9b=20.9 mm, h=41.9h=41.9 mm minimum; adopt 21×4221\times42 mm (δ=1.97\delta=1.97 mm)

Justification. Stiffness (the 2 mm limit) governs, not strength. Because δ∝1/b4\delta\propto1/b^4, a small increase in size reduces the deflection sharply. The energy method is valid here since there is only one load and the deflection wanted is at its point of application.

U4-Q116Q116 | L6 Create | E1 | P | 8 marks

Derive the strain energy of a tapered circular rod (diameter varying linearly from d1d_1 to d2d_2 over length LL) under axial load PP, and evaluate it for d1=20d_1=20 mm, d2=40d_2=40 mm, L=0.6L=0.6 m, P=40P=40 kN, E=200E=200 GPa.

Solution

Design problem. Derive and apply the variable-section axial energy formula U=∫P22AEdxU=\displaystyle\int\dfrac{P^2}{2AE}dx (course notes, C.4.1).

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic; constant axial force PP; the taper is gentle so that the stress is uniform over each cross-section (a standard approximation); units N and mm.

Derivation.

  1. Diameter at distance xx from the small end: d(x)d(x)​=d1+(d2−d1)Lx=d_1+\dfrac{(d_2-d_1)}{L}x, so A(x)=πd(x)24A(x)=\dfrac{\pi d(x)^2}{4}.
  2. UU​=∫0LP22A(x)Edx=\displaystyle\int_0^L\dfrac{P^2}{2A(x)E}dx​=2P2πE∫0Ldxd(x)2=\dfrac{2P^2}{\pi E}\int_0^L\dfrac{dx}{d(x)^2}.
  3. Let k=d2−d1Lk=\dfrac{d_2-d_1}{L}, then ∫0Ldx(d1+kx)2\displaystyle\int_0^L\dfrac{dx}{(d_1+kx)^2}​=1k(1d1−1d2)=\dfrac1k\left(\dfrac1{d_1}-\dfrac1{d_2}\right)​=1k⋅d2−d1d1d2=\dfrac1k\cdot\dfrac{d_2-d_1}{d_1d_2}​=Ld1d2=\dfrac{L}{d_1d_2}.

U=2P2LπE d1d2U=\dfrac{2P^2L}{\pi E\,d_1d_2} (and for d1=d2=dd_1=d_2=d it reduces to P2L2AE\dfrac{P^2L}{2AE} ✓)

Evaluation.

  1. UU​=2(40 000)2(600)π(200 000)(20)(40)=\dfrac{2(40\,000)^2(600)}{\pi(200\,000)(20)(40)}​=1.92×10125.027×108=\dfrac{1.92\times10^{12}}{5.027\times10^{8}}​=3820=3820 N mm =3.82=3.82 J.
  2. Check by numerical integration of ∫P22AEdx\int\dfrac{P^2}{2AE}dx: 3819.7 N mm ✓.
  3. Comparison: uniform 20 mm rod =7639=7639 N mm; uniform 40 mm rod =1910=1910 N mm. The tapered rod lies between them (the geometric-mean diameter d1d2=28.3\sqrt{d_1d_2}=28.3 mm gives exactly 3820 N mm).
  4. Maximum stress occurs at the small end: σ=40 000314.16=127.3\sigma=\dfrac{40\,000}{314.16}=127.3 MPa; at the large end 31.831.8 MPa.

U=2P2LπEd1d2=3820U=\dfrac{2P^2L}{\pi Ed_1d_2}=3820 N mm ≈3.82\approx3.82 J

U4-Q117Q117 | L6 Create | E2 | P | 8 marks

Develop a general expression for the strain energy of a shaft of two equal-length portions with diameters ndnd and dd under torque TT. Evaluate Un/U1U_n/U_1 for n=1.5n=1.5 and comment on the design implication.

Solution

Design problem. Compare the torsional energy of a stepped shaft with that of a uniform shaft.

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic; same torque TT in both portions; each portion has length L/2L/2; J=πd432J=\dfrac{\pi d^4}{32} for the diameter dd portion, so Jn=n4JJ_n=n^4J for the diameter ndnd portion; stress concentration neglected.

Derivation (course notes C5).

  1. UU​=∑T2Li2GJi=\displaystyle\sum\dfrac{T^2L_i}{2GJ_i}​=T2(L/2)2G(n4J)+T2(L/2)2GJ=\dfrac{T^2(L/2)}{2G(n^4J)}+\dfrac{T^2(L/2)}{2GJ}.
  2. UnU_n​=T2L4GJ(1+1n4)=\dfrac{T^2L}{4GJ}\left(1+\dfrac1{n^4}\right).
  3. A uniform shaft of diameter dd and length LL (n=1n=1): U1=T2L2GJU_1=\dfrac{T^2L}{2GJ}.

UnU1\dfrac{U_n}{U_1}​=12(1+1n4)=\dfrac12\left(1+\dfrac1{n^4}\right)

Evaluation for n=1.5n=1.5. 1. n4=1.54=5.0625n^4=1.5^4=5.0625, so 1n4=0.1975\dfrac1{n^4}=0.1975. 2. UnU1\dfrac{U_n}{U_1}​=12(1.1975)=\dfrac12(1.1975)​=0.599=0.599​≈0.60\approx0.60. 3. Reference: n=2n=2 gives 12(1+116)\dfrac12\left(1+\dfrac1{16}\right)​=1732=\dfrac{17}{32}​=0.53=0.53 (the notes' result).

Design implication. For the same torque, the maximum shear stress is set by the smaller diameter, so enlarging one half does not allow a larger torque but removes about 40% of the stored energy: the enlarged half is lightly stressed. A shaft meant to absorb torsional energy (a torsion bar, a shock-absorbing coupling) should therefore be of uniform section, or turned down to the minimum size, as in Q038 and Q093. A larger diameter is justified only for stiffness, a shoulder or bearing seat.

U4-Q118Q118 | L6 Create | P2 | P | 8 marks

Develop a design chart for thick cylinders: for pi/σallow=0.2p_i/\sigma_{allow}=0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 compute ro/rir_o/r_i using Lamé's theory, plot it and comment on the limit as pi→σallowp_i\to\sigma_{allow}.

Solution

Design problem. Tabulate and plot the thickness ratio against the pressure ratio.

Assumptions and sign convention. Lamé's theory, internal pressure only; the maximum hoop stress at the bore equals σallow\sigma_{allow}; x=pi/σallowx=p_i/\sigma_{allow}.

Formula. From σθ,max\sigma_{\theta,max}​=piro2+ri2ro2−ri2=p_i\dfrac{r_o^2+r_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}​=σallow=\sigma_{allow}: rori\dfrac{r_o}{r_i}​=σallow+piσallow−pi=\sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_{allow}+p_i}{\sigma_{allow}-p_i}}​=1+x1−x=\sqrt{\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}}.

Solution.

pi/σallowp_i/\sigma_{allow} ro/rir_o/r_i wall thickness t/rit/r_i
0.21.2/0.8=1.225\sqrt{1.2/0.8}=1.2250.225
0.41.4/0.6=1.528\sqrt{1.4/0.6}=1.5280.528
0.61.6/0.4=2.000\sqrt{1.6/0.4}=2.0001.000
0.81.8/0.2=3.000\sqrt{1.8/0.2}=3.0002.000
(0.9)1.9/0.1=4.359\sqrt{1.9/0.1}=4.3593.359

Comment on the limit. As x→1x\to1 the denominator 1−x→01-x\to0, so ro/ri→∞r_o/r_i\to\infty: no finite wall thickness is enough when pi=σallowp_i=\sigma_{allow}, and a single-material cylinder cannot be designed for pi≥σallowp_i\ge\sigma_{allow}. The curve is also steep at high ratios: raising xx from 0.6 to 0.8 raises ro/rir_o/r_i from 2 to 3, and 0.9 needs 4.36. The chart shows that a high-pressure design wastes material in thick walls (Q035), so a better material (higher σallow\sigma_{allow}) is the effective remedy.

ro/rir_o/r_i​=1.225,=1.225,​1.528,1.528,​2.00,2.00,​3.003.00 for pi/σallowp_i/\sigma_{allow}​=0.2,=0.2,​0.4,0.4,​0.6,0.6,​0.80.8; unbounded as pi→σallowp_i\to\sigma_{allow}

U4-Q119Q119 | L6 Create | P2 | P | 8 marks

A closed-end thick cylinder with ri=80r_i=80 mm carries pi=45p_i=45 MPa. Design the outer radius so that the maximum in-plane shear stress at the inner surface does not exceed 60 MPa.

Solution

Design problem. Choose ror_o so that τmax\tau_{max} at the bore is at most 60 MPa.

Given. ri=80r_i=80 mm, pi=45p_i=45 MPa, po=0p_o=0, τallow=60\tau_{allow}=60 MPa; closed ends.

Assumptions and sign convention. Lamé's theory; tension positive; in-plane shear =σθ−σr2=\dfrac{\sigma_\theta-\sigma_r}{2} at the inner surface (the largest shear in the wall); the closed-end axial stress σL=A\sigma_L=A lies between σr\sigma_r and σθ\sigma_\theta, so it does not change this value.

Formula. τmax\tau_{max}​=σθ−σr2=\dfrac{\sigma_\theta-\sigma_r}{2}​=piro2ro2−ri2=\dfrac{p_ir_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}.

Solution.

  1. 45ro2ro2−6400\dfrac{45r_o^2}{r_o^2-6400}​≤60\le60​⇒45ro2\Rightarrow45r_o^2​≤60ro2−384 000\le60r_o^2-384\,000​⇒15ro2\Rightarrow15r_o^2​≥384 000\ge384\,000​⇒ro2\Rightarrow r_o^2​≥25 600\ge25\,600.
  2. ro≥160r_o\ge160 mm (wall thickness 80 mm, ro/ri=2r_o/r_i=2).
  3. Check: σθ(ri)\sigma_\theta(r_i)​=4525 600+640019 200=45\dfrac{25\,600+6400}{19\,200}​=75=75 MPa; σr=−45\sigma_r=-45 MPa; τmax=75+452=60\tau_{max}=\dfrac{75+45}{2}=60 MPa ✓.
  4. Closed-end axial stress: σL=45(6400)19 200=15\sigma_L=\dfrac{45(6400)}{19\,200}=15 MPa, between −45-45 and 7575 ✓.
  5. Larger ror_o lowers the shear towards a limit of pi=45p_i=45 MPa as ro→∞r_o\to\infty, so the required thickness is finite as long as τallow>pi\tau_{allow}>p_i.

ro=160r_o=160 mm (minimum), i.e. wall thickness 80 mm; at this size σθ=75\sigma_\theta=75 MPa, σr=−45\sigma_r=-45 MPa, σL=15\sigma_L=15 MPa, τmax=60\tau_{max}=60 MPa

U4-Q120Q120 | L6 Create | P1 | P | 9 marks

A filament-wound cylindrical pressure vessel (r=100r=100 mm, p=5p=5 MPa) carries pressure only through helical fibres at angle α\alpha to the axis. Develop the condition for α\alpha that makes the fibres carry both hoop and axial loads, find α\alpha, and calculate the fibre thickness needed if the fibre stress is limited to 1500 MPa.

Solution

Design problem. Find the winding angle and the fibre thickness for a vessel whose fibres alone carry the pressure.

Method. The lecture notes and slides have no filament-winding formula, so the syllabus method for thin cylinders is used: equilibrium of a free body cut across and along the cylinder (the hoop and axial force balances of the notes, B.2 and Q030), with the only unknown, the fibre force, resolved along the hoop and axial directions. No formula from outside the syllabus is used.

Given. r=100r=100 mm, p=5p=5 MPa, fibre stress σf=1500\sigma_f=1500 MPa; fibres at ±α\pm\alpha to the axis (two symmetric helical layers), total fibre thickness tft_f.

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin wall; fibres carry tension only; the matrix carries no load; the fibre stress is uniform; closed ends so the axial force pπr2p\pi r^2 must also be carried; angle α\alpha measured from the axis.

Derivation.

  1. Fibre force per unit length of wall (across a section): σftf\sigma_ft_f in the fibre direction. Resolved along the hoop direction it is σftfsin⁡2α\sigma_ft_f\sin^2\alpha per unit axial length (fibre force ×sin⁡α\times\sin\alpha, number of fibres crossing a hoop section ∝sin⁡α\propto\sin\alpha); along the axis it is σftfcos⁡2α\sigma_ft_f\cos^2\alpha per unit circumference.
  2. Hoop balance (cut along the axis through a strip of unit length): pr=σftfsin⁡2αpr=\sigma_ft_f\sin^2\alpha. (Compare σht=pr\sigma_h t=pr for an isotropic wall.)
  3. Axial balance (cut across the vessel): pπr2p\pi r^2​=σftfcos⁡2α (2πr)=\sigma_ft_f\cos^2\alpha\,(2\pi r), so pr2=σftfcos⁡2α\dfrac{pr}{2}=\sigma_ft_f\cos^2\alpha.
  4. Dividing 2 by 3: tan⁡2α=2\tan^2\alpha=2, independent of pp, rr and σf\sigma_f.

Condition: tan⁡2α\tan^2\alpha​=2  =2\;​⇒  α\Rightarrow\;\alpha​=arctan⁡2=\arctan\sqrt2​=54.74∘=54.74^{\circ} (from the axis), so sin⁡2α=23\sin^2\alpha=\tfrac23 and cos⁡2α=13\cos^2\alpha=\tfrac13

Thickness.

  1. From the hoop balance: tft_f​=prσfsin⁡2α=\dfrac{pr}{\sigma_f\sin^2\alpha}​=5(100)1500(2/3)=\dfrac{5(100)}{1500(2/3)}​=5001000=\dfrac{500}{1000}​=0.50=0.50 mm.
  2. Check from the axial balance: tft_f​=pr2σfcos⁡2α=\dfrac{pr}{2\sigma_f\cos^2\alpha}​=5002(1500)(1/3)=\dfrac{500}{2(1500)(1/3)}​=0.50=0.50 mm ✓ (both agree because α\alpha satisfies the condition).
  3. For comparison, an isotropic wall with the same allowable stress would need t=prσ=0.33t=\dfrac{pr}{\sigma}=0.33 mm for hoop (the filament wall needs more because the fibres are not aligned with the larger hoop stress).

α=54.74∘\alpha=54.74^{\circ} and total fibre thickness tf=0.50t_f=0.50 mm (split between the two ±α\pm\alpha layers)

Justification. At 54.7∘54.7^{\circ} the fibres work equally hard for hoop and axial loading: a smaller angle would leave the hoop direction under-reinforced, a larger one the axial direction. Practical filament-wound vessels use this near-55∘55^{\circ} angle for the cylindrical part.

Assignment problems (Unit 4 assignment, 20 questions)

The Unit 4 assignment has 20 Bloom's-level questions (Remember 3, Understand 4, Apply 5, Analyse 4, Evaluate 2, Create 2). Its question wording was read from the page images. The assignment's own answer key (page 5) gives final values for Q8 to Q20; each numerical answer below was recomputed and is compared with that key. Where an assignment question repeats a question-bank topic, the full answer is given again here (so each can be studied on its own) and the question-bank number is cited.

U4-A01Assignment Q1 | L1 Remember | Transformation of stresses

Define principal planes, principal stresses and maximum in-plane shearing stress.

Solution

Definitions. - Principal planes: the two mutually perpendicular planes through a point on which the shear stress is zero. - Principal stresses σ1,σ2\sigma_1,\sigma_2: the normal stresses on the principal planes; they are the maximum and minimum normal stresses at the point. - Maximum in-plane shearing stress: the largest shear stress on planes that contain the zz axis, τmax=σ1−σ22=R\tau_{max}=\dfrac{\sigma_1-\sigma_2}{2}=R; it acts on planes at 45∘45^{\circ} to the principal planes, together with the normal stress σavg=σx+σy2\sigma_{avg}=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}.

tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2τxyσx−σy=\dfrac{2\tau_{xy}}{\sigma_x-\sigma_y},   σ1,2=σx+σy2±R\;\sigma_{1,2}=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}\pm R, RR​=(σx−σy2)2+τxy2=\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^2+\tau_{xy}^2}

(See QB Q004 to Q006.)

U4-A02Assignment Q2 | L1 Remember | Pressure vessels

Define hoop stress and longitudinal stress in a thin cylinder. State the criterion used to classify a pressure vessel as thin or thick.

Solution

Definitions. - Hoop (circumferential) stress σh\sigma_h: the tensile stress acting around the circumference of the wall; σh=pD2t\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t}. - Longitudinal (axial) stress σL\sigma_L: the tensile stress along the axis of a closed cylinder; σL=pD4t=σh2\sigma_L=\dfrac{pD}{4t}=\dfrac{\sigma_h}{2}.

Criterion. A vessel is thin-walled if the wall thickness is small compared with the radius, t≤r10t\le\dfrac{r}{10} (equivalently D/t≥20D/t\ge20); the hoop stress is then taken as uniform and the radial stress as negligible. If t>r/10t>r/10 the vessel is thick-walled and Lamé's equations must be used (QB Q013, Q033).

U4-A03Assignment Q3 | L1 Remember | Energy methods

Define strain energy, strain energy density, resilience, proof resilience and modulus of resilience.

Solution

Definitions. - Strain energy UU: the energy stored in a deformed body, equal to the work done by the slowly applied loads, U=∫P dxU=\displaystyle\int P\,dx (area under the load-deformation diagram); for a linear member U=12PxU=\tfrac12Px. - Strain-energy density uu: strain energy per unit volume, u=∫σ dεu=\displaystyle\int\sigma\,d\varepsilon (area under the stress-strain diagram); in the elastic range u=σ22Eu=\dfrac{\sigma^2}{2E}. - Resilience: the total strain energy stored in a body within the elastic limit, which is recovered on unloading. - Proof resilience: the maximum strain energy that can be stored without permanent deformation, i.e. the resilience at the elastic limit (yield): Uproof=uY×VU_{proof}=u_Y\times V. - Modulus of resilience uY=σY22Eu_Y=\dfrac{\sigma_Y^2}{2E}: the proof resilience per unit volume.

(See QB Q010, Q036, Q037.)

U4-A04Assignment Q4 | L2 Understand | Transformation of stresses

Derive the expressions for the normal and shearing stresses on an oblique plane in a body under plane stress, and hence obtain the principal stresses and the maximum shearing stress.

Solution

Principle. Equilibrium of a wedge element with one face on the oblique plane (normal x′x' at θ\theta counter-clockwise from xx); tension positive, τxy=τyx\tau_{xy}=\tau_{yx}.

Derivation. Let the inclined face have area dAdA; the xx face has area dAcos⁡θdA\cos\theta and the yy face dAsin⁡θdA\sin\theta.

  1. Forces along x′x': σx′\sigma_{x'}​=σxcos⁡2θ+σysin⁡2θ+2τxysin⁡θcos⁡θ=\sigma_x\cos^2\theta+\sigma_y\sin^2\theta+2\tau_{xy}\sin\theta\cos\theta.
  2. Forces along y′y': τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−(σx−σy)sin⁡θcos⁡θ+τxy(cos⁡2θ−sin⁡2θ)=-(\sigma_x-\sigma_y)\sin\theta\cos\theta+\tau_{xy}(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta).
  3. With double angles:

σx′\sigma_{x'}​=σx+σy2+σx−σy2cos⁡2θ+τxysin⁡2θ=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}+\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\cos2\theta+\tau_{xy}\sin2\theta, τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−σx−σy2sin⁡2θ+τxycos⁡2θ=-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\sin2\theta+\tau_{xy}\cos2\theta

Principal stresses. Put dσx′dθ=0\dfrac{d\sigma_{x'}}{d\theta}=0: tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2τxyσx−σy=\dfrac{2\tau_{xy}}{\sigma_x-\sigma_y} (equivalent to τx′y′=0\tau_{x'y'}=0). Substituting back:

σ1,2\sigma_{1,2}​=σx+σy2±(σx−σy2)2+τxy2=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}\pm\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^2+\tau_{xy}^2}

Maximum shear. Put dτx′y′dθ=0\dfrac{d\tau_{x'y'}}{d\theta}=0: tan⁡2θs\tan2\theta_s​=−σx−σy2τxy=-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2\tau_{xy}}, i.e. θs=θp±45∘\theta_s=\theta_p\pm45^{\circ}, and

τmax\tau_{max}​=(σx−σy2)2+τxy2=\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^2+\tau_{xy}^2}​=σ1−σ22=\dfrac{\sigma_1-\sigma_2}{2}, on planes with σ′=σx+σy2\sigma'=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}

Full derivations: QB Q061 and Q062; the wedge figure is in Q061.

U4-A05Assignment Q5 | L2 Understand | Mohr's circle

Explain, step by step, the construction of Mohr's circle for plane stress and how principal stresses, maximum shear stress and their planes are read from it.

Solution

Principle. The transformation equations are the parametric equations of a circle in the (σ,τ)(\sigma,\tau) plane (parameter 2θ2\theta), so the stresses on every plane lie on one circle (QB Q026).

Sign convention for plotting. σ\sigma to the right (tension positive); shear that turns the element clockwise is plotted upward, so X=(σx,−τxy)X=(\sigma_x,-\tau_{xy}) and Y=(σy,+τxy)Y=(\sigma_y,+\tau_{xy}).

Steps. 1. Draw the σ\sigma and τ\tau axes with a suitable scale. 2. Plot X=(σx,−τxy)X=(\sigma_x,-\tau_{xy}) and Y=(σy,+τxy)Y=(\sigma_y,+\tau_{xy}). 3. Join XYXY; it cuts the σ\sigma axis at the centre C=σx+σy2C=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}. 4. Draw the circle with centre CC through XX and YY; radius RR​=(σx−σy2)2+τxy2=\sqrt{\left(\tfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^2+\tau_{xy}^2}. 5. Principal stresses: the points AA and BB where the circle cuts the σ\sigma axis: σ1=C+R\sigma_1=C+R, σ2=C−R\sigma_2=C-R. 6. Principal planes: the angle from CXCX to CACA is 2θp2\theta_p (measure it in the same sense as the element turns); the σ2\sigma_2 plane is 90∘90^{\circ} further on the element (180∘180^{\circ} on the circle). 7. Maximum shear: the top and bottom points DD, EE: τmax=R\tau_{max}=R, with normal stress CC; the planes are 2θs=2θp±90∘2\theta_s=2\theta_p\pm90^{\circ} on the circle, 45∘45^{\circ} on the element. 8. Any plane: turn XYXY through 2θ2\theta in the same sense as the element; the new end X′X' gives (σx′,−τx′y′)(\sigma_{x'},-\tau_{x'y'}) and Y′Y' gives σy′\sigma_{y'}.

Checks. The centre stays fixed, so σx′+σy′=σx+σy\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'}=\sigma_x+\sigma_y; RR never changes. (See QB Q027, Q028, Q048.)

U4-A06Assignment Q6 | L2 Understand | Pressure vessels, thin

Derive the hoop and longitudinal stresses in a thin cylindrical shell under internal pressure and show that the hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress.

Solution

Principle. Equilibrium of a free body cut through the shell; pressure force balanced by wall force.

Hoop stress (cut by a plane through the axis, length LL). Pressure force on the projected area =pDL=pDL; resisted by two wall strips: 2σhtL2\sigma_htL​=pDL=pDL​⇒σh\Rightarrow\sigma_h​=pD2t=\dfrac{pD}{2t}.

Longitudinal stress (cut across the shell). Pressure force on the end area =pπD24=p\dfrac{\pi D^2}{4}; resisted by the wall ring of area πDt\pi Dt: σLπDt\sigma_L\pi Dt​=pπD24=p\dfrac{\pi D^2}{4}​⇒σL\Rightarrow\sigma_L​=pD4t=\dfrac{pD}{4t}.

σh=pD2t=2σL\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t}=2\sigma_L

The same pressure acts over the area DLDL in the hoop cut but is resisted by a wall area 2tL2tL (ratio D/2tD/2t); in the axial cut the pressure acts over πD2/4\pi D^2/4 and is resisted by πDt\pi Dt (ratio D/4tD/4t). (QB Q030.)

U4-A07Assignment Q7 | L2 Understand | Pressure vessels, thick

State Lamé's equations and explain the variation of radial and hoop stresses across the wall of a thick cylinder under internal pressure.

Solution

Lamé's equations (tension positive, radius rr):

σr=A−Br2\sigma_r=A-\dfrac{B}{r^2}, σθ=A+Br2\quad\sigma_\theta=A+\dfrac{B}{r^2}, with A=piri2−poro2ro2−ri2A=\dfrac{p_ir_i^2-p_or_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}, BB​=(pi−po)ri2ro2ro2−ri2=\dfrac{(p_i-p_o)r_i^2r_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}

(Slide form: radial pressure pr=br2−ap_r=\dfrac br^2-a, σc=br2+a\sigma_c=\dfrac br^2+a.) Boundary conditions: σr=−pi\sigma_r=-p_i at rir_i and −po-p_o at ror_o.

Internal pressure only (po=0p_o=0). - σθ\sigma_\theta​=piri2ro2−ri2(1+ro2r2)=\dfrac{p_ir_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}\left(1+\dfrac{r_o^2}{r^2}\right): tensile, maximum at the inner surface, piro2+ri2ro2−ri2p_i\dfrac{r_o^2+r_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}, falling as 1/r21/r^2 to 2piri2ro2−ri2\dfrac{2p_ir_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2} at the outer surface. - σr\sigma_r​=−piri2ro2−ri2(ro2r2−1)=-\dfrac{p_ir_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}\left(\dfrac{r_o^2}{r^2}-1\right): compressive, equal to −pi-p_i at the bore and rising to zero at the free outer surface. - σr+σθ=2A\sigma_r+\sigma_\theta=2A is constant through the wall.

The inner surface is the critical one: highest hoop stress and highest shear σθ−σr2=piro2ro2−ri2\dfrac{\sigma_\theta-\sigma_r}{2}=\dfrac{p_ir_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}. (QB Q034, Q053, Q074.)

U4-A08Assignment Q8 | L3 Apply | Principal stresses

At a point in a body, σx=80\sigma_x=80 MPa, σy=−40\sigma_y=-40 MPa and τxy=30\tau_{xy}=30 MPa. Determine the principal stresses, the orientation of the principal planes and the maximum in-plane shearing stress.

Solution

Given. σx=80\sigma_x=80, σy=−40\sigma_y=-40, τxy=30\tau_{xy}=30 MPa.

To find. σ1,σ2\sigma_1,\sigma_2, θp\theta_p, τmax\tau_{max}.

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; tension positive; θ\theta counter-clockwise from xx.

Formula. σ1,2=σavg±R\sigma_{1,2}=\sigma_{avg}\pm R, tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2τxyσx−σy=\dfrac{2\tau_{xy}}{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}, τmax=R\tau_{max}=R.

Solution.

  1. σavg=80−402=20\sigma_{avg}=\dfrac{80-40}{2}=20 MPa; σx−σy2=60\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}=60 MPa.
  2. RR​=602+302=\sqrt{60^2+30^2}​=67.08=67.08 MPa.
  3. σ1\sigma_1​=20+67.08=20+67.08​=87.08=87.08 MPa; σ2\sigma_2​=20−67.08=20-67.08​=−47.08=-47.08 MPa.
  4. tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2(30)120=\dfrac{2(30)}{120}​=0.5=0.5​⇒2θp\Rightarrow2\theta_p​=26.57∘=26.57^{\circ}, θp=13.28∘\theta_p=13.28^{\circ} (the σ1\sigma_1 plane); the σ2\sigma_2 plane is at 103.28∘103.28^{\circ}.
  5. τmax=R=67.08\tau_{max}=R=67.08 MPa on planes at 13.28∘+45∘13.28^{\circ}+45^{\circ}​=58.28∘=58.28^{\circ} and −31.72∘-31.72^{\circ}, with σ′=20\sigma'=20 MPa.
  6. Check: 87.08−47.0887.08-47.08​=40=40​=σx+σy=\sigma_x+\sigma_y ✓.

σ1=87.08\sigma_1=87.08 MPa, σ2=−47.08\sigma_2=-47.08 MPa, θp=13.28∘\theta_p=13.28^{\circ}, τmax=67.08\tau_{max}=67.08 MPa

Agrees with the assignment key (87.08, −47.08-47.08, 13.28°, 67.08). Same data as QB Q101.

U4-A09Assignment Q9 | L3 Apply | Transformation of plane stress

An element is subjected to σx=60\sigma_x=60 MPa, σy=20\sigma_y=20 MPa and τxy=−20\tau_{xy}=-20 MPa. Determine the normal and shearing stresses on a plane rotated 30∘30^{\circ} counter-clockwise from the xx axis.

Solution

Given. σx=60\sigma_x=60, σy=20\sigma_y=20, τxy=−20\tau_{xy}=-20 MPa; θ=30∘\theta=30^{\circ} CCW.

To find. σx′\sigma_{x'} and τx′y′\tau_{x'y'} (and σy′\sigma_{y'} as a check).

Assumptions and sign convention. Plane stress; tension positive; θ\theta counter-clockwise positive.

Formula. σx′\sigma_{x'}​=σavg+σx−σy2cos⁡2θ+τxysin⁡2θ=\sigma_{avg}+\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\cos2\theta+\tau_{xy}\sin2\theta, τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−σx−σy2sin⁡2θ+τxycos⁡2θ=-\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\sin2\theta+\tau_{xy}\cos2\theta.

Solution. σavg=40\sigma_{avg}=40 MPa, σx−σy2=20\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}=20 MPa, 2θ=60∘2\theta=60^{\circ} (cos⁡=0.5\cos=0.5, sin⁡=0.8660\sin=0.8660).

  1. σx′\sigma_{x'}​=40+20(0.5)+(−20)(0.8660)=40+20(0.5)+(-20)(0.8660)​=40+10−17.32=40+10-17.32​=32.68=32.68 MPa.
  2. τx′y′\tau_{x'y'}​=−20(0.8660)+(−20)(0.5)=-20(0.8660)+(-20)(0.5)​=−17.32−10=-17.32-10​=−27.32=-27.32 MPa.
  3. σy′\sigma_{y'}​=40−10+17.32=40-10+17.32​=47.32=47.32 MPa; σx′+σy′\sigma_{x'}+\sigma_{y'}​=80=80​=σx+σy=\sigma_x+\sigma_y ✓.

σx′=32.68\sigma_{x'}=32.68 MPa,   τx′y′=−27.32\;\tau_{x'y'}=-27.32 MPa (σy′=47.32\sigma_{y'}=47.32 MPa)

Agrees with the assignment key (32.6832.68, −27.32-27.32).

U4-A10Assignment Q10 | L3 Apply | Pressure vessels, thin

A thin cylindrical shell 1.5 m in diameter, 4 m long and 12 mm thick is subjected to an internal pressure of 1.6 MPa. Find the hoop and longitudinal stresses and the changes in diameter, length and volume (E=200E=200 GPa, ν=0.3\nu=0.3).

Solution

Given. D=1500D=1500 mm, L=4000L=4000 mm, t=12t=12 mm, p=1.6p=1.6 MPa, E=200 000E=200\,000 MPa, ν=0.3\nu=0.3.

To find. σh\sigma_h, σL\sigma_L, ΔD\Delta D, ΔL\Delta L, ΔV\Delta V.

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin closed cylinder, internal diameter; tension positive; σr≈0\sigma_r\approx0.

Formula. σh=pD2t\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t}, σL=pD4t\sigma_L=\dfrac{pD}{4t}, εh=σh−νσLE\varepsilon_h=\dfrac{\sigma_h-\nu\sigma_L}{E}, εL=σL−νσhE\varepsilon_L=\dfrac{\sigma_L-\nu\sigma_h}{E}, ΔVV=2εh+εL\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}=2\varepsilon_h+\varepsilon_L.

Solution.

  1. σh\sigma_h​=1.6(1500)2(12)=\dfrac{1.6(1500)}{2(12)}​=100=100 MPa; σL=50\sigma_L=50 MPa.
  2. εh\varepsilon_h​=100−0.3(50)200 000=\dfrac{100-0.3(50)}{200\,000}​=4.25×10−4=4.25\times10^{-4}; ΔD\Delta D​=4.25×10−4(1500)=4.25\times10^{-4}(1500)​=0.6375=0.6375 mm.
  3. εL\varepsilon_L​=50−0.3(100)200 000=\dfrac{50-0.3(100)}{200\,000}​=1.0×10−4=1.0\times10^{-4}; ΔL\Delta L​=1.0×10−4(4000)=1.0\times10^{-4}(4000)​=0.40=0.40 mm.
  4. ΔVV\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}​=2(4.25×10−4)+1.0×10−4=2(4.25\times10^{-4})+1.0\times10^{-4}​=9.5×10−4=9.5\times10^{-4}.
  5. VV​=π4(1500)2(4000)=\dfrac{\pi}{4}(1500)^2(4000)​=7.069×109=7.069\times10^{9} mm3^3; ΔV\Delta V​=9.5×10−4(7.069×109)=9.5\times10^{-4}(7.069\times10^{9})​=6.715×106=6.715\times10^{6} mm3^3.

σh=100\sigma_h=100 MPa, σL=50\sigma_L=50 MPa; ΔD=0.6375\Delta D=0.6375 mm, ΔL=0.40\Delta L=0.40 mm, ΔV=6.715×106\Delta V=6.715\times10^{6} mm3^3

Agrees with the assignment key. (The key writes Δd\Delta d for ΔD\Delta D.)

U4-A11Assignment Q11 | L3 Apply | Pressure vessels, thin sphere

A thin spherical vessel of 1.2 m diameter is to withstand an internal pressure of 1.5 MPa. Find the minimum wall thickness if the allowable stress is 80 MPa.

Solution

Given. D=1200D=1200 mm, p=1.5p=1.5 MPa, σallow=80\sigma_{allow}=80 MPa.

To find. Minimum thickness tt.

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin sphere; internal diameter; same stress in all directions; joint efficiency 1 (none given).

Formula. σ\sigma​=pD4t=\dfrac{pD}{4t}​⇒t\Rightarrow t​=pD4σallow=\dfrac{pD}{4\sigma_{allow}}.

Solution.

  1. tt​=1.5(1200)4(80)=\dfrac{1.5(1200)}{4(80)}​=1800320=\dfrac{1800}{320}​=5.625=5.625 mm.
  2. Adopt the next whole size, 6 mm. Check: σ=18004(6)=75\sigma=\dfrac{1800}{4(6)}=75 MPa <80<80 ✓. Thin-wall: t/r=6/600=0.01t/r=6/600=0.01 ✓.

tmin=5.625t_{min}=5.625 mm; adopt t=6t=6 mm

Agrees with the assignment key (5.625 mm, adopt 6 mm).

U4-A12Assignment Q12 | L3 Apply | Strain energy, normal stresses

A steel bar 2 m long and 25 mm in diameter carries an axial tensile load of 60 kN. Find the strain energy stored (a) when the load is applied gradually and (b) the maximum stress and strain energy when the same load is applied suddenly (E=200E=200 GPa).

Solution

Given. L=2000L=2000 mm, d=25d=25 mm, P=60 000P=60\,000 N, E=200 000E=200\,000 MPa.

To find. (a) σ\sigma and UU for gradual loading; (b) σmax\sigma_{max} and UU for sudden loading.

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic; uniform bar; units N and mm; for sudden loading the load acts at its full value through the whole elongation, and all its work is stored as strain energy at the instant of maximum extension (no energy losses).

Formula. U=σ22EAL=P2L2AEU=\dfrac{\sigma^2}{2E}AL=\dfrac{P^2L}{2AE}. Sudden load: work =Pδmax=U=P\delta_{max}=U with δmax=σmaxLE\delta_{max}=\dfrac{\sigma_{max}L}{E}.

Solution.

  1. AA​=π(25)24=\dfrac{\pi(25)^2}{4}​=490.87=490.87 mm2^2.
  2. (a) σ=60 000490.87=122.23\sigma=\dfrac{60\,000}{490.87}=122.23 MPa.
  3. (a) UU​=P2L2AE=\dfrac{P^2L}{2AE}​=(60 000)2(2000)2(490.87)(200 000)=\dfrac{(60\,000)^2(2000)}{2(490.87)(200\,000)}​=36 670=36\,670 N mm =36.67=36.67 J.
  4. (b) Energy balance: PδmaxP\delta_{max}​=σmax22EAL=\dfrac{\sigma_{max}^2}{2E}AL with δmax=σmaxLE\delta_{max}=\dfrac{\sigma_{max}L}{E} and P=σstaticAP=\sigma_{static}A. So σstaticAσmaxLE\sigma_{static}A\dfrac{\sigma_{max}L}{E}​=σmax2AL2E=\dfrac{\sigma_{max}^2AL}{2E}​⇒σmax\Rightarrow\sigma_{max}​=2σstatic=2\sigma_{static}.
  5. (b) σmax\sigma_{max}​=2(122.23)=2(122.23)​=244.46=244.46 MPa.
  6. (b) UU​=σmax22EAL=\dfrac{\sigma_{max}^2}{2E}AL​=(244.46)2400 000(490.87)(2000)=\dfrac{(244.46)^2}{400\,000}(490.87)(2000)​=146 680=146\,680 N mm =146.68=146.68 J (=4×=4\times the gradual value).

(a) σ=122.23\sigma=122.23 MPa, U=36.67U=36.67 J. (b) σmax=244.46\sigma_{max}=244.46 MPa, U=146.68U=146.68 J

Agrees with the assignment key. The doubling of stress with sudden loading follows directly from the energy balance (the energy principle of notes C2).

U4-A13Assignment Q13 | L4 Analyse | Mohr's circle

For an element with σx=−60\sigma_x=-60 MPa, σy=40\sigma_y=40 MPa and τxy=−40\tau_{xy}=-40 MPa, draw Mohr's circle and determine the principal stresses, maximum in-plane shearing stress and the corresponding planes. Verify the results analytically.

Solution

Given. σx=−60\sigma_x=-60, σy=40\sigma_y=40, τxy=−40\tau_{xy}=-40 MPa.

To find. σ1,σ2\sigma_1,\sigma_2, τmax\tau_{max} and the planes; analytical check.

Assumptions and sign convention. Tension positive; Mohr's circle plots X=(σx,−τxy)X=(\sigma_x,-\tau_{xy}) and Y=(σy,+τxy)Y=(\sigma_y,+\tau_{xy}) with clockwise shear upward; θ\theta counter-clockwise from xx.

Construction and reading.

  1. X=(−60,+40)X=(-60,+40) and Y=(40,−40)Y=(40,-40).
  2. Centre C=−60+402=−10C=\dfrac{-60+40}{2}=-10 MPa.
  3. Radius RR​=502+402=\sqrt{50^2+40^2}​=64.03=64.03 MPa.
  4. σ1\sigma_1​=−10+64.03=-10+64.03​=54.03=54.03 MPa; σ2\sigma_2​=−10−64.03=-10-64.03​=−74.03=-74.03 MPa; τmax=R=64.03\tau_{max}=R=64.03 MPa (top and bottom points) with σ′=−10\sigma'=-10 MPa.
  5. Angles: CXCX lies 5050 to the left of CC and 4040 above it, so it is 141.34∘141.34^{\circ} counter-clockwise from the +σ+\sigma direction. Going from XX to BB (σ2\sigma_2, at 180∘180^{\circ}) is 38.66∘38.66^{\circ} counter-clockwise, so 2θp2=38.66∘2\theta_{p2}=38.66^{\circ}, θp2=19.33∘\theta_{p2}=19.33^{\circ} (plane of σ2\sigma_2). The σ1\sigma_1 plane is 90∘90^{\circ} further: θp1=109.33∘\theta_{p1}=109.33^{\circ}.
  6. Planes of maximum shear are 45∘45^{\circ} from these: θs\theta_s​=19.33∘+45∘=19.33^{\circ}+45^{\circ}​=64.33∘=64.33^{\circ} and −25.67∘-25.67^{\circ}.

Analytical verification.

  1. σ1,2\sigma_{1,2}​=−10±(−50)2+(−40)2=-10\pm\sqrt{(-50)^2+(-40)^2}​=−10±64.03=-10\pm64.03 ✓.
  2. tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2(−40)−60−40=\dfrac{2(-40)}{-60-40}​=0.8=0.8​⇒2θp\Rightarrow2\theta_p​=38.66∘=38.66^{\circ} (or 218.66∘218.66^{\circ}).
  3. At θ=19.33∘\theta=19.33^{\circ}: σx′\sigma_{x'}​=−10=-10​+(−50)cos⁡38.66∘+(-50)\cos38.66^{\circ}​+(−40)sin⁡38.66∘+(-40)\sin38.66^{\circ}​=−10−39.04−24.99=-10-39.04-24.99​=−74.03=-74.03 MPa. So this plane carries σ2\sigma_2, and σ1\sigma_1 acts at 109.33∘109.33^{\circ} ✓. The shear there is −(−50)sin⁡38.66∘+(−40)cos⁡38.66∘-(-50)\sin38.66^{\circ}+(-40)\cos38.66^{\circ}​=31.24−31.24=31.24-31.24​=0=0 ✓.
  4. σ1+σ2\sigma_1+\sigma_2​=−20=-20​=σx+σy=\sigma_x+\sigma_y ✓.

σ1=54.03\sigma_1=54.03 MPa (at 109.33∘109.33^{\circ}), σ2=−74.03\sigma_2=-74.03 MPa (at 19.33∘19.33^{\circ}), τmax=64.03\tau_{max}=64.03 MPa on planes at 64.33∘64.33^{\circ} and −25.67∘-25.67^{\circ}

Agrees with the assignment key (centre −10-10, radius 64.03, σ1=54.03\sigma_1=54.03, σ2=−74.03\sigma_2=-74.03; θp=19.33∘\theta_p=19.33^{\circ} for σ2\sigma_2 and 109.33∘109.33^{\circ} for σ1\sigma_1).

U4-A14Assignment Q14 | L4 Analyse | Pressure vessels, thick

A thick cylinder of 200 mm internal and 300 mm external diameter is subjected to an internal pressure of 30 MPa. Using Lamé's equations, find the hoop stress at the inner and outer surfaces and plot the variation of radial and hoop stresses across the wall.

Solution

Given. di=200d_i=200 mm so ri=100r_i=100 mm; do=300d_o=300 mm so ro=150r_o=150 mm; pi=30p_i=30 MPa, po=0p_o=0.

To find. σθ\sigma_\theta at rir_i and ror_o; plot of σr\sigma_r and σθ\sigma_\theta.

Assumptions and sign convention. Lamé's theory; tension positive; σr=−pi\sigma_r=-p_i at the bore.

Formula. A=piri2ro2−ri2A=\dfrac{p_ir_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}, B=piri2ro2ro2−ri2B=\dfrac{p_ir_i^2r_o^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}, σr=A−Br2\sigma_r=A-\dfrac B{r^2}, σθ=A+Br2\sigma_\theta=A+\dfrac B{r^2}.

Solution.

  1. ro2−ri2r_o^2-r_i^2​=22 500−10 000=22\,500-10\,000​=12 500=12\,500 mm2^2.
  2. A=30(10 000)12 500=24A=\dfrac{30(10\,000)}{12\,500}=24 MPa; BB​=30(10 000)(22 500)12 500=\dfrac{30(10\,000)(22\,500)}{12\,500}​=5.4×105=5.4\times10^{5} MPa mm2^2.
  3. Inner (r=100r=100): Br2=54\dfrac{B}{r^2}=54, σθ=24+54=78\sigma_\theta=24+54=78 MPa; σr=24−54=−30\sigma_r=24-54=-30 MPa (=−pi=-p_i ✓).
  4. Outer (r=150r=150): Br2=24\dfrac{B}{r^2}=24, σθ=48\sigma_\theta=48 MPa; σr=0\sigma_r=0 ✓.
  5. Intermediate points for the plot:
rr (mm) σθ\sigma_\theta (MPa) σr\sigma_r (MPa) sum (MPa)
10078.0−30.0-30.048.0
112.566.7−18.7-18.748.0
12558.6−10.6-10.648.0
137.552.6−4.6-4.648.0
15048.00.048.0

σθ(ri)=78\sigma_\theta(r_i)=78 MPa, σθ(ro)=48\sigma_\theta(r_o)=48 MPa; σr=−30\sigma_r=-30 MPa (inner), 00 (outer)

Agrees with the assignment key (78, 48, −30-30, 0). The hoop stress is largest at the bore and falls as 1/r21/r^2; the sum σr+σθ=2A=48\sigma_r+\sigma_\theta=2A=48 MPa is constant.

U4-A15Assignment Q15 | L4 Analyse | Principal stresses, combined loading

A 60 mm diameter shaft is subjected to a bending moment of 1.5 kN m and a torque of 2 kN m. Determine the principal stresses and the maximum shearing stress at the critical point on the surface.

Solution

Given. d=60d=60 mm, M=1.5M=1.5 kN m =1.5×106=1.5\times10^{6} N mm, T=2T=2 kN m =2×106=2\times10^{6} N mm.

To find. σ1,σ2\sigma_1,\sigma_2 and τmax\tau_{max} at the critical surface point.

Assumptions and sign convention. The critical point is on the surface at the extreme fibre of the bending stress (where σ=Mc/I\sigma=Mc/I is largest and τ=Tc/J\tau=Tc/J is also at its surface value); xx along the shaft: σx=σ\sigma_x=\sigma, σy=0\sigma_y=0, τxy=τ\tau_{xy}=\tau; tension positive (the sign of τ\tau does not change the principal values). Shear from transverse loading is zero at this fibre.

Formula. σ=McI\sigma=\dfrac{Mc}{I}, I=πd464I=\dfrac{\pi d^4}{64}, τ=TcJ\tau=\dfrac{Tc}{J}, J=πd432J=\dfrac{\pi d^4}{32}, σ1,2\sigma_{1,2}​=σ2±(σ2)2+τ2=\dfrac\sigma2\pm\sqrt{\left(\dfrac\sigma2\right)^2+\tau^2}.

Solution.

  1. c=30c=30 mm; II​=π(60)464=\dfrac{\pi(60)^4}{64}​=6.362×105=6.362\times10^{5} mm4^4; J=2I=1.272×106J=2I=1.272\times10^{6} mm4^4.
  2. σ\sigma​=1.5×106(30)6.362×105=\dfrac{1.5\times10^{6}(30)}{6.362\times10^{5}}​=70.74=70.74 MPa.
  3. τ\tau​=2×106(30)1.272×106=\dfrac{2\times10^{6}(30)}{1.272\times10^{6}}​=47.16=47.16 MPa.
  4. σ2=35.37\dfrac\sigma2=35.37 MPa; RR​=35.372+47.162=\sqrt{35.37^2+47.16^2}​=58.95=58.95 MPa.
  5. σ1\sigma_1​=35.37+58.95=35.37+58.95​=94.31=94.31 MPa; σ2\sigma_2​=35.37−58.95=35.37-58.95​=−23.58=-23.58 MPa.
  6. τmax=R=58.95\tau_{max}=R=58.95 MPa (in-plane; the opposite signs of σ1,σ2\sigma_1,\sigma_2 make it the absolute maximum too).
  7. tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=2(47.16)70.74=\dfrac{2(47.16)}{70.74}​=1.333=1.333​⇒θp\Rightarrow\theta_p​=26.57∘=26.57^{\circ} from the shaft axis (for σ1\sigma_1).
  8. Check: σ1+σ2=70.74=σ\sigma_1+\sigma_2=70.74=\sigma ✓.

σ1=94.31\sigma_1=94.31 MPa, σ2=−23.58\sigma_2=-23.58 MPa, τmax=58.95\tau_{max}=58.95 MPa

Agrees with the assignment key (σ=70.74\sigma=70.74, τ=47.16\tau=47.16, 94.31, −23.58-23.58, 58.95).

U4-A16Assignment Q16 | L4 Analyse | Strain energy, impact

A weight of 1 kN falls through 50 mm onto a collar attached to the lower end of a vertical steel bar 1.5 m long and 500 mm2^2 in area. Determine the maximum instantaneous stress and elongation, and compare them with the values for the same load applied gradually (E=200E=200 GPa).

Solution

Given. W=1000W=1000 N, h=50h=50 mm, L=1500L=1500 mm, A=500A=500 mm2^2, E=200 000E=200\,000 MPa.

To find. σmax\sigma_{max} and δmax\delta_{max} under impact; ratio to the gradual values.

Assumptions and sign convention. Linear elastic; no energy loss (the weight's whole loss of potential energy goes to strain energy of the bar at maximum elongation); the weight falls the height hh and then moves with the collar through the elongation δ\delta (so its fall is h+δh+\delta); the collar and bar mass are neglected; units N and mm.

Formula. Energy balance (the impact principle of notes C2, UmU_m = energy supplied): W(h+δmax)W(h+\delta_{max})​=σmax22EAL=\dfrac{\sigma_{max}^2}{2E}AL with δmax=σmaxLE\delta_{max}=\dfrac{\sigma_{max}L}{E}.

Solution.

  1. Substitute δmax\delta_{max}: W(h+σLE)=σ2AL2EW\left(h+\dfrac{\sigma L}{E}\right)=\dfrac{\sigma^2AL}{2E}, i.e. AL σ2−2WL σ−2EWhAL\,\sigma^2-2WL\,\sigma-2EWh​=0=0.
  2. Numbers: AL=750 000AL=750\,000 mm3^3; 2WL=3.0×1062WL=3.0\times10^{6}; 2EWh2EWh​=2(200 000)(1000)(50)=2(200\,000)(1000)(50)​=2.0×1010=2.0\times10^{10}.
  3. σ\sigma​=2WL+(2WL)2+4AL(2EWh)2AL=\dfrac{2WL+\sqrt{(2WL)^2+4AL(2EWh)}}{2AL}​=3.0×106+9.0×1012+6.0×10161.5×106=\dfrac{3.0\times10^{6}+\sqrt{9.0\times10^{12}+6.0\times10^{16}}}{1.5\times10^{6}}​=3.0×106+2.4497×1081.5×106=\dfrac{3.0\times10^{6}+2.4497\times10^{8}}{1.5\times10^{6}}​=165.31=165.31 MPa.
  4. δmax\delta_{max}​=165.31(1500)200 000=\dfrac{165.31(1500)}{200\,000}​=1.240=1.240 mm.
  5. Gradual load: σst=1000500=2\sigma_{st}=\dfrac{1000}{500}=2 MPa; δst\delta_{st}​=2(1500)200 000=\dfrac{2(1500)}{200\,000}​=0.015=0.015 mm.
  6. Ratios: σmaxσst\dfrac{\sigma_{max}}{\sigma_{st}}​=165.312=\dfrac{165.31}{2}​=82.7=82.7; δmaxδst=82.7\dfrac{\delta_{max}}{\delta_{st}}=82.7.
  7. Check with the closed form: σmax\sigma_{max}​=σst[1+1+2hEAWL]=\sigma_{st}\left[1+\sqrt{1+\dfrac{2hEA}{WL}}\right]​=2[1+1+2(50)(200 000)(500)1000(1500)]=2\left[1+\sqrt{1+\dfrac{2(50)(200\,000)(500)}{1000(1500)}}\right]​=2(1+6667.7)=2(1+\sqrt{6667.7})​=165.31=165.31 MPa ✓. Ignoring the extra fall δ\delta would give 163.3163.3 MPa (1.2% lower).

Impact: σmax=165.31\sigma_{max}=165.31 MPa, δmax=1.24\delta_{max}=1.24 mm. Gradual: σ=2\sigma=2 MPa, δ=0.015\delta=0.015 mm. Impact stress ≈82.7×\approx82.7\times the gradual value.

Agrees with the assignment key (165.31 MPa, 1.24 mm, 82.7 times). A falling weight is far more severe than a gradually applied load.

U4-A17Assignment Q17 | L5 Evaluate | Pressure vessels, joint efficiency

A boiler shell 1.8 m in diameter with 16 mm plates operates at 2 MPa. The longitudinal and circumferential joint efficiencies are 75% and 50%. If the allowable stress is 150 MPa, evaluate whether the shell is safe and identify which joint governs.

Solution

Given. D=1800D=1800 mm, t=16t=16 mm, p=2p=2 MPa, ηl=0.75\eta_l=0.75, ηc=0.50\eta_c=0.50, σallow=150\sigma_{allow}=150 MPa.

To find. The joint stresses, safety verdict and governing joint.

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin shell (internal diameter, t/rt/r​=16/900=16/900​=0.018=0.018); the hoop stress is resisted by the longitudinal joint and the longitudinal stress by the circumferential joint; the joint stress is the plate stress divided by the joint efficiency; tension positive.

Formula. σh=pD2tηl\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t\eta_l},   σL=pD4tηc\;\sigma_L=\dfrac{pD}{4t\eta_c}.

Solution.

  1. Longitudinal joint (carries the hoop stress): σh\sigma_h​=2(1800)2(16)(0.75)=\dfrac{2(1800)}{2(16)(0.75)}​=360024=\dfrac{3600}{24}​=150=150 MPa.
  2. Circumferential joint (carries the longitudinal stress): σL\sigma_L​=2(1800)4(16)(0.50)=\dfrac{2(1800)}{4(16)(0.50)}​=360032=\dfrac{3600}{32}​=112.5=112.5 MPa.
  3. Compare with σallow=150\sigma_{allow}=150 MPa: the longitudinal joint is exactly at the limit (FS=1.0FS=1.0); the circumferential joint is at 112.5/150=75%112.5/150=75\% (FS=1.33FS=1.33).

Evaluation. The shell is just safe, with no reserve, and the longitudinal joint governs (it carries the hoop stress, which is twice the axial stress, and the lower efficiency of the circumferential joint is offset by its lighter load). A small rise in pressure or a poor weld would make it unsafe; a thicker plate or a better longitudinal weld is advisable. The circumferential joint has spare capacity.

Longitudinal joint σ=150\sigma=150 MPa (=σallow=\sigma_{allow}, just safe, governs); circumferential joint σ=112.5\sigma=112.5 MPa (safe)

Agrees with the assignment key (150 MPa governs; 112.5 MPa safe).

U4-A18Assignment Q18 | L5 Evaluate | Pressure vessels, thin vs thick

A cylinder has an internal diameter of 200 mm and a wall thickness of 20 mm. Compare the maximum hoop stress given by the thin-cylinder formula with that given by Lamé's equation, evaluate the percentage error, and decide which theory should be used.

Solution

Given. di=200d_i=200 mm so ri=100r_i=100 mm; t=20t=20 mm so ro=120r_o=120 mm; internal pressure pp.

To find. Thin-wall and Lamé maximum hoop stresses (as multiples of pp), the error, and the theory to use.

Assumptions and sign convention. Internal pressure only; the maximum hoop stress is at the inner surface in Lamé's theory; the thin formula is evaluated with the inner diameter and also with the mean diameter; Lamé taken as exact.

Formula. Thin: σh=pD2t\sigma_h=\dfrac{pD}{2t}. Lamé: σθ,max\sigma_{\theta,max}​=pro2+ri2ro2−ri2=p\dfrac{r_o^2+r_i^2}{r_o^2-r_i^2}.

Solution.

  1. Thin (inner D=200D=200): σh=p(200)2(20)=5.0 p\sigma_h=\dfrac{p(200)}{2(20)}=5.0\,p.
  2. Thin (mean D=220D=220): σh=p(220)2(20)=5.5 p\sigma_h=\dfrac{p(220)}{2(20)}=5.5\,p.
  3. Lamé: σθ,max\sigma_{\theta,max}​=p14 400+10 00014 400−10 000=p\dfrac{14\,400+10\,000}{14\,400-10\,000}​=p24 4004400=p\dfrac{24\,400}{4400}​=5.545 p=5.545\,p.
  4. Error (inner DD): 5.545−5.05.545\dfrac{5.545-5.0}{5.545}​=9.8%=9.8\% low. Error (mean DD): 5.545−5.55.545\dfrac{5.545-5.5}{5.545}​=0.8%=0.8\% low.
  5. Thin-wall limit: t/rit/r_i​=20/100=20/100​=0.20=0.20​>0.1>0.1, so the vessel is thick by the course criterion.

Thin (inner dd): 5.0p5.0p; thin (mean dd): 5.5p5.5p; Lamé: 5.545p5.545p. The thin formula with the inner diameter under-estimates by 9.8%.

Decision. Use Lamé's equation: the ratio t/r=0.2t/r=0.2 exceeds the thin-wall limit, the thin formula (with the inner diameter) is 9.8% unsafe, and Lamé also gives the radial stress (−p-p) and the variation through the wall. The mean-diameter value happens to be close here, but that is a coincidence of this ratio and cannot be relied on. (Compare QB Q077.)

Agrees with the assignment key (5.0p, 5.5p, 5.545p, 9.8%, use Lamé).

U4-A19Assignment Q19 | L6 Create | Pressure vessels, design

Design the wall thickness of a cylindrical air receiver 1 m in diameter for a working pressure of 1.2 MPa, allowable stress 100 MPa, longitudinal joint efficiency 80% and corrosion allowance 2 mm. Also design the thickness of hemispherical end covers for the same allowable stress (efficiency 100%).

Solution

Design problem. Size the shell and the end covers.

Given. D=1000D=1000 mm, p=1.2p=1.2 MPa, σallow=100\sigma_{allow}=100 MPa, ηl=0.80\eta_l=0.80 (longitudinal joint), corrosion allowance c=2c=2 mm; end covers: hemispherical, η=1.0\eta=1.0.

Assumptions and sign convention. Thin walls; internal diameter; the hoop stress governs the shell and is resisted by the longitudinal joint; the circumferential-joint efficiency is not given, so only the hoop requirement is used (the longitudinal stress is half as large and a circumferential joint of the same efficiency would need only half the thickness, tL=3.75t_L=3.75 mm for η=0.8\eta=0.8, so it does not govern); corrosion allowance added to the pressure thickness.

Formula. Shell: tt​=pD2σallowηl+c=\dfrac{pD}{2\sigma_{allow}\eta_l}+c. Hemispherical end (a sphere): tt​=pD4σallowη+c=\dfrac{pD}{4\sigma_{allow}\eta}+c.

Solution.

  1. Shell, pressure thickness: 1.2(1000)2(100)(0.80)\dfrac{1.2(1000)}{2(100)(0.80)}​=1200160=\dfrac{1200}{160}​=7.5=7.5 mm.
  2. Add corrosion allowance: 7.5+2=9.57.5+2=9.5 mm; adopt t=10t=10 mm.
  3. End covers, pressure thickness: 1.2(1000)4(100)(1.0)\dfrac{1.2(1000)}{4(100)(1.0)}​=3.0=3.0 mm.
  4. Add corrosion allowance: 3.0+2=5.03.0+2=5.0 mm; adopt t=6t=6 mm (the assignment key adopts 6 mm for the covers).
  5. Check of the shell after corrosion (t=10−2=8t=10-2=8 mm): σh\sigma_h​=12002(8)(0.80)=\dfrac{1200}{2(8)(0.80)}​=93.8=93.8 MPa <100<100 ✓.
  6. Check of the covers after corrosion (t=6−2=4t=6-2=4 mm): σ=12004(4)=75\sigma=\dfrac{1200}{4(4)}=75 MPa <100<100 ✓.

Shell: t=7.5+2=9.5⇒10t=7.5+2=9.5\Rightarrow10 mm. Hemispherical ends: t=3+2=5⇒6t=3+2=5\Rightarrow6 mm

Justification. A sphere needs half the thickness for the same stress (Q031). Using 6 mm rather than the 5 mm minimum gives a convenient size and some margin at the shell-to-cover junction; matching the radial expansion of shell and cover would, strictly, be checked separately (QB Q072).

Agrees with the assignment key (9.5 mm, adopt 10 mm; ends 5 mm, adopt 6 mm).

U4-A20Assignment Q20 | L6 Create | Transformation of strains, experimental

Plan an experiment using a 0∘0^{\circ}-45∘45^{\circ}-90∘90^{\circ} strain-gauge rosette to determine the principal stresses on the surface of a pressurised component. Derive the data-reduction equations and work out the principal stresses for readings ε0=400μ\varepsilon_0=400\mu, ε45=250μ\varepsilon_{45}=250\mu, ε90=−100μ\varepsilon_{90}=-100\mu (E=200E=200 GPa, ν=0.3\nu=0.3).

Solution

Design problem. Find the surface stress state from three strain readings.

Method note (flag). The Unit 4 notes and slides contain no strain-transformation or rosette section (searched). The strain-transformation equation below is derived from the geometry of the deformation (the same form as the stress-transformation equations with γ/2\gamma/2 in place of τ\tau). The conversion from strains to stresses uses Hooke's law for plane stress, which is in the course (the biaxial form εh=(σh−νσL)/E\varepsilon_h=(\sigma_h-\nu\sigma_L)/E of the thin-vessel notes, inverted). Logged in progress.md.

Experimental plan. 1. Choose the point on the free surface (plane stress, σz=0\sigma_z=0). Clean and bond a 0∘0^{\circ}-45∘45^{\circ}-90∘90^{\circ} rosette with its 0∘0^{\circ} gauge along a reference axis xx. 2. Wire each gauge in a Wheatstone bridge with a temperature-compensating dummy; zero at no pressure. 3. Pressurise, record ε0,ε45,ε90\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_{45},\varepsilon_{90}, and repeat during unloading to check for drift. 4. Reduce the data as below; check against a calculated or analytical value where one exists.

Derivation of the data-reduction equations. The normal strain in a direction at angle θ\theta from xx in a plane strain state (εx,εy,γxy\varepsilon_x,\varepsilon_y,\gamma_{xy}) is

εθ\varepsilon_\theta​=εxcos⁡2θ+εysin⁡2θ+γxysin⁡θcos⁡θ=\varepsilon_x\cos^2\theta+\varepsilon_y\sin^2\theta+\gamma_{xy}\sin\theta\cos\theta.

  1. θ=0∘\theta=0^{\circ}: ε0=εx\varepsilon_0=\varepsilon_x.
  2. θ=90∘\theta=90^{\circ}: ε90=εy\varepsilon_{90}=\varepsilon_y.
  3. θ=45∘\theta=45^{\circ}: ε45\varepsilon_{45}​=εx+εy2+γxy2=\dfrac{\varepsilon_x+\varepsilon_y}{2}+\dfrac{\gamma_{xy}}{2}.

εx=ε0\varepsilon_x=\varepsilon_0,   εy=ε90\;\varepsilon_y=\varepsilon_{90}, γxy\gamma_{xy}​=2ε45−ε0−ε90=2\varepsilon_{45}-\varepsilon_0-\varepsilon_{90}

Principal strains (same form as the stress equations): ε1,2\varepsilon_{1,2}​=εx+εy2±(εx−εy2)2+(γxy2)2=\dfrac{\varepsilon_x+\varepsilon_y}{2}\pm\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\varepsilon_x-\varepsilon_y}{2}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\gamma_{xy}}{2}\right)^2}, tan⁡2θp=γxyεx−εy\tan2\theta_p=\dfrac{\gamma_{xy}}{\varepsilon_x-\varepsilon_y}. Plane-stress Hooke's law (principal axes): σ1\sigma_1​=E1−ν2(ε1+νε2)=\dfrac{E}{1-\nu^2}(\varepsilon_1+\nu\varepsilon_2), σ2\sigma_2​=E1−ν2(ε2+νε1)=\dfrac{E}{1-\nu^2}(\varepsilon_2+\nu\varepsilon_1).

Numerical solution.

  1. γxy\gamma_{xy}​=2(250)−400−(−100)=2(250)-400-(-100)​=200μ=200\mu.
  2. εx+εy2\dfrac{\varepsilon_x+\varepsilon_y}{2}​=400−1002=\dfrac{400-100}{2}​=150μ=150\mu; εx−εy2=250μ\dfrac{\varepsilon_x-\varepsilon_y}{2}=250\mu; γxy2=100μ\dfrac{\gamma_{xy}}{2}=100\mu.
  3. Radius =2502+1002=\sqrt{250^2+100^2}​=269.3μ=269.3\mu.
  4. ε1\varepsilon_1​=150+269.3=150+269.3​=419.3μ=419.3\mu; ε2\varepsilon_2​=150−269.3=150-269.3​=−119.3μ=-119.3\mu; tan⁡2θp\tan2\theta_p​=200500=\dfrac{200}{500}​=0.4=0.4​⇒θp\Rightarrow\theta_p​=10.9∘=10.9^{\circ} from the 0∘0^{\circ} gauge.
  5. E1−ν2\dfrac{E}{1-\nu^2}​=200 0000.91=\dfrac{200\,000}{0.91}​=219 780=219\,780 MPa.
  6. σ1\sigma_1​=219 780 [419.3=219\,780\,[419.3​−0.3(119.3)]×10−6-0.3(119.3)]\times10^{-6}​=219 780(383.5×10−6)=219\,780(383.5\times10^{-6})​=84.28=84.28 MPa.
  7. σ2\sigma_2​=219 780 [−119.3=219\,780\,[-119.3​+0.3(419.3)]×10−6+0.3(419.3)]\times10^{-6}​=219 780(6.52×10−6)=219\,780(6.52\times10^{-6})​=1.43=1.43 MPa.
  8. Cross-check via the gauge axes: σx\sigma_x​=219 780(400−30)×10−6=219\,780(400-30)\times10^{-6}​=81.32=81.32 MPa, σy\sigma_y​=219 780(−100+120)×10−6=219\,780(-100+120)\times10^{-6}​=4.40=4.40 MPa, τxy\tau_{xy}​=Gγxy=G\gamma_{xy}​=200 0002(1.3)(200×10−6)=\dfrac{200\,000}{2(1.3)}(200\times10^{-6})​=15.38=15.38 MPa; then σx+σy2±(σx−σy2)2+τxy2\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}\pm\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^2+\tau_{xy}^2}​=42.86±41.42=42.86\pm41.42​=84.28,=84.28,​1.431.43 MPa ✓.

γxy=200μ\gamma_{xy}=200\mu; ε1=419.3μ\varepsilon_1=419.3\mu, ε2=−119.3μ\varepsilon_2=-119.3\mu; σ1=84.28\sigma_1=84.28 MPa, σ2=1.43\sigma_2=1.43 MPa

Agrees with the assignment key (γxy=200μ\gamma_{xy}=200\mu, ε1=419.3μ\varepsilon_{1}=419.3\mu, ε2=−119.3μ\varepsilon_2=-119.3\mu, σ1=84.28\sigma_1=84.28, σ2=1.43\sigma_2=1.43 MPa). Note that σ2≈1.4\sigma_2\approx1.4 MPa is almost zero although ε2\varepsilon_2 is negative: the Poisson contraction caused by σ1\sigma_1 (−νε1≈−126μ-\nu\varepsilon_1\approx-126\mu in strain terms) accounts for almost all of ε2=−119μ\varepsilon_2=-119\mu.
